paragraphs.text: THE LETTERS OF MAGNUS FELIX ENNODIUS, IN NINE BOOKS.
BOOK ONE.
1. ENNODIUS TO JOHN.

While you go in search of the sea with words composed in a quiet harbour, and describe the uncertainties of the liquid element in calm speech; while, as a careful helmsman, you steer the skiff of discourse among the rocks of language and, having built an artful course, weigh it out like a balance-keeper: you showed my eyes that the sea of waters you were portraying was a sea of eloquence. Good God, into how many uses a rich tongue spreads itself! When it wishes, it rages like a beast, runs like a river, heaves like the deep, and whatever likeness it paints with the coloured images of words it presents with the warrant of truth. You hint that you fear writing, as though shy of countenance, while a profession that flees praise actually demands the pomp of declamation and grows greedy of glory, while it makes a show of sparing modesty and feigns a fear that is foreign to it. I give and feel thanks that you have consecrated the noble first fruits of your eloquence to the praises of one who is, as you judge, a friend. And although I do not recognize as mine the things you say, I nevertheless embrace the scruple of the speaker and praise the devotion of the heart, which you have dedicated to the light of a favour shining through a clear sky. That torch which you, a charming speaker, kindle in your opinion of me is held up for you: as for me, though I do not flee the night of my conscience, I know how to assess it. Credulity entrusted to another's kindness suffers grave lapses, although whoever wishes to deceive one who trusts outdoes every crime. Yet you have filled my joy in you with the gifts of your letter, showing freshness of thought with serenity of language and surpassing the glories of an ancient lineage with the brilliance of youthful discourse. It would have been enough for your parents' wishes that you should emulate the older ornaments of the family; that you could surpass them, just as no one believed, so no one hoped. Do you see how much a manner of life polished to the fingernail adds to the merits of one well born? What the splendour of blood supplied, the diligence of your teacher has surpassed. I believed the sum of my prayers would be exhausted if you proved yourself worthy of your birth, without weighing what the one who lives alongside you would pour into your distinction. Perhaps my understanding was cheated in the estimate of my judgment. I believed that no one would reach Olybrius, whom a swift pursuer [?] at close heels. You will overtake him—making him happy, surely, if you surpass him. I pray God that in you, in your youth, the shoots of good fruit, which show perfection in their beginnings, may grow strong. At home you have living examples to take of what I urge. May your father make you like him in tranquillity of character, and your father-in-law in eloquence. If the heavenly kingdom deigns to grant my prayer, I ask one thing: that you deign to remember me, and that you do not strive to equal in forgetfulness also the man whose perfection you study among the models of speaking. But I shall return to the custom of a letter, which your affection has drawn out at length. Farewell, my lord, and cherish one who loves you with frequent services of letters, lest your profession of love be thought, as is usual with some people, to have existed only in your earlier letter.
2. ENNODIUS TO FLORUS.

I know that I have taken on a hard task and lift a heavy burden on weak shoulders, I who have roused with the goads of words your Sublimity, which, as far as I was concerned, was at rest. So feeble youth provokes beasts threatening with their teeth, and while it challenges things greater than its strength, it thinks that what it hopes will happen is a spectacle, not a battle. So a mind ignorant of combat brings its eagerness to the contest before it knows the danger. I judge the rage of a lion, and the beast that Libya breeds, milder than you in tongue. What ignorance hurled me headlong? What heat of mind led me, a stranger to knowledge of you, astray, so that I did not know what one who is provoked owes to an attacker—you who are always first to begin the insults, who in the gymnasia of abuse never deserved to be placed second? You are certainly the most practised reviler of the clergy, who always showed them the bite of a fresh and sharp tooth, whom even a life drawn true to the fingernail could not escape, to whom all learning has yielded, and whom the whole body of the religious flees like a comet: this is the man I, shameless and weak of countenance, have roused. With the same confidence I might have provoked the winds to blow, the rivers to run, my Faustus to eloquence, as that with which I, sparing of speech, have spurred you on to garrulous talk with the iron-shod heels of words. Forgive me, I pray, and in those who love you despise the taciturnity you think a vice in others; refrain from replies, condemn the challenger with contempt. Let one brought forth from the very heart of the senate house contend with you; toward a Gaul, keep silent about lineage; if you are the stronger, let him be punished in retaliation by your silence. Take care, my lord, that by provoking a lesser man to talkativeness you do not begin to be thought lowly. For what labour is it to overcome one who lies prostrate in that respect, and to triumph over one who confesses himself unequal before the conflict? Yet be for me, with my lord Faustus, the clasp of my love, if you are eager to escape complaints, however petty and rustic.
3. ENNODIUS TO FAUSTUS.

The case of my desire has been won thanks to my complaints: impudence has earned what courtesy was denying. I have drawn out the devotion of your holy heart, which an artful silence was concealing; I have put an end to the taciturnity that had been prepared as fuel for my ardour; by sending out cheap pages I have received the victor's prize. So rich earth repays the farmer with interest for the clods he has worked, and from single seeds the soil brings forth a noble offspring; so the hidden recesses of the mountains answer the voice of one man, and while the small cry is overcome, the elements show their strength. Having obeyed the Gospel oracles by such conduct, I have won a morsel of the truth of the precept whose teaching declares that God often rises and gives to one who knocks, if not because of merit, then because of importunity. Henceforth let the ill-advised questioning of unbelievers cease: on the evidence of present events I stand as a fit witness to the soundness of that saying. By frequent prayer I have won what I wanted: what was denied to scrutiny was granted to persistence in entreaty. I owe you friendship, my complaints, and I shall love you the more since you bring my wishes to fulfilment. Though you took your origin from just grievance, I shall often start you up even when unharmed, now that you have proved effective. Embracing the soothing plea of your letter, I give and feel thanks that you did not wish me to share your sorrows for long. You did this perhaps from the wish and zeal of one looking out for me; but I put it down to my sins that, while you softened your words, I was tossed about by greater anxieties. To me alone what was provided turns out the opposite, since in grief I always judge graver the things that are kept silent; for I believe that words are often exchanged about moderate illnesses, whereas the nearness of death imposes silences that must soon be broken. Thanks be to God, who in his mercy turns to good what are thought hard things, and by his compassion causes what we reckoned would come from our deserts to pass us by. Yet I would have wished that your Graciousness had kept such affection toward my littleness that you would have chosen to share adversities also with the one you often admitted as a companion in joys. Or do you think I will count it a kindness received if I am shut out from the turmoil of your heart as though untrustworthy? You have not, as I see, weighed the reasoning of my view. I consider that your favour is lost to me unless you nourish it by sharing everything with me. Cease, I pray, to look out for me in this respect, for I crave your words at any cost; if the letters I long for are denied me, I shall wither like earth on which nothing drips from heaven, and which does not pour into its veins the sap of soaking moisture, from which it might supply nourishment to the stalks born in it and bring heavy ears to the sickle. As a fish drawn from the water, stripped of its life-giving garment, dies, so I perish when the streams of your words are withdrawn. Let others seek what delights; I demand things that pertain to the soul: your words bring me not so much pleasure as well-being. I confess the matter coloured with no dyes, painted with no lying mists, for I am no artist of pretence: I felt that something was torn from my life while you were silent. You poorly claim to be faithful if only misfortunes that are lamented by everyone in general reach my ears through you—as though any Christian could be permitted not to know an evil under which Rome is collapsing. I conjecture that barbarian nations, separated from our frontier by almost the whole world, groan over these things in continual lamentation and lend their tears to our consolation. Your Magnitude avoids acting as informant on this matter, with the result that, to my ruin, the wishes of lying messengers tell their falsehoods with diabolical assurance, so that there is no one to whose truth I may return after the tales, nor anyone to sustain my mind by showing the truth. Beware of doing so, my lord: my dealings with you are a different matter; the law of the forum is one thing, the law of the dining room another. Let the household of your home hear you recount what you have learned in public life: feed the minds of your dependants and those hearts you think faithful with the food of your reports, lest the hungry hearts of your friends, unfed by such dishes, die.
4. ENNODIUS TO FAUSTUS.

Trusting the reader's word, and stirred by the flavour of persuasive speech, I almost believed a virtuous act to be a vice, and, while I believe that the diadems of words are worth more than conscience, I incurred a guilt my mind did not recognize. Not so does the beguiling hunter trick deer with artful whistling snares, nor does a master's hand so arrange nets that are sought of their own accord, with feather-lines of varied colours feigning terror, as the words of your Magnitude held me captive, offering my mouth freely to the halter. Unaware of any offence, while you pressed your attack, I long inquired whether I was innocent. I thought one thing of your letter, another of my own intention. Who, I ask, was such a charming perpetrator of a crime that he would believe it an excuse to confess that he served his own misdeed at another's command, when no one can justly believe in another's crime on the word of one who has confessed his own? But I believe the person was without knowledge of statute and law and made up entirely of cunning, one whom practice permits even to imitate the likeness of truth in another's handwriting, and whom shameful allurements win a semblance of authenticity. I do not wish to attack anyone's name, nor to take on the role of accuser against my conscience: it is enough that my modesty is set in harbour; let the uncertain winds toss others. Yet even if I had been driven by the spurs of beloved reading to order such things, I would defend myself by imitating the patriarchs. By theft Jacob overcame the seniority of his firstborn brother, and by that means obtained the primacy which nature had not given him. David, while he wandered the byways and narrow places of the earth in flight, drove off his hunger with the showbread and, against the prohibitions of the law, whose stings are lesser, put the body's hunger to flight. I had to endure, with long-wasting entrails, the starvation my unfed soul had conceived for the divine books, until the disease I had contracted ran through the hidden vital organs. The prophet Daniel took away divine teachings from the royal inner chambers—a chaste robber worthy of imitation, who added them to his own instruction. What use is it to go through them one by one, when a single one of the persons mentioned suffices to defend a conscience under attack? And yet that conscience, by first asking for what it needed, looked out for its own modesty and, so to speak, its natural weakness. For judge whether, after being refused, I am one who has made himself guilty. You claim that the African teacher wept over the pears he had stolen. Rightly must that be atoned for with lamentation which the belly acquires at the cost of decency. What he took was perhaps worthless, bound to perish through neglect or use or weather; yet the robber was not free of guilt, according to the apostle: he loved the flesh more than the soul. The prophet Tobias confronts offenders of this kind and testifies with a divine voice, saying: “It is not lawful for us to eat anything stolen.” When he said “eat,” he did not say: “It is not lawful for us to read anything stolen.” Josiah, as the history relates, was instructed by a purloined scroll. Would I, a little man, not do this, I whom you goad with the spurs of words to love knowledge beyond the strength of my talent? But I return to that excellent man, perpetrator, as you write, of the aforesaid crime, who, breaking faith on both sides, granted neither you security nor me, if I did write, the completion of the deed. May it be granted me, with all respect to your Magnitude, to thrash the back of so great a man in your presence, according to God's commandments, as my mind is inclined.
5. ENNODIUS TO FAUSTUS.

Having prayed for God's abundant mercy, I commend to him the auspices of a happy year, and, exalted now by the gifts of his kindness, I approach a consular man as though an equal. Until now, ornaments from outside supplied our family with the pomp of the consular robe and buskin, and we rejoiced that we were connected to the man who gave his name to the year more by marriage than by blood. It was a favour, not a due, that in the stories of those who loved us we were counted among the holders of curule chairs. How often did the tongue that exalted us before others make us beholden to it, so that, the order of things reversed, the insignia of our nobility were owed to the service of others? But now let envy depart. A restorer of ancient fasces, a consul has dawned upon the young, and with a strong push he has opened the decayed doors of our dignities. The trembling thresholds of rotting hinges grow young again in revived vigour—thresholds which, I believe, with God's favour, have been opened never again to be shut by any bars. For my Avienus's consulship is not the only one but the first. As forerunner he has gone ahead of the ranks that will carry the eagles of his line, and has shown the road of virtue to the highest service. If there is any reverence for worldly dignities, if there is any honour in a man's living on after the tomb, if the shrewdness of the ancients provided any means by which the years allotted to men might be overcome, then rightly are the consular lists thought to have devised such a plan, for their long duration defies both old age and ending. Good God, what a thing it is that the name of one man can either establish or annul the labour spent in drafting laws! Hail, young man of outstanding virtues, who along the obliterated path of your mother's lineage have brought back the life-giving axes of office, with which to cut away the aged barriers on a most splendid road, lest they hold back your posterity. Let the praises of the ancients yield to this—praises whose nobility was produced by the writings of the learned, and which buy their merit from the narrator through the decked-out loftiness of words. For the slenderness of a theme must be enlarged by the narrator's wealth, so that an endowment not found in the material may be inserted by the processions of the pen. To say nothing of the Fabii, Torquati, Camilli and Decii having been surpassed: you yourself, my lord, who have surpassed them all, have, I think, gladly yielded to his beginnings. You, already of riper years, walked along the well-trodden track of the consular staffs of great-grandfathers and grandfathers, almost joined at the side of those who went before, so that you advanced in an unbroken union of good fortune. It falls to the virtues of my still-tender Avienus both to continue the fasces in your family and to restore them to ours. I give thanks for the effort that will profit our common advancement, through which, by God's favour, the brilliance of noble birth, hitherto shut off, has shone out again, and through which shining blood has recognized its day. How I would have wished to behold in person the sum of my prayers, had not the greatness of my sins denied to my eyes the heavenly gift it could not deny to my desires, and were it not wrong for a man to obtain all his wishes at one and the same time! Yet I believe this must be counted among the greatest rewards of our Redeemer, that my consul crossed the threshold of a happy childhood with the honour of an old man. In hope I anticipate what is in store for his labours, when such things are shown at the outset. Increases of advancement with unforeseen successes are to come to one whom we see beginning from the fasces. Less is that with which old renown flatters itself about prosperous outcomes in the praises of the ancients. What grey hair worn down by dust, what a life spent under the burden of office scarcely earned, what an aged man, never sure of obtaining it, longed for—this the gift from on high has heaped upon my oft-mentioned young man. Add to this that, trained at the start of life in the best disciplines, he seems to have deserved what he has obtained, and he does not deign to attribute wholly to good fortune what in his case can be credited even more to virtue. Having pursued the schools and the study of letters to adorn his nature, an emulator of his father's perfection, by his own diligence he has made himself such a son as another could scarcely have chosen. Whatever is most excellent in the Attic tongue, whatever in the Roman, he has learned; he has weighed the gold of Demosthenes and the iron of Cicero; as a Latin speaker he has mastered both styles of eloquence. He embraced the bars of grammatical instruction and those lawful constraints of speaking as though they were freedom. Pursuing the pomp of oratory, with the arms of manly diction he drew his peers to oratory. But I recognize where the onrush of an affection that refuses limits is carrying me: turned aside from my purpose, I, unequal in talent, am addressing a learned consul. I return to you, with whom I share a common joy, an equal longing, an equal supplication. Let us pray God, since our prayers refuse all measure, that he himself may make perpetual what he has granted and never set a limit to his gifts toward us, he who has felt no loss by giving. But you, rejoice in so excellent a blessing of yours, to whom it is granted, after your own consular robes, to have a consular son obedient to you. If, however, heavenly power is at work in my judgment and my whole mind does not lie bowed beneath human faults, the dignity obtained for your offspring is the reward of your faithful prayers. The intercessors one house possesses would be enough for a city. Happy mother, mistress of so many men of command, the brave matron raises you up before God by her prayers. Through so many the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, for by their merits what is asked is exacted from divine mercy. For we remember it is written that the Lord said to his disciples: “If two or three of you agree, whatever you ask you will obtain.” I believe that the Redeemer, foreseeing the rarity of the just, said that two would be enough to ask for salvation. One may weigh by conjecture whether anything could be denied to three asking for the good of their own. Encouraged, then, by these hopes and exalted by kinship with the just, I trust in heavenly kindness that I too shall attain the abundance of the grace I long for. If by Abraham's merits Lot is admitted to the throngs of the saints, if those who lacked merits of their own deserved to be raised to the heights by the virtues of their relatives, this year will bring forth dignities for your family. For if I am dear to you, I am easily brought to heavenly grace by obtaining what I desire. My lord, paying the reverence of my greeting, I ask pardon for the length of my letter, because it is difficult for one rejoicing in great things to be content to say little.
6. ENNODIUS TO FAUSTUS.

Good God, how nothing is hard for those whose concern is with great things, and how calmly divine minds describe what they have seen! With what gifts are those places adorned on which a rich tongue, skilled in speaking, has turned its gaze, if my religious calling may say so without prejudice to my profession! God, the maker of the world, by the astonishing generosity of his hidden counsel, granted certain blessings to certain provinces: some he bade pour out wine more abundantly, others wine of better quality; to others he gave the joy of a rich wheat harvest; many he endowed with the variety or usefulness of their fruits. Those to which the opposition of nature itself denied these merits, he made sublime through one who would describe them. The soil starved by rocks has no reason to despair, nor need fields that do not answer the farmer's toil lie in disgrace. Merits are bestowed on lands by the genius of tongues, and as well as a man has been able to speak, so highly does he raise the thing of which he spoke. You will grow, provinces, through the cultivation of speech: whatever in you has amazed the reader belongs to the mouth. Rich soil, land that boasts of fruitful vines, that feeds the farmer though he only scratches your back with shallow furrows, that lays open rich veins at the very first ploughing, that returns the seed it receives in a multiplied harvest, you have nothing in common with the greatest if lord Faustus, the embodiment of Roman eloquence, has not graciously come to you. See Como, once a dark place and all but consigned to silence, which until now boasted of no advantage and, as they say, of no beauty: how it rejoices in the privilege of genius! Como, which through steep valleys and the wide gaps between linked mountains knows how to display a wretched harmony of summer snows; where, amid the dangers of farmers hanging over the road, one must sow soil on the rocks before sowing seed; whose kind of calamity is to have adorned the borders of the banks of Larius with hoary groves, so that, smiling with alluring looks, it promises its owners a fertility it does not have, with a charming face, and nurtures an accursed beauty to the ruin of its possessor; where the owners first pay the taxes on their buildings through their villas, while they strive with sparing frugality to repair the extravagances of their forebears and to prop up roofs that devour their patrimony; where an abundance of natives is kept only so that a number exceeding even the assessor's wishes should not be lacking for public duty; which nourishes peoples of fish not for delicacy but for horror, through which we learn what praise the taste of fish caught elsewhere deserves; where the air is perpetually rainy, the sky threatening, and life is passed, as it were, without full light; where the waters of Larius are sweet to the eyes of passers-by and invite to swim those whom they will destroy. Who could bear that lovely flood deceiving under such treachery? What shall I say of the island made habitable only by report? Who would not marvel at this? There life, once preserved, is less loved; there it was a lot to have escaped accusation [?]; around it fish are served a meal of human corpses. For none who have died there have earned any tomb but the waters of Larius. You have praised the seas, the river and the Adda, whose distinct course amid mingled channels the swelling of the lake reveals, though its waters could never be recognized within it except by their muddy current. To display the riches of eloquence in things that lack all praise was worth more than all these things would have been worth had they received the blessings of nature. May the Lord of heaven, who granted you this power, guard his gifts for ever; for I have written these things not as one who disagrees with you, but so that the reader may learn from them that Como is better read about through your pen than seen.
7. Ennodius to Faustus.

How heavy is the burden of ill will, how easy the road to harm, whenever the accused labors under a prior reputation! No one, as I see, considers what has been done or left undone: only the charge itself is summoned as a witness to lend credit to the attack. May almighty God turn the altered order of things for the better, and pour the brightness of a golden age over our condition, which has grown dim through the decay of time or the clouds of our deserts. When did the shelter of an innocent office not cover the most shameful crimes of men, and when did the serenity of heavenly service not excuse whatever came down from the cloud of bad morals? But now the clerical state is dragged into the snare of a credulous and ill-disposed interpreter, and what it would have been unseemly to commit before religious profession, we are believed to do without regard for honor after we have renounced our faults by taking an ecclesiastical title. Into what a storm, what a gale of monstrous sins, have you driven me, into an office of ill repute? In that very office in which all the branches of error are usually cut off by the sickle that teaches us how to live, you cause deceivers to believe every crime of me. That man has lamented that his slaves were taken away by me, and has thought that royal protection must be invoked against the power of a soldier of the Church. I ask you, what writer would put this even on the stage? What poet would furnish a fable with such pretenses or invented characters? The Lord knows, and may he rise with a strong hand as my champion to aid you, that I am wholly ignorant of this whole trick. Some time ago two boys, who claimed that violence was being done to them by the aforesaid, took refuge in the help of the Church by public petition. I remember making entreaties that the wishes of the deceased concerning them be kept; he promised, with deceitful and coaxing blandishments, that he would heed them. In the presence of the holy bishop your father, who was giving them help, and with the knowledge of the city, I urged them to return to the service to which they had been assigned. What happened afterward I did not know until I received the name of wrongful detainer. I am lying if these things are not confirmed by the testimony of my very assailant, to whom, however, I give thanks, because on whatever pretext he drew from you the letters I longed for, letters which nevertheless caused me much pain by the doubt in your command. For I see that [?] has been decided about me, if I find you in doubt whether I will heed what you command. Yet no blame before God will touch either me or your greatness on that account, since I soon compelled the aforesaid to go back into that good man's service without weighing the matter in any hearing. Offering my lord the most abundant greeting: if you will not refuse pages to such affairs, how I should like either to make up accusers myself or, what is more in keeping with my habits, to go wrong often!
8. Ennodius to Firminus.

Pleasant is the exchange of letters, when they are composed by a learned author, letters in which the splendor of perfectly polished speech flashes out, where rich discourse is held in by the reins of skill. When a laborious searcher has brought to light an abundant vein of language, then come forth the courtesies that will satisfy the desires of the one who receives them. But where rough speech betrays the narrowness of a poor talent, and, failing to set its thought in order, spreads night by its very effort at expression, and by the ambiguity of a cloudy narrative breeds some [?] about its own meaning, who, set on the heights [?] of eloquence, would not scorn the affection of such a person? The love of an unlearned man is a burden to the conscience of the accomplished. But the force of love, aided by the bonds of close kinship, cannot be held back: one whom love drives with its goads does not know how to test what he is able to do. Yet the accomplished are accustomed to judge worthy of pardon those whose faltering steps have failed them on the paths of letter-writing. You are accustomed to attend to what we meant whenever our words do not express our wishes. I have, however, added to the load of a suitable bearer, and she who could have presented me with living speech I have sent with a letter for company, trusting that there is less danger for me in having erred in the presence of a good intercessor. Farewell, then, my lord, and cherish one who loves you with your special kindnesses: so may divine favor raise your eminence still higher, if there is any height left to which it may grow.
9. Ennodius to Olybrius.

While you speak honeycombs and, in waxen cells, compose the honey of liquid substance with the nectar of eloquence, you have poured onto my lips the foreign flavor of a rich banquet, making mention of the contest of Hercules and the triumphant falls of Antaeus. This is how wrestling-grounds trained in the gymnasia of letters display themselves; this is how limbs moistened with the oil of study submit to the arts of speech. But I confess I would rather not have been stung by the mention of that fight, as they say. The old fable says that Antaeus, who was not conquered when thrown, lost his mother's comfort once he began not to fall: through the contrivance of a cunning enemy he is said to have been overcome while standing, and to have breathed out his life on his opponent's breast. A story worth remembering, no doubt, but unworthy of the purpose of friendship. I remember that we too undertook contests in our covenant, but contests in which we conquer by the services of mutual love, so that, while we strive in such wrestling, we both wish to be conquered and to conquer. We must live, rather than die, through the shared secrets of our hearts, united by the help of mother Church, who, to speak truly, nourishes us both as a nurse with the rich milk of faith. Let the fictions of old-womanish poets cease; let fabulous antiquity be rejected; let an innocent state never be mixed up with another's ruin. If we please to recall the examples of our forebears for a new use, it is more fitting to remember the grace and fidelity of Pylades and Orestes, Nisus and Euryalus, Pollux and Castor (provided the indecency of secret acts takes nothing away from them), whom an equal harmony of spirits so bound together that two of them welcomed a death sought together with their friend, and one brought his friend life at the price of his own death. These are worth remembering whenever, among new bonds of concord, a noble shoot is grafted and wedded to a strong stock along the moist bark, so to speak, of souls. Those minds promise the fruits of concord which know how much sweat the work of cultivation requires. I rejoice, however, that we are now joined in character by an indissoluble partnership, and from the threshold of affection weigh the growth of love in the balance of the scale.
10. Ennodius to John.

I would return the compliment, were it not that praise given back burdens the devotion of a friendly heart. I would not have us seem to scratch each other's backs with praises, lest affection be stained by the suspicion of flattery and love run into vice, while we unfittingly heap on each other what we ought to do in the presence of others. The merits of those we love should be kept within friendly letters, not spoken of, lest we merely burden our consciences with empty phrases by recounting praise. There are places where I may celebrate your good qualities, my friend, so that before you I keep silent out of affection: in what I think of your progress, I owe you only a reverent silence. I could, of course, following the vices of the age, now lay open your praises in endless proclamation and color the whole page with painted flatteries. But far be this from my purpose, let it be gone from my ways, that I should wish one whom I hold in my heart to be content with such a reward alone. I owe you not soothing speech but the voice of one who corrects. Not mocking you with painted artifices of words, but holding you wholly in the depths of my mind, I could say: you have reached the citadel of knowledge without any handicap from your tender age; you have attained the summit of perfection; no care need trouble you, but you should adorn yourself with your goods like a wealthy owner. But these things, as I said, are foreign to me. I say this to you face to face, with a parent's goad: though great are the things you promise in the white blossom of your eloquence, yet I do not rejoice except over the harvest, like the greedy farmer who measures the year's yield only in his granaries. Already we see in you ears that, if not yet heavy, are swelling with much milk; already our hopes have almost reached the threshing floor. But there is more to fear whenever a hope close at hand inflames our desires. Work hard, then, at your studies; love light in your conversations [?]; apply yourself devotedly to reading, so that the fruit of your eloquence may be cleansed by the winnowing of many authors. Beautiful are the things you write, but I love strong things more; they are wreathed with flowers, but I prefer fruit. Greetings, my lord; take these words to heart with the sincerity in which I have conveyed them, and weigh my love by the faithfulness of my admonition. Know that I am not to withhold your letters from any of the learned, so that what has escaped me through ignorance may be corrected by those who are thoroughly learned; and therefore prepare yourself with much sweat for the cultivation of writing, so that the hopes I have conceived for you, because of the merits of your venerable father and my love for him, may come to fulfillment through this effort of your distinguished self.
11. Ennodius to Castorius and Florus.

You ought to refresh one who loves you with the favor of conversation, and to show your friendly devotion by the testimony of your words, for silent love almost plays the part of ingratitude, and the force of love is cut off by abstaining from letters. The only remedy for the minds of the absent is the offering of letters, which by a kind of mental art paint in writing the one with whom they speak. We think it superfluous to assert this to you, whom noble training sharpens, who have at hand blood, learning and good company. There is nothing in the liberal arts of which you could be ignorant without the fault of negligence, since after the light of your birth Faustus, the glory of Rome, has trained you. So it must rather be confessed that I do not deserve what I ask than that you do not know what you ought to offer. My lords, paying the debt of greeting with the most abundant humility, I pray that at long last, not forgetting admonition and covenant, you will write back; in such works it is not fitting for you to be sluggish, since neither a holy conscience can be lacking to your way of life nor rich speech to your conversation.
12. Ennodius to Avienus.

Should you ask why my lavish brow of shame, though punished by your silence, does not hold its tongue, and why affection, by an ill interpretation, is called impudence; should you say that my chatter ought to have been checked when it bore no fruit: I appeal to you, most illustrious of men, by that sincerity which is native to your family; I embrace your sworn promise as a hostage of your mind. I grieve indeed at the causes you have contrived for so long a silence, while both love and kinship are neglected; but since your love claims me wholly for itself, I still believe that what you have done can admit of excuse, and I suppose there are grounds for your acquittal in this matter, though I cannot find them. I have always heard, to my prayers' fulfillment, that you are living in good health; you have often polished your labors for the distinction of your family in the brilliance of letter-writing. Silence shows nothing but contempt whenever it has no necessity. I, however, taking hope of a reply, have always written, and have dictated things to be read as though in some way in the presence of your excellence: it seemed to me, as I spoke, that my page reproduced you, that it tasted of you and lent my words colors painted from your likeness. Weigh carefully, I beg you, what sweetness there would be in a letter from you, if I were granted to receive it, when even words that come from us embrace you as they reach you [?]. Now, I beg you, rise to the desire of writing and pour your flowing speech upon my dryness, so that I may learn what my ministry can obtain from God, if I receive letters from you that rival your father's perfection. I do not want you to be afraid because I speak of one who is formidable to the most learned and bring him, as it were, before your eyes as a model of style. It is the custom of skilled physicians to detect the strength of bodies in the veins and to question their fingers about a man's recovery. Nor can the talents of beginners be known in any other way than when those who ought not [?], seeking vigorous declamations from tender years, give joy over a future abundance and reveal the harvest of skill in its root. My lord, having paid, as above, the honor and reverence of greeting, I hope that, if my merit does not show that you remember me, at least my importunity, which is tireless, may make it known.
13. Ennodius to Agapitus.

My mind is troubled, since your greatness, most observant of justice and steadfast in friendship, has turned to such neglect in forgetting me that, unmindful of courtesy, you let rumor rather than a happy letter announce the blessings of a better age that have come with the advancement of your honors. Where are those venerable inner sanctuaries of your holy conscience in your dealings with others? When could a mind anxious for the happiness of one it loves have found anything more worth reporting? But I wonder whether some malicious person has let a south wind loose on the flowers or a butting beast into the rose beds. For good fortune is never hidden from friends without some offense: it comes from ill feeling that one does not tell those living far away what one rejoices in. Far from your character be the foulness of malice. I think I have deserved not to know of your good fortune, since such silence will be made up for by frequent letters. No cultivation of love can soothe a friend who falls short of one's desires. However much, my lord, you paint these things with the noble images of words that your learning supplies, misdeeds are seldom cured by conversation, and pain that springs from a fact cannot be healed by talk; you will hardly erase by writing what you scorned to write. But I return to my purpose, from which, if God has mercy, I must never depart. I owe it to God that I was the first in Liguria to learn of your prosperity, though you contrived silence. You have lost the fruit of your studied silence: the good fortune of good men is celebrated by the tongue of the world; what has come to the highest cannot remain unknown. In honors, those are more to be embraced which are rendered as due: it is ill that a man is raised to the fasces whose mind, among the stars of the senate, does not recognize in his titles the votes of his own brilliance. Grey-haired dignity has come to you, [late] but due. It was summoned by your eloquence, which it follows; it was demanded by your innocence, which you once possessed in step with your years. But now I return to the grace of familiar address, even after offense. Greetings, my lord; and restore by abundance of speech what you neglected, to the detriment of our promised covenant.
14. Ennodius to Faustus.

I would rather not, I confess, disclose the causes of my delays, lest my mind, only lately brought back to peace and gladness, be disturbed again by a sad report, and I find in the telling a fresh beginning of my sorrow. For a man almost brings his troubles on himself if he does not shrink from going over them again once they are past. Who would revive his anxieties, once brought to an end, through the need for untimely speech? But with you I have a bond of faith and of truthfulness in facts, and to you sincerity is owed in replies, whatever the cause. I gladly suffer the stings of recalled grief, provided nothing is lost to the truth, and so as not to dishonor my page with falsehood through the weakness of a tender mind, I willingly bear what I relate. The health of the holy bishop your father, which was brought almost into doubt, held me back. In his illness, although the whole Church wept, a special grief afflicted me, who owe more to his love. I saw the peace of our city, under the pressure of discord, crossing its thresholds and slipping away from our eyes like some uncertain or wandering divinity. But let a brief account suffice for sad things. Now to good health: the health of the holy father, so longed for and so dear, is reviving. For as soon as my mind returned to its post, it at once turned to your commands. I have sent servants to inform me by faithful report of the prosperity of your eminence and of your whole holy household. I hang in suspense again and am torn between hope and fear in doubtful judgment, I who must be anxious for the well-being of my other parent. Who could stretch himself to the measure of my cares? Who could match the turmoil of one torn by such a division? But these things are more rightly referred to God, whose clemency it is to surpass the prayers of suppliants and to prepare a harbor for wavering desires. Meanwhile I return to my habit of complaining. I submit that your letters ought to have followed me at once, and that writing ought to have been continued for my comfort, or because of my recent request, so that my mind would not have hung in doubt about your journey, dependent on hearsay. But I believe this fault in writing can be amended by frequency. It remains for God to cause you to report what it is a joy to learn. My lord, offering your reverence an abundant greeting, I pray that the matters I have asked to be brought to your attention may be accomplished.
15. Ennodius to Florianus.

Not to keep within bounds in humility is the same as overstepping them in arrogance. To be more submissive than is right is an affectation of haughtiness: it is common for grand talkers to invent new flatteries, and for a lofty tragic buskin in eloquence to feign fear, or, though sure of praise, to dread examination. For my part, I would hold diligently to my resolve if I did not owe something to our kinship. I received your letter, rich with a Roman dowry and displaying a Latin style in the very brilliance of its opening. Affection compelled me to reply to it, though the unskillfulness of my hand objected, since the hope of keeping silent had long made the zeal for writing obsolete in me and counted silence in place of glory. But had I not replied, you would not know that you had been found out, in that you made sport of less polished talents with artful eloquence and the paint of Roman cleverness. A polished blade and one that rust has taken over do not have equal power to cut, nor can practice and sluggishness enter the contest on equal terms. Now, content with a short letter, I turn to the debts of greeting, to make up with good will what I could not with eloquence, returning friendship for the figures and pomp of speech. See, I have written in haste, as much as I could steal from my business. God will grant that, if you desire replies, you will find the heart you knock at free of cares.
16. Ennodius to Florianus.

Your Fraternity could have given my love one thing, which, as true generosity, would have served both the giver's economy and my modesty: namely, that since you already held a letter that showed my inclination, you should have spared yourself the trouble of writing. Does anyone paint a face with colourful enticements and shake a reputation with a vigorous assault, and then, not content with a plain excuse, think that what he has proved is not enough for a mistrustful conscience? Such a man whets the appetites of greedy friends with the varied flavour of his talk, so that by offering sweet things he may change what has been settled. For after I had written back that I love silence, I received, as if in answer to my plea, longer pages, and after my refusal I drew out a rich store of eloquence that had perhaps long been laid up. What would you have done if I had promised a contest, if I had carelessly attacked the ardour of your studies with some sort of tooth, and, being no fit judge of myself, had failed to keep my inner recesses safe? I believe the depth of Cicero's flood, the precision of Sallust and the elegance of Varro would have been brought to bear against me, and I would have found help nowhere. It did not even help me that I avoided contests in writing; I was provoked anyway, even while I kept silent. Even if awareness of skill and vigour of speech lifted me up, after seeing the varied perils of writers I would still dread the praise that you seek with so much sweat. Besides, you said that I have a rhetorician's cunning, when it has long since been true that devotion to prayer has cut me off from the orator's style. I cannot busy myself with flowers of speech, since the call of my office summons me to groans and prayers. So hold back the soothing and misleading persuasions of your talk. If what you write is invented and adorned with the brush of falsehood, change your purpose, at least now that you see your intention in doing it has become known. If it is true and comes from the scales of judgment, shut it up in the deep secret of your heart, so that you may show the reverence of affection by keeping things intact for a friend. Keep an unchanging heart toward me, and soothe others with your talk. See, in wanting to answer a long page I have gone beyond the measure of a letter. But a fault that has its author in another's errors should not be punished with a special penalty. My lord, returning the greeting I owe, I pray that if you persist in prying into the wishes I have formed out of love of silence, you will at least excuse the occupations that hinder me.
17. Ennodius to Faustus.

If a loving mind holds back from its habit of courtesies, it takes that very pause as an ill omen. For anyone who does not believe that what he loves is always living close by brings grief on himself. Would anyone think a person has gone far away when he reaches him with his mind? For if the spirit is the divine element in man, it cannot feel the losses imposed by great distances of land. I have stated the reason that makes me send letters. I pay the duty of greeting, which is why letters are sent, and I pray God that by the gift of heavenly kindness these words may reach Your Magnificence in good health. I commend to you in return the bearer, who gave me the opportunity to write, so that he may be well received.
18. Ennodius to Avienus.

How well and how happily you imitate what you modestly decline! While complaining that Your Magnificence is being urged on by difficult examples, you have yourself displayed, as an able champion, the very splendour of narration that you shun. I embrace the lovable plea of fear, which the vein of a rich talent in you makes attractive. I would not have you dread the father, revered by all good men, whom I set before you as an example in my exhortation: what you say comes from him. I know which land brings forth the nobler gold, in whose soil the metals nourished in its bosom gleam redder; often my labour has been rewarded, and my search has shown me the nourishing veins of that tawny element. I know which shells enclose gems proud in price, and where the stone comes from that is to lend splendour to empires. Do not put down what I did to inexperience or to error. The son of a brave man recognises the look of arms in his father's embrace, and in obeying nature he learns to love what is terrifying. Virgil, the root of the learned and the shaper of your eloquence, tells of a son so encouraged by his father's words that he says: "Learn courage, boy, from me," and elsewhere: "and his father Aeneas." Was that boy already rising to battle with strong arms, or thought able to wage the coming wars with a man's strength? No, but his courage, kindled better by fresh examples than by admonitions, was waiting for his body to grow. Those who know such things say that eagles, at the very threshold of life, when their chicks are stripped of the shell, hold them up to the rays of the sun, and recognise the light of their offspring by setting it against that immense splendour. Is there impiety in so strict a test, when the judgment in choosing is right? They do not want any of their brood to perish, but they do not acknowledge as their own those who give way. Rightly is that lofty bird considered the mother of victors among birds. Now then, my dear one, pursue what you have begun so well, and with God's favour, as you reproduce your grandfather in name, reproduce your father in learning. Do not think my advice burdensome. And since I judge you by your stock, do not you be afraid of beginnings. Even the man who is now feared was once a beginner; and whenever a finger scratches the ground to draw a channel of water through the dust, whatever comes first flows muddy. For the rest, farewell, my lord, and honour one who loves you with frequent gifts of letters; in those studies, if you remember me, it does not become you to be lazy.
19. Ennodius to Deuterius.

How gladly would I often omit the duty of visiting, if the fault brings so sweet a reward, and knowingly and deliberately neglect the sentence of a heavenly command, if blameworthy acts bring my desires such abundance! To me alone it has happened that what I deserved for an offence has turned out to be something to rejoice at: I have now learned to go after errors when they bring such recompense. What I am compelled to bring into the open, excellent teacher, is not contrary to the sacred bond of friendship. On the contrary, to make a confession worthy of my calling, I never, like an ungrateful man, wished your health to be in doubt; indeed, as far as lay in me, I set the hands of prayer against the ailments that assailed you. But see how lively your mind is, a mind not founded on the sound health of the limbs, as your page shows, in which you shone with both kinds of light. Are your eyes, I ask, dimmed by a cloud of pain, you whose poems are so bright? And do you, who speak light, complain about your sight? How I fear that I shall be found to praise your merits too sparingly. It is rightly said of you that you give eyes to all and make the darkness of minds shine with a light not their own. Do you then think that what you bestow is not strong in you? Drive from your mind, I beg you, anxieties perhaps born of needless worry or caution. God will grant that whatever bodily trouble has come upon you will be cleansed in turn by the brightness of your soul, which gleams as in a clear sky.
20. Ennodius to Faustus.

Thanks indeed to the Trinity, our God, whom we venerate and worship, who has bidden us devoutly to believe in and adore one substance under the distinction and wonderful equality of the persons; who has turned our mourning into joy and changed the tears that accompany sorrow into the service of gladness, so that I may truly say with the prophet: "Who will give water to my head, and to my eyes a fountain of tears?" so that I may answer the greatness of heavenly benefits with this devotion. For it befell me to receive heavenly gifts before asking for them, and to read of the good that had happened before I felt the evils my sins threatened. It is your doing, almighty Steward, that in the anxiety that came before I did not fear for the serene children and their inheritance of future innocence; I who received even the news of their restored health as if stunned, and, thrown into a kind of confusion, could hardly believe that the blessings granted beyond my merit had really come about. Truly the human mind cannot weigh the riches of heavenly reward. The weak are so tempered in spirit that they see the safe harbour before they grasp the uncertainties of the dangers. Good God, over what precipice did we hang then, when, so that the testimony of the little ones' restored health might be complete, the heavenly power [?] was shaken all the more through our deserving [?]! I speak sincerely and wrap the voice I owe to my calling in no cloud of falsehood (I mingle my words with sobs, and amid solid rejoicing my eyes overflow all the more with weeping): I often look back on what I have escaped. Where in the world were we? From what ruin has heavenly mercy restored us to human life? Let us then render to the giver of this good what we owe, in brief words but with long groans; let us invite him, whom we have found to bring help in our straits, to guard his own gifts. Let us ask him who surely knows how to preserve what he has granted and to prolong the living witnesses of his power. Such are the prayers for you that I share with the venerable community of the servants and friends of God settled throughout Liguria; your holy house rests on such support. Prayers are poured out without ceasing for the serene children. God is my witness that I speak the truth, the Godhead which, since it is itself truth, loves truth: to all who can trust in the innocence and integrity of their lives your sorrow was exceedingly bitter. But now I return to the custom of a letter. Greetings, my lord. Receive the bearer of this letter, the honourable Bassus, with the graciousness you usually show to those dear to me, since among all who are disposed to keep my friendship for your sake, he has risen to a kind of citadel of purity. Help his petitions, then, so that he may reap the fruit of his expenses and be prepared for greater things.
21. Ennodius to Faustus.

For a long time my mind hung in uncertainty about Your Eminence's arrival. But once divine mercy released me from that anxiety, I at once turned to my customary duties, although I had not neglected the service of letters even while you were far away. In this letter, then, I tell you of my health and reveal the sickness of mind I have contracted from grief. I am anxious about the health of our dear lights, placed as I am in a spot that the awaited messenger reaches only with difficulty. My consolation is this: I pray God not to let his servant be worn down by care any longer, but to bring swift healing to my turmoil by fully restoring their wellbeing. Greeting you with the service I owe, I beg that once you know these things, about which my mind is tossed between hope and fear, you will diligently come to my aid with the kindness of a letter that brings good cheer.
22. Ennodius to Opilio.

Your Greatness had begun, with a hope that surpassed my wishes, to raise my lowliness by your favour, and, after the manner of heaven's ordering, to make your benefits more glorious by weighing my merits on no scale of judgment, or, setting assessment aside, to give value to gifts which you showed to be undeserved. For affection shown to the humble is under no obligation, and it displays its beauty with a splendour shining as in a clear sky. For a long time, then, supported by such confidence, after God, I did not fear whatever the poison of slanderers threatened. But when your forgetfulness brought me back to my old dust, as tends to happen to those stripped of a protector, by way of consolation I sent out letters that carried, as it were, my complaints, promising myself a reply in return for their persistence. But perhaps Your Greatness is indicating, by the growth of your hindering occupations, that you do not attend to such duties. I will reply that your lofty position was the same before, when you used to send letters. Yet I bring myself back to the custom of letter-writing, lest excessive length breed tedium and the very plea that asked for letters cause them to be refused. My lord, I pay the duty of greeting and, as one bound to you in spirit, I ask about your health, wishing through your report to attain both my desires.
23. Ennodius to Senarius.

Affection loses its health when weakened by the torpor of silence, and the flow of devotion does not abound as it should if it is deprived of the sharing of conversation. Mute love almost looks like not loving, and not to reveal in words what you love is a semblance of hatred. I told Your Sublimity this face to face, when you promised letters to console me for my absence. But now what forgetfulness of me has invaded your mind, that over such long stretches of time I have received no letters to tell me of your good health? Was it, I wonder, so that I should not come upon letters that reveal the heart as proof of love? Turn, then, your irreverent conduct toward one who loves you for the better, and, remembering the faith you promised, send me writings. My lord, paying the dues of greeting, I pray that if this letter finds you still holding your old regard for me, it may earn a reply, since I think the twin bonds between us, of love and of blood, cannot be broken.
24. Ennodius to Asturius.

What on earth is the reason that you are so stingy with kindness and so lavish with complaint, and demand frequent letters that you yourself do not give, eyeing another's offences with a viper's eyes while cutting back your own faults with no pruning hook? It is several years since you, a senator and a learned man, chose to live near the Alps, where, as you gazed at the frosty ridges, the ill-omened snow appeared on your own head, and where, as you indicated in writing, you even eat acorns. The style of your letters confirmed this, when the mark of that food showed itself in the belching of a swollen breast and in Alpine speech. Yet I wonder that amid the ice-bound rivers of that place and its unrelenting cold, the flame of your liver burns all the hotter, and your breast takes no moderation from where you live. Your years are cooling into old age; there is a place that turns waters into metal and against nature rules the torrents by its own law; and yet amid all this you are said to live as though your fire were fed by the fuel of cold. I goad you with a parent's voice, because I owe you, and my calling, the voice of one who corrects. It is up to you after this, if you choose to receive my letters often, to welcome the admonition. For my part, besides greeting you with honour, I have found nothing more that I could write to those living in that filth of the flesh which you love.
25. Ennodius to Olybrius and Eugenes [?].

Out of longing for your letters my modest brow has grown bold, and since a letter sent out promises a reply, it can no longer keep its long-standing speechlessness shut up in the chamber of bashfulness. I ought indeed, out of regard for our kinship and my calling, to have kept the grace of silence, after our first exchanges denied the fruit of my hope. But I do not know whether one should call it perverse obstinacy when an intention, at no cost to anyone else, multiplies the risks of a trial that love makes anxious. Farewell, my lords, and return with me to harmony in writing, lest you act against the warnings of the Gospel by refusing to importunity what affection might perhaps justly have obtained.
26. Ennodius to Faustus.

A letter satisfies my wishes and desires when, coming from one who loves you, it serves the needs of others. How I would wish, if my calling did not forbid it, that the peace of many might often be shaken, so that by giving voice to those in difficulty I might pay the debt of steadfast love! I devote the service of this letter to the commands of my lord, your father, whose mind, while providing for the security of all, disregards its own quiet in this endeavour. He is confounded to see that the evils of the Ligurians have not yet died with the death of Mauricellus. For our province is suffering from renewed plots, as though the tomb did not hold that man. Certain persons are striving through wicked men to obtain the post of advocate of the treasury, and even before their wishes are granted they show what they intend to do in it. For my part, I did not conceal Your Magnificence's resolution concerning the public good, but declared that, with God's help, you would not entrust that office to any such person. But the anxiety of the provincials believes that everything it fears can come about. I took on this task of pleading from my lord the bishop, so that I might address your conscience through the service of a letter, lest anyone's underhanded scheme bring this matter to pass. Keep your most faithful promise with careful integrity of purpose. Paying the duties of greeting, I have set out what I undertook to plead. I hope, however, to be informed by letter of what has been decided on that matter.
Book Two.
1. Ennodius to Armenius: a consolation.

For a long time, dearest brother, though my wish was eager, I did not send you a letter of consolation. I did not want to be thought to be withholding my own tears while I arranged words, making ornaments of speech out of groans amid the losses of lamentation and dissipating due mourning in figures of speech. Yet, against the sacred bond of friendship and the ties of kinship, a hostile conscience lays bare its secret if, when you can weep for the dead in two ways, you do not, that is, if you do not join the office of the mouth to the service of the eyes. When the eyes weep, driven by the goads of grief, should the mourner's words keep holiday? But I, most sincere of men, who owe service to your sadness in every way I can, wished to bear witness in writing to the grief in which I am your companion, so that the memory of the tears shed should not be cut off within a single generation, and so that posterity should not reckon that at your son's death I owed only what I paid. On this path I have the examples of venerable bishops, by imitating whom those whose merits have kept them in obscurity are ennobled. Our Ambrose followed his departing brother with a little book that bears witness to his affliction. When later generations read it over, they both remember the writer with affection and join their laments for the death of his brother Satyrus. For through his foresight it came about that his grief is fresh as he speaks, that he shows before the eyes of his readers the limbs of a man long dead as though still breathing out his spirit, and that by the faithfulness of his account he never lets a funeral grow old which the passing years could have buried. This being so, restrain [?] your eyes, and turn your mind, if you please, to the words of one who comes to you as a weeping comforter. That you have lost an almost only son, of good disposition, whom a father's love longs for no less, the wailing of the province shows, since the whole community, joining its own groans to console yours, bears witness to what it thought of him. Yet amid all this you shut yourself up as though crushed by a private sorrow, not knowing that what is shared and spread through the hearts of many should be moderated. Why then should you think your own an anguish that very many have made theirs out of affection for you? With you, to say nothing of your kindred people, the Goth grieves; and do you still bow down as though you alone were subject to your own torments? Let the glories of our ancestors of old instruct you, I pray, and bring you back from your bent toward grief to sound health. Abraham, as a devout father, offered his only son to death, and, what is more, he did so gladly; the merciful father made ready the blade to slay his son. You, as one bereaved, seek one who has been transferred by heavenly judgment, and you burden with tears one who has been called away, whom it would have been sacrilege not to offer. In this matter let David's example come to mind: rejoicing and giving thanks to God, he went before his son's bier, because the favour of heaven had summoned from the seed of the venerable prophet one whom it perhaps meant to reward. If you do not imitate him by breaking out into joy, at least temper your sadness by imitating him in some measure. Perhaps you will reply that such things can hardly be urged on those sick at heart, that counsel has no place in heavy tribulation, that the bereaved pay no heed to anything that urges them to live, and that the desolate have one resource, to call for death. To this you may add that you have lost a worthy son, one who surpassed his tender age by the modesty of his ways, and you may claim that your young man closed with a glorious end those immature years that are friendly to sin, and that in the shipwreck of youth he was brought by God to the harbour of the soul [?]. Against these sources of your sorrow, though grieving myself, I would set the following: he sinned the less for being cut off before his time; he joined to the everlasting life of a better world what he preserved in this one; the penance you say he performed, even if it found nothing in him to wash away, found something to adorn, for whenever penance is given to the innocent it wins them a crown for their humble disposition. To this you may answer: "Where shall I turn, brother, when I have nothing in this present light but tears?" I will add that a man who takes no joy in nearness to men can find nearness to God, and that in place of a son a conscience can take its place which will find God's saints as its heirs. So, if you will deign to listen, I will show you more than one way to a better life, although your perfection needs no one to admonish it, and a man whom the improvements and honourable qualities of his conduct have made conspicuous needs no teacher. I ask only that you weigh carefully the good faith of this exhortation, which you owe to your own counsel and prudence, and recall yourself to love of the heavenly gifts, from which we both receive and love the breath of life, and by which the benefit becomes dear to us whose author we worship and revere. These are the great matters I have woven together in my grief in a few words, sending, in place of a rich style, a testimony broken by sobs, as I turn laments into conversation.
2. Ennodius to Speciosa.

Grief demanded my silence. While it brooded on revenge, it let the losses to our love grow. What else could I do but repay in kind, by keeping silent, one who refused me letters? You made your contempt for me known by withholding your venerable words, and so, by withdrawing my own conversation, I wanted to strike back with an equal blade. Perhaps you will say that revenge is hostile to our religious calling. But I count every fault as obedience to law when you happen to be its author. Would anyone think it a fault to do what you have done, or judge something worthy of divine punishment when he knows it came from you? So bear calmly the wrong I have done: in leading the way in this matter, light of the Church, you willed it yourself. I keep the resolve I promised, to be your imitator in all things, if I am worthy. The proof of this is that I am silent when you are silent and speak when you speak. Now that I have been bidden, I have returned to the duty of writing. Until now I kept within the modest inner chamber of my heart words that were not welcome, and I am ready to obey in my pages with the same compliance. Farewell, my lady, splendour of a good conscience without a cloud. May you be preserved for a long time as an example of holy living, and deign to remember me, if I deserve it. Pardon the brevity of this letter, which the haste of the carrier has squeezed into a narrow space.
III. ENNODIUS TO SPECIOSA

How heavily sinners are weighed down by the burden of their deeds! Whatever is offered to them is snatched from their eyes, and, so that their desires may not slip into oblivion, all that they long for comes near and yet may not be touched. I had undertaken a longed-for errand to the city of Ticinum and had come through all the hardships of a wearisome journey. I thought the bishop would believe that what really served my own affection was being spent on his commands. Then suddenly, near the goal of my wishes, the fruit I had sought with the greatest labour escaped from the very threshing floor. Alas, grief, you call me away from the language of a letter to tragedy! For your sake I had looked on the walls of that city, venerable to me second only to its holy places, and I was already preparing the words of a pleasant conversation. I am afraid to tell what followed, lest in telling it I be forced to endure it all over again. Chance unexpectedly thrust before my eyes the illustrious Erduic, whom you, glory of the Church, had made me long for. There my companions saw what I was seeking. There the turmoil of my heart became known, which until then I had kept hidden under cover of the person I have mentioned. Amid the torments of love I could not hide what I wanted, nor colour my conscience with any disguise. The man who cut short the reasons for a longer journey led me back home grieving. I confess that I did not welcome being spared that fatigue. See, I have set out the proof of my devotion and of my heart. If I have spoken the truth, it is for you to question yourselves and to judge my heart by the measure of your own affection. My lady, I greet you, and I ask that you be willing to hear from the bearer of this letter what he has to tell you.
IIII. ENNODIUS TO OLYBRIUS

No wise man doubts that the pledge of a sacred promise is kept, and that friendship, once wedded to fruitful kindling, rejoices in a noble harvest. I appeal to your conscience, which is now bound by faithful compacts. As the rightful owner of a good tree gathers its yield, so I gather fruit from our mutual love. Let neither party, by hunting for a pretext to withdraw, deny that what it wanted to happen has been fulfilled. Before God, vows earn either punishment or reward. Considering the religious calling on my side and the most noble station on yours, I judge that what was begun between us has come to fulfilment in concord. I could not refuse an exchange of words to a young friendship and to fruits just breaking into the light, since anyone who lives nearby and will not be the first to begin deserves blame. In this matter, then, I wish to avoid any loss of modesty, but I do not mind being thought rash, so long as I show that I have reached the fulfilment of a perfect friendship. I have loaded a most suitable bearer with the burden of my unskilled speech. My fault is one of affection, and whoever errs in this way deserves both pardon and favour. As I pay the debt of a most abundant greeting, I ask, if you hold me dear, that you show it by sending me a long and rich letter. You are an eloquent speaker and a generous champion of love, and you do not know how to deceive anyone with the flattering varnish of words.
V. ENNODIUS TO LACONIUS

Among those who love each other, an offence is never well punished by silence. A new kind of revenge strikes its inventor harder than the one who erred, and it is wrong to apply faults to correct faults, for then the healer falls sick from his zeal to cure. I wanted to imitate the silence that you, forgetful of me, have kept toward me until now, but I am a gentle man and could not match the disdain of strong spirits. I confess that the frailty of my nature overcame me. Loving more, I did something I believe you count among the vices: I answered your abstaining from the pen with a flood of talk and soothed the pain of a long silence with an abundance of words. I was indeed waiting for you to send the first letter, but I did not want to deny myself a reply by staying silent for a long time. I reckoned that I could not show you how to speak except by speaking. Therefore, my lord, as I pay the homage of the greeting I owe, receive with your usual graciousness the bearer of this letter, who has been sent specially to you. Take up again the practice of writing you have dropped, so that this sparing of words does not lead to the loss of our friendship.
VI. ENNODIUS TO POMERIUS

How long will so much abstinence be allowed? How long will a noble reputation grow old, deprived of the exchange of letters? I do not mind being thought rash, so long as I can come to know a perfect man. I want to be the first to send letters, so that the riches of Gaul may pass into Italy and lose nothing of their form in the crossing. Or did you perhaps think you could hide somewhere, when the light of your learning pointed you out to people far away? Perhaps the report I have heard, though from my own people, is poor through its own lack of skill and cramps me in praising you, and the thinness of the reporter narrows the full proclamation of your merits. Even so, you, the clasp of a perfection that comes from two sides, have taken the largest bites from both libraries, and you made sure that your mind would grow rich on such abundance. I pass over the full measure of heavenly favour granted to you, and the fact that you were furnished with gifts from above without human help. For whatever has no example among men is rightly judged to come from above. But I think these things are better kept for later, if I live. I come now to the point on which you instructed me, though you are so far away. As far as the account of the holy Felix, the bearer of this letter, went, you, a nursling of the Rhone, were looking in my carelessly dictated letters for Roman evenness and the true vein of the Latin stream. I believe that a careful and diligent examiner found something for the file to polish as he ran through such rough-hewn words. Do we not know in what spirit a man has read when he delivers his verdict so deliberately? Especially since it is written: "Homer himself, father of poets, prince of Helicon, received the darts of a judge's stern censure." I ask you: granted that Latinity shines among its natives and among those trained in the wrestling ground of its studies, is it not wonderful to say that it loves foreigners? I ought not to make trial of the pomp of eloquence, and I do not presume to test how well anyone can manage it, since for my profession it is enough to study simple doctrine. Yet if anyone had bitten me with such a tooth long ago, when I still delighted in the novelty of liberal studies, I would have prepared either a fitting excuse or something I would not be ashamed to have criticized. Now farewell, my lord, and show me your favour rather in church learning. Write or send word about what parents Melchizedek had, the explanation of the ark [?], the secret of circumcision, and what lies hidden in the prophetic mysteries. Let these figures of worldly rhetoric be rejected. They are bent on perishable persuasions and are like Penelope's web. [?]
VII. ENNODIUS TO FIRMINUS

Love may demand what perfection cannot achieve, and charity may win its point, so that the bold use of speech destroys the hope of a silence that could have adorned me. This is especially so since, as Tully says, speaking is an inept business unless it is necessary. Yet on the paths of narrative and the roads that the sickle of learning must open, affection reigns and does not know how to be held back by any thought of its own strength. Love, once fixed in the inner chambers of the heart, rules like an emperor. It believes that someone anxious for the welfare of an absent kinsman is not won by the weight or pomp of words. It does not imagine that offence can arise from kindness, and it reckons that there is joy enough if a letter brings news of the hoped-for good health. But you have been weighed in the scale of eloquence by the balance of skill. You possess a rich tongue, disciplined speech, a Latin flow and a well-built style. No wonder, then, that you look in others for what you practise yourself and seek what you love. We, cut off from the gymnasia of the schools, challenge the streams of the ocean with the drops of a parched wit, as if we were going to fight the rays of the sun with lamps. The leanness of my learning shows itself from far away. Unless family affection excuses my chatter, what I have loved will cost me my modesty. The vein of the tongue is indeed drawn from the fountain of one's family, and noble offspring are usually stirred by an inborn fire. I am unequal to my lineage. The fullness of learning has not touched me, as if I were a stranger to your endowments. I can only praise you, not imitate you. Mature eloquence has not yet come into flower in me, and, weighed down by a debt of gratitude, I lack the means to pay it. Nevertheless I entrust a slender skiff to a calm sea, since mute thanks differ little from ingratitude. Hence it comes about, I beg you, that the good news of you I learned from the bearer's report is counted among my blessings from heaven. I ought to have repaid you with the courtesy of letters, but the carelessness of carriers caused the letters you sent to be either held back or lost. Even so, I have led my modesty out from its safe anchorage into uncertain waters and commit the whole of myself to your taste to be read. Farewell, my lord, and cherish one who loves you with frequent gifts of letters. In such pursuits it is fitting for neither the diligent nor the eloquent to be slow.
VIII. ENNODIUS TO APOLLINARIS

Other people's needs fight on the side of our own desires when, at someone's request, we perform a service that brings us joy. Who would not pay a price for his own sake to obtain what is granted to another on such an occasion? The bearers of this letter now owe me what I myself owed. Far from dragging me to pay, they confess themselves my debtors. It is not through neglect that I rarely send letters: such good opportunities often slip away, as I have now found. So if you love me, let these bearers reap the fruit of this kindness. Just as they demanded from me what was to be offered, so they bring to you, I think, the exchange of letters we both desire. My lord, returning the homage of a greeting, I pray God that this may reach you in good health, and that a letter may come back at once asking after my health and announcing yours.
VIIII. ENNODIUS TO OLYBRIUS

Rarely have things I long desired turned out as I wished, as they have now. The wave of your rich eloquence has quenched the thirst I had conceived from longing for your letters, and its streams, smiling on my lips, have put out the heat that long waiting had doubled. But why should I claim to have reached the height of my wishes, when attainment gives birth to a greater desire and my heart burns from the very river of your words? It shows me clearly how ignorant of things the human mind is. Once it understands the value of what it strives for, it learns to love more what it reaches late, and while it has plenty in the present to rejoice in, there remains still more for it to seek. Now, I confess, as a judge of myself, I was alarmed at the needless caution in your letter.
