The sails of your speech were carried out into the deep by favouring winds, and everything that breathes served you obediently, and yet you say that your discourse lacks oars. A fear painted in words, apart from any concern for truth, is not permissible. Oars are needed whenever ships get no help from the push of the winds. A ship whose voyage the devoted conspiracy of the winds has made favourable has no need of them. The sun is not helped by torches, and the companies of lesser stars have never added light to the brightness of the moon's globe. My lord, offering you the honour of a greeting, as above, I pray that I may not lose the fruit of my zeal with your Greatness, now that I have not hidden from you what I desire. Repay with frequent or abundant letters the effort of writing that you have made so far.
X. ENNODIUS TO FAUSTUS

If the Ruler of heaven paid regard to my merit, I would receive either small blessings or great punishments, and, judging myself fairly, I would not reach in prayer for what I could not attain by merit. But thanks be to him who prunes our faults so that we are not puffed up, yet leads our hope on to wider things. I owe these preliminary words to the compositions of the lord Avienus. Though he was not yet restored to good health, he had loosed my mind from the chain of anxiety while my anxious prayers still hung between hope and fear. Looking to his own nature, he showed with what eloquence he thunders. I had indeed foreseen this by judgement, and in the treasures it had produced I recognized the vein that nourishes noble metal. Yet even in this, sinner that I am, I could hardly believe that what I did not deserve to obtain would come about. I speak the truth, with divine mercy as my witness: if there are any in Liguria who can judge the genius and splendour of letters, they believed that you had laboured over that composition, which a grey-haired wisdom, running ahead of his years, has already cultivated in a boy. But I have spoken of these things rather, with tearful joy, to those whom shed blood or a glorious confession has enrolled on the register of the heavenly senate, so that they may confirm our beginnings with happy success. Greeting you with the humility and obedience of a servant, I wish that, among all other things, while you relax your mind with these, you may rejoice over the troubles of your adversaries. For here there is nothing in which we can feel any harm from our enemies. This is what God has bestowed on us, and earthly envy cannot take it away.
XI. ENNODIUS TO FAUSTUS

What am I to do, when you write out in advance what I would write back, and, by the gift of foreknowledge that heaven graciously grants you, relate whatever another's heart could have worked out? Clearly it is beyond human power to play two parts in this way, but let all this be referred to him who granted it. I did not, however, promise to send back the speech that will thrust old Tully into the shade. I had returned the quire I received more quickly than suited my wits, because I was serving good faith and disregarded what might have been to my advantage. Nothing of that venerable composition remained with me, except what my thieving memory had stolen from the one who demanded it back, for the sake, I suppose, of a good reputation. I will not say what the part I unwillingly returned was like, or the part I loved, lest you believe that you had plainly foretold what would be alleged, at no cost to yourself [?]. Yet in this matter the kindness of my serene light, the lord Avienus, a beginner but already proven, came to the aid of my concerns. That purple of nobility pressed on me a certain sheet, which he was able to keep. I have had it until now, and from it I have both spoken and grown wise. But since I have been ordered to give up even the gifts of others, I will send it by the next bearer. For my sins, I do not find in myself such goodwill that I would trustingly refuse nothing that might strengthen the minds of outsiders, though I know that to deal with people so guardedly conflicts with my calling [?]. I speak the truth, with him to whom all things are known as my witness: not even torture would compel me to give anyone those compositions of yours that the whole world celebrates. I believe this comes from my ignorance. My lord, offering the greeting due to your reverence, I solemnly declare that neither negligence assails my judgement nor flattery my affection.
XII. ENNODIUS TO ASTURIUS

Your Sublimity pays homage to the prophetic oracles and confirms the ancient decrees by new excesses. You made sure that admonition would not be left too feeble, its force withdrawn and consigned to neglect. For the worshippers of God have written that the teaching of the wise passes by some people's ears, while others it draws with the savour of salted speech, and they declare that warnings given to people of another mind are wasted. I, however, am humble in rank and a beggar in speech. Before, I put words on paper only under the goad of necessity, and in my earlier letter, as proof of my devotion, I gave you a reply in the frankness of kinship. Now I am troubled in mind that, finding no fruit in your insults, you have perhaps put on a show of boastfulness under a pretended wit. You do not know that the darts an unskilled hand hurls at another fly back at their author. Who would consider something an insult when it wounds only the conscience of the one who sends it? It is the nature of the wicked to think of everyone what they themselves deserve, and, for comfort in their own wrongdoing, to see innocence nowhere. A stained way of life is tormented if it cannot believe that others share in it. I have written this in the spirit in which, mindful of my calling, I am bound to hate crimes. My tooth has bitten no one except someone who confesses about himself. When we attack vices, it is anger that reveals the guilty. I would be unjust if I felt a ploughshare in place of a pen, or counted as addressed to me what I do not recognize when I reread it. The Lord knows that if the letter had not been marked with my name, I would not have known to whom it was addressed. Keep your witticisms to yourself, or save them for those with whom the clamour of your deeds speaks without need of words, through the bond of secret intimacy. Now, paying the honour of a greeting, I beg you to pay heed to places, times and persons when you send letters, so that what I do not count as written to me does not perhaps wound someone else. For I judge that you have sent the text of this letter to a great many people, merely changing the names, and passed it on to each one without regard to what they deserve.
XIII. ENNODIUS TO OLYBRIUS

As a certain lofty authority on eloquence teaches, negligence is the law in letters, and carelessness proves to be the craftsman of their character. In such work, whatever sweat, the witness of torment, has found is lost to charm. Someone who reports on his own health and asks after another's does not demand words smelted in the smith's furnaces. It is better [?] to meet in these exchanges with a plain face of expression. The simple dress of conversation forswears diadems, and correspondence wins whenever it flees affected ornament. But the rich and carefully worked narration of your Greatness cannot be shut within beggarly limits, nor can it confine the treasure of its speech within any borders. Like great rivers, it scorns the reins of its banks. When your wealthy tongue oversteps the carefully arranged excuse of being busy, it shows that it serves only those studies to which it has been led even by chance. Our own quiet bears witness that the helm of the state has been entrusted to you, that whatever is arranged anywhere is the business of your labour, and that the care of Italy has entered a single breast. Did we not know this, we would almost think you were worn out only by your care and diligence in writing letters. These gifts are owed to God, who gave you a mind that loves knowledge and did not deny you the file of study to shape your speech. A swift arrow driven by the bowstring does not cleave the air as your speech sets out the discoveries of your mind. It flags at no barrier and is slowed by no obstacle. Whatever difficulty meets it becomes passable, and in a wonderful way the very nature of a case is changed by the pleader's skill. You make whatever case you favour seem to have had merit, and whatever you present as truth is truth. Hence even cautious judges may not resist. The most meticulous examiners count it a gain for their reputation to follow wherever your commanding oratory drags its captives. To this tongue and to these riches, to which I was the first to run, I confess that I owe a singular reverence. I wish there were a great many tasks entrusted to me to carry out for the sake of the bond of love. But as for what you enjoined concerning the religious women Speciosa and her sisters, I am distressed that I could not carry it out. I no longer have any close acquaintance or tie with them, especially since they live in different cities. Still, I at once forwarded to them the letter sent to me, and they have put off their reply until the time when they see one another. So as not to keep your Greatness in suspense, I have sent this letter. Whatever they instruct, if they are pleased to have it made known, will soon reach you. Now, offering the honour of a greeting, I ask your Sublimity to entrust to me instead any business that needs to be done with the Church. I think I did not hide the devotion of my heart toward you in the case of your kinswomen, or of the matron's friend.
XIIII. TO THE AFRICANS

The enemy might perhaps have counted it a gain if, amid the dangers he declared against Christians, he had subdued the souls of believers, and if the Lord's flock had been scattered in every direction so that not even a few were left by whose persevering faith he could be trampled underfoot. But he still reigns among your number who has taken pleasure not so much in numbers as in devotion. For it is written that power was given to Satan to sift the servants of Christ, so that whatever wheat could be found might be gathered into the granaries, and whatever chaff might pass over to feed the fires. To you in particular it was said: "Do not be afraid, little flock; it has pleased your Father to give you the kingdom." The sword of the faithless came among you to cut away the withered limbs of the church and to bring the sound ones to heavenly glory. The contest shows what soldiers Christ has; war reveals who deserve the triumph. Do not be afraid because they have taken from you the insignia of the pontifical dignity. With you is that Priest and Victim who is wont to rejoice not so much in honours as in hearts. The rewards of confession are greater than the gifts of a titled rank. Human favour often brings even persons of lesser merit to the latter; the former are bestowed only by grace from above. For he himself both fought and conquered in you, he whom faith deserves to have as its companion even amid the tortures inflicted by men. There is no need for lengthy discourse to kindle the heavenly fervour in you; the fire of divine power has its own means of increase. Nor is there need to extol with praises those already set upon the trophy, who conquered without anyone to urge them on. Whatever the flatteries of praise bring only burdens a Christian's conscience. What you have done is indeed an act of virtue, but it is to be surpassed by the repayment of the highest reward. Yet what you hoped for in the letter you addressed to our son the deacon, when you asked for the blessing of the blessed martyrs Nazarius and Romanus, we do not deny to the faithful. Receive the venerable protection of these unconquered soldiers, since the Emperor has already recognized your faith in battle; bring the gifts of confession to a happy completion. God will grant, when it pleases him, that quiet return to the churches, so that he may console with the sweetness of peace the grief that adversity has brought on.
XV. Ennodius to Euprepia.

By the dispensation of a heavenly mystery, a sister's affection has been restored to me and a mother's to Lupicinus at one and the same time, and the bond of a twofold kinship has been found worthy to receive back the wanderer after a long interval. Through the kindness of a letter you have come back to life among us, after the death of affection that you yourself had brought about: we have seen love rising as though from a kind of burial. The news of your well-being reached our ears unexpectedly, for we believed that, though still alive, you had filled the grave through your contempt of us. I believe that you have suffered hard things, but I declare that you have inflicted the hardest. What you endured you share with the good; what you did, with the cruel. Where in the world has a mother's care been hiding all this time? Where did what was owed to a brother wander off to? Your mind had gone farther away than your body. If adversity, the companion of exile, had driven you to the farthest borders of the earth, a sister's loyalty and a mother's concern ought to have followed you there. But in the setting of the sun, close to which you are said to have been, you kept a heart cold to dutiful love. Had you imitated the heavenly star, whose failing is happily reborn, in the diligence you owed, you would not have kept a mind on permanent holiday from kindness. You took on the mentality of the provincials to whom you went: you changed your region and renounced your resolve of devotion. For by forswearing communion with Italy you rejected not only your friends but even your closest kin. In the end a change of soul came upon you along with the change of land. How I fear that I am assailing your neglect with too long a reproach! What will one do when offended, who scorned us when unhurt? I have given just grief to the conduct of one who did not love; I have set out the charges that may yet make you innocent. But this reproach, if looked at in itself, is harsh; if its origin is examined, it is seasoned with all the honey of sweetness. He who freely accuses a kinswoman's silence takes neglect of love hard. If you cannot correct your errors by your presence, you can do so by frequent writing. Therefore, offering you the kindness of a greeting, I ask you to remember me, who have anticipated your prayers and wishes concerning our common son. For I considered what I ought to do before I learned what you wanted. Do you appease God by devotion and dispose him toward us by constant prayers, so that he who sees my intention for the boy's progress and the secrets of my heart may grant by his help what I promise by my labour.
XVI. Ennodius to Faustus.

It would indeed have been fitting, since the eminent Pamfronius was making the journey, to transfer the service of a letter to the offices of living speech, and not to burden with a packet of letters a man who has come to know not so much my words as my sentiments. But in these matters I yield to his command. This searcher of hidden minds asks for a page to assist him, and so, lest any part of my compliance toward him be found wanting, I have granted him a letter, which, though not necessary as a recommendation, suits his instructions. For with what words should one be escorted who may hope for everything from the favour of Your Greatness? It will turn out that the petitioner's words fall short of the bearer's merits. For what help can one give a man who deserves more than whatever one asks on his behalf? These lines, then, are added as an exercise for my pen, not for the benefit of the traveller. It pleases my mind to remember you on any occasion, even though by writing I confer nothing on the man I name. Yet see, since I have been so ordered, I add the words of recommendation that are given to strangers. Help in particular a man who seeks you out, strengthening his confidence by your graciousness: may he find whatever he anticipates in hope, so that, if he is a modest judge of his own merits, he may credit to me whatever he obtains. Paying the homage of greeting, I beg you to think fit to relieve me with frequent letters, since amid the burdens of grief I can have no support other than the solace of your words.
XVII. Ennodius to Constantius.

No one condemns skill for its showy eloquence, nor thinks that what accompanies modesty is to be despised: whoever preaches in elaborately worked speeches that the cultivation of language should be renounced is his own opponent. I, however, in the letters of Your Greatness have always weighed the care, not the words, and I have never judged eloquence, the helper of malice, to be of greater value than simplicity, which with unpainted face declares the secret of the mind. This I have always loved and cherished in holy men. I now give and feel thanks that you visit my littleness with the address of a letter, and that amid the business and vigils with which Ravenna keeps everyone occupied, your care for me is not laid aside. I therefore return the duties of a most abundant greeting, hoping that, in keeping with the graciousness with which you cherish one who trusts you, you will make my presence welcome to my lords, who love you.
XVIII. Ennodius to John.

I have good reasons to assail Your Unanimity with the bite of my pen, rusty and grimy though it is, reasons which, abundant as you are in natural gifts and rich in talent, you cannot clear away. Did I ever believe that news of your return could be carried to anyone else sooner than to me? Did I ever suppose that care for me, amid any business whatever, would leave that breast consecrated to friends? See, before my very eyes letters are delivered to others, and a friend's expectation is frustrated with utter disregard for my trust. I do not wish to fill this letter with a greater gall of reproach: for those who are grieved a brief account suffices. My mind still remains in the same state in which it admonished Your Greatness at your departure: it is up to you, if you scorn the evils of the times, to keep the friendship you promised. Farewell, my lord, and relieve one who loves you with the fellowship of speech, so that by writing you may erase the grief which you see has befallen a friend through your abstaining from writing.
XIX. Ennodius to Constantius.

I overflow with joy, and my gladness is firmly convinced that certain contests arise by the devil's inspiration precisely so that you, who have advanced beyond the reproof of all, may rejoice in the honour of a triumph. Liguria, I see, is not worn out: even at the very end of the ages she has not laid aside her nobility in bearing children. She still nourishes, even in her ashes, a fire hostile to vice, in whose embers the flame that avenges crimes does not die, nor is the fire that is the enemy of errors smothered. How I feared that she had ceased, as though exhausted, while I anxiously weighed the face of your letter, darkened by the deceptions of others, like a startled parent who, sending a dear child to war, does not allow himself to be sure even of proven courage. To increase his anxieties he counts his son's triumphs, not his times of rest; he fears more for a tested success to which affection supplies dread, because a mind schooled in victories knows nothing of caution, and in battle the love of praise is forgetfulness of safety. The taste of a trophy commands one to renounce the love of life: the savour of life holds only those who have learned none of the goods that come from conflict; whatever is taken from care for one's own safety is always added to glory. But for the present I must refrain from writing of this kind. The contests of our soldier are not so much to be praised as to be supported. Where javelins are needed, words contribute nothing. Although it would amount to publishing my own opinion while I proclaim yours, and to praise your reply would itself be to reply, still, having prayed for God's help, I add words that will be obedient to the faith, turning the cultivation of my pen to him who, whenever the barren earth must be written on with the curved ploughshare, promises that he will give his servants the seeds they are to sow, saying: "Do not think what you are to say, for it is your Father who speaks in you." May he himself, then, come to ratify the truth of his promise, and himself strengthen the faltering infancy of my speech, so that the composition of my wandering thoughts may not seem uncouth. But why do I talk around things that would take long to unfold? One thing I ask: that my reply be judged according to my small measure, and that what I do not know not be thought lacking either to the law or to its defence. So, as you testify in your letter, a man has been found who, just as Christ himself promised would happen, should on this occasion sift the servants of Christ, by asserting, concerning freedom of choice, that man has been granted licence to choose in one direction only, the worse? O schismatic proposition, which, as in the Apocalypse, has blasphemies written on its forehead! What sort of freedom is this—let him explain, if he can—where one is given only to will what brings punishment? Or why does he call it a choice, when he asserts that only one direction has been allowed? If this were true, divine judgements would have no place. For what good could our God rightly require of us, if he had withdrawn the desire for it from our will? But, in the words of the Apostle: "Is God unjust? By no means." If among men one who demands from his subjects what he has not put in their power departs from a right disposition, consider with what conscience such a thing could be thought of God. Where is that saying of the Apostle, crying out and bearing witness to freedom of choice: "To will is present with me, but how to accomplish it I do not find"? What else is this but to say: I know how to choose the right road, but unless grace from above helps me as I walk it, I shall grow weary? No one doubts, no one condemns this: that the path of righteousness is opened to men with grace as its author and protector. For grace is the leader and forerunner of good things, when from heaven we are invited to rest by manifold exhortation, when it is said to us: "Come, children, listen to me"; "Come, you blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you"; "Where I am, there shall my servant be also." But unless both our will, which is free, and our labour render obedience to such admonitions, we roll down into peril and Gehenna, not by any command but of our own accord. So either devotion earns a reward or contempt earns punishment. Otherwise the recompense will not be just, if it either inflicts punishment on those who sin by necessity or offers a good wage for work to which people are dragged against their will. Therefore we owe it to grace that we are called; we owe it to grace that, by hidden paths, unless we resist, the savour of life is poured into us; yet it is our own choice that we follow the benefits shown to us. For the way of wickedness is said to be not our mistress but our servant, since it is said of sin: "Its desire shall be under you." What, too, is the meaning of the whole utterance of the prophet, garlanded as it were: "Do not emulate evildoers"; "Do not put your trust in princes"; "Do not be like the horse and the mule"; and of the Apostle: "Do not become slaves of men"? What is the point of so many "Do not"s in heavenly admonition, if it was not permitted to will otherwise? Then again, though speaking in the person of Christ, the same prophet provides us with testimony for freedom of choice: "I have willed to do your will, my God"; and elsewhere: "Willingly will I sacrifice to you"; and: "I will pay my vows to the Lord"; and again: "Vow and pay." And that example of the blessed Apostle by which he believes himself protected actually sides with us, if he attends to what follows, when that enemy of arrogance said: "By the grace of God I am what I am." For at once, lest he be thought to flee glory so far as to stray a long way from the truth, the wise master builder added: "I laboured more abundantly than all of them, and the grace of God in me was not in want," which is to say: Christ found in me someone whom he could reward worthily and abundantly. For divine grace is not poor; but it is thought to be diminished by a certain leanness or thinness in our merits. It is reckoned not to be flowing in its own channels when the vein of our dryness receives nothing from its streams. O, if only the narrow limits of a letter allowed the secrets of the sacred books to be unlocked! But I fear that one who, by God's inspiration, will be able to find no grounds for slander in our faith may complain of the length of my page. What of that passage—in what spirit does he take it: "Behold water and fire; stretch out your hand to whichever you will"? What of the other passages which you yourself, as a copious defender, have set out? I suppose he passed them by with his ear shut, as they say, like the asp. I see how far the poisons of this Libyan pest extend. The serpent of the sands has more deadly things than those he reveals: what he confesses must be weighed as a measure of his hidden misdeeds. For he wants to arrive at this: that no one perishes through his own fault or negligence, if man is deprived of the choice between both things, good and evil, granted to him by his own power. He boasts that only those could be saved, without any labour and without any love for the commandments, whom heavenly favour alone has snatched away while they were strangers to merit; and accordingly—so that the blame would fall on God himself—he holds that those perished whom divine grace did not wish to set free. Farewell, my lord; "see to it that you remain master of yourself," and if this slave of death cannot be healed, give up the dispute, lest, while you strive, propped up by the strong root of faith, he should seize the occasion of this controversy to shake the offspring of the divine seed from the womb of some before the time of birth.
XX. Ennodius to Constantius.

You will forgive me for replying so quickly, for I still owe my age an unteachable haste. Maturity and gravity become you. So cherish one who trusts you, and withdraw my trifles from public severity, because if our page is an uncertain and doubtful thing, it shelters under the patronage of your command, on the principle that no one disdains what he himself has ordered. So, as I bid you farewell, I commend to you what is to be read: for it will come about that hereafter, if well received, we shall be spurred to obey by the goads of a soothing obedience.
XXI. Ennodius to Albinus.

Four times I have dispatched letters to Your Greatness, and still I am accused of being idle. My tongue has served my affection, yet my assiduity earns no credit for diligence. I believe that either the carelessness or the jealousy of the letter-carrier has brought me into this disfavour. Yet see, I multiply my letters, and, giving news of my own well-being as you wished, I long to rejoice in your good fortune. Farewell, my lord, and relieve one who loves you with all graciousness, for you do something close to God when, by your patronage, you relieve with full faith and fellowship one who trusts in you.
XXII. Ennodius to Faustus.

He who strives to help the sun with torches toils at superfluous expense in doing a kindness. Fullness of favour needs no addition, nor does one whom his merits have brought to an abundance of friendships require any increase of recommendation. My pen's care escorts the illustrious patrician Albinus, your kinsman, to whom by this letter I give not what is necessary but what is desired; and though I add nothing to his advantage, I yet earn his love, because I have carried out his commands. So, imparting to my venerable lord the homage of a greeting, I pray that this magnificent man may receive, in return for his attentiveness, what he showed to me because he honours you. For I know that this most distinguished man will quickly be brought into the inmost recesses of your heart, and that his blameless purpose will commend him to you by its own endowments.
XXIII. To his lord Faustus, Ennodius the deacon.

Those who happen to belong to you are bereaved without loss of guardianship: those whom you cherish do not lack a father's help. I speak of Lupicinus, son of our Euprepia: the general statement above applies to him. Concerning his property, the eminent Count Tancila, your admirer, told me that something has been obtained from our lord the king which it is grievous to report. For he asserts that all his mother's small possessions have been claimed by Torisa and others. I had nothing else I could offer to the misfortune of the orphan except to inform you and perform the office of a truthful reporter. It is for you, with God's inspiration, to provide what may help the poor boy; it fell to me to make known what had been disclosed to me. Presenting the homage of greeting to my true lord, I ask the divine mercy that heavenly aid may accompany your labour.
XXIV. To his lord Faustus, Ennodius the deacon.

I consider it a loss to diligence not to endow the hands of any traveller with the gift of a letter, for letters, when read, are wont to carry even faces to distant places and to present the likenesses of dear ones through the service of speech. To this is added the opportunity of a bearer, the most eminent Luminosus, who deserves well of us both, and who adds the fruit of his own favour to the reverence owed to your merits. Who would allow a twofold affection to be dulled by any negligence, if I were to refrain from the letters your graciousness demands, and if the man I have named were not given them to deliver? Thanks be to God—this ought to have been placed at the head of my letter—that your happiness is raised up and increased by the successes you desired, and that the swollen neck of the enemy, weighed down by Christ our God, has given way. I had anticipated in hope what the outcome has shown. For he rightly foresees the end of a heavenly decree who knows how to infer its nature from the serenity of human affairs. Farewell, then, for long, my lord, and relieve one who loves you by using your pen, so that the offering of letters may make up for whatever the distances between our lands take away.
XXV. Ennodius the deacon to Faustus the quaestor.

In keeping with the heavenly disposition, it is fitting that news of my return should be given by no one rather than by a friend hastening to Ravenna, whose faithful report would have sufficed even without a letter. But I could not abstain from my habit, for if I were to refrain from it through any neglect, I would seem to have condemned the frequent writing that I have loved. Add to this that I could not hold out refusing hands to the aforesaid man, who knows how to demand confidently from those who love him what he knows how to render faithfully to them out of conscientious devotion. Having left Ravenna, then, which holds whatever I have that is sweet in this present life, I reached Milan in sound bodily health, with Christ escorting me, though I am vexed that, with winter pressing on me, I perhaps wished for a speed in returning that went against my desires. But all things must be referred to God, whose it is to order human affairs and to change bodily attachment by the savour of eternal love. Now, having offered a humble greeting, I turn to the purpose of my writing and to the recommendation of the bearer. If he rejoices in benefits that answer to the serenity of your mind, he will recognize either that he has received back what he rendered to your people, or how he ought to be stirred to love. Compel him, even if he is unwilling, to return quickly, for his presence is necessary to my affection, and, if God fulfils his promise, when he so commands, he is awaited as one well suited to be of use.
XXVI. Ennodius to Liberius.

Diligence is either nourished or sustained by writing; epistolary conversation is the handmaid of affection; silent love presents the image of an ungrateful man; a friendship that does not break out into speech cheapens its own nature. The secret of the heart is well unlocked with the key of speech. By your leave, I already hold the advantage. According to the strength of my talent I have dedicated these first offerings of an exchange of letters, by which I presume to claim for myself the merit of loving more. For no one keeps his lips behind the bar of silence if speech, the betrayer of the mind, does not desert him while he remembers the compact that has been made. I therefore hold first place in the fellowship of letters and deserve greater regard, since I was the first to disclose by the testimony of my tongue what I longed for. See, I have set out without a cloud the duty of sending a letter. It is for you to cherish in me what you have received, lest, if I am neglected, the judgements of Your Eminence be subjected to scrutiny. For whoever does not protect what he has chosen exposes his own judgement to censure. My lord, paying the reverence of a greeting with full homage, I ask God to multiply the increase of his benefits toward you, for he alone is the full sum of my advantages who has raised Your Highness to the heights that are your due.
XXVII. Ennodius to Honoratus.

In your recent letter you told me that you are living nearby, and to the loss of my joys you added that your health is impaired. I do not deny it: I deserve to have bitter things always joined with the sweet. Until now misfortune kept you busy with your duties at Ravenna. Now that you have happened to be released, your bodily strength has been shaken, so that we were not allowed to win all we hoped for. How harsh is the condition of human affairs! Whenever it answers our desires with some taste of sweetness, it soon takes back what it granted, even at the door. Still, I dreaded the trap you set in your letter with an orator's all too Daedalian foresight: that you would believe I was unwilling to act for your benefit if I told you I could not manage it. O secret of an artful mind, which looks more to advantage than it trusts in love! God is my witness that I will not refuse you whatever I can do. You, for your part, ask God not to let my efforts be hindered by the misfortunes of the luckless letters you love. For there is nothing I fear more as an obstacle to the task laid on me than what I know well: that a man of letters gains nothing. Rather turn your talent to the rough business of the law, through which whatever a harsh tongue has demanded it has soon obtained, or, if it did not deserve it, has soon seized. My lord, as I pay you the courtesy of a greeting, I hope that you will help my labours with abundant prayers, since, though I lack the merit of a learned or educated man, I often suffer in lawsuits the fate of an accomplished one.
XXVIII. Ennodius to Avienus.

Thanks be to God, for that must come first, who made Your Magnificence ask for what I ought to have offered. You have rewarded the talkativeness that until now I barely kept within the modest inner chamber. Now that it has been drawn out, I make use of the gift of the pen, which I had sternly held back from importunate writing. Because my voice was compelled, I possess a merit through this unusual talkativeness. For when you ordered me to send you pages, you commended my silence to my own mind. Well done, my brow, so long lavish [?]: at last it has been my lot to reach an abundance of affection without any loss to you. Let us learn not to hate what helps us. The favour of silence has brought it about that we now speak to you freely: conversations from me that were often found tiresome are now awaited. I will not go further. As I see it, the tongue's office is vindicated by the rarity of its speech. In this respect the confidence of my joy is not lame, and my view is supported by the endorsement of truth. Look: he who scarcely sipped with the tip of his lips the letters of learned men, rich with the harvest of weighty discourse, does not disdain to receive the stubble of my tablet. Modesty, you have done me good with a double joy: you stand firm at your post, and addresses often scorned are now desired. See, the opinion of the man we love has become better. So by modesty we have provided for ourselves, and by his improvement for our consul. But my page should not run on and pass its appointed limits, nor should I show by saying much that my silence was not deliberate. Farewell, my lord, and honour those who love you with this fellowship, since the lofty summits of your honours admit only those increases that are born of humility.
BOOK THREE
I. Ennodius to Bishop Senator.

The first thing that undoubtedly befits a holy calling is to do of one's own accord, for justice's sake, whatever others usually do only when admonished. Next to that, or second in honour, is not to resent right suggestions. In this respect, even if the one admonished does not hold first place, he still has God's grace, because he does not resist the promptings of truth. I explain the reason for this preface so that I too may not seem to delay my own business with long-winded speech. Some time ago I humbly asked in person that, of the slaves your people were known to have enticed away from my household, the one who remained be returned to me. You answered my plea with a holy promise: even if the boy belonged to you by right, you would still put kindness ahead of profit. When I returned from Ravenna, though it is shameful to say, your priestly decision could not take effect, on account of my sins. I put it down to my own deserts that a lie violated what had been settled, though lying is condemned by your own mouth. See, I again commit myself to your conscience; see, I do what befits a son. Through the sublime and magnificent lord Victor I humbly submit whatever the authority of secular law could have secured for me. Judge whether I am at fault, I who chose a man suited to the character of bishops, who could soften even the untamed hearts of those who resist what is fair. I have already promised myself success in this business, since I know the worth of my envoy. Consider whether it befits religion, whether it is worthy of a bishop, that a man who can command even rocks should be scorned. Two things are on my side: the honesty of my case and the character of the one who pleads it. Whatever stands against this will soon incur the verdict of good men.
II. Ennodius to Eugenes.

The exchange of letters belongs more to joy than to grief, and speech lamed by recent distress does not bring well into the light the secret of the heart or the care of friendship. Even so, I shall consider whether less frequent speech harms love; at any rate, if no letter at all is sent, it betrays speechlessness. God gave the tongue its office as a witness of affection. But you may say, my lord, that this is out of place for a man whom I know to be taken up with the greatest sorrows. You may say that a heart weighed down with anguish is not lifted to words of love, and that laments feel nothing soothing. You may say that what weighs on the mind rejects what delights the ear, and that a brother who was the greater part of your soul, now among those above, has carried that part with him to the tomb. What should be asked of a man half of whose life the grave has shut away? In the depths of affliction a voice overcome by groans cannot complain, and in the time of tears any narrative is composed out of season. I will answer that an equal grief at this bitter loss has entered my own heart. Nor can I be separated from the sorrow of one whom happy times have sometimes joined to me through likeness of will. Yet I point out that in mourning speech has often been the sign of a heavier evil, and that the remedies of silence are cut off by betraying talk. I will say this: whoever denies pages to his lament wants what he mourns to perish within a single generation. The memory of a brother and a learned man does not deserve that what we thought of him should die with our weeping. When the mouth keeps holiday in mourning, the mind grows sparing. The remembrance of a loved one committed to writing breaks violently into the hearts of those dear to him with its stings, and an account of a death set down in letters never lets that death grow old. So, as a weeping comforter, I appeal to Your Magnificence with this aim: that through the kindness of exchanged letters the affection we promised, calling on God, may be nourished between us, and that a figure of eloquence, whose merits do not allow it to set, may come to life again in our conversation too.
III. Ennodius to his lord Faustus.

When a chance to write offers itself, one both domestic and friendly, why should I refrain from writing as though I lacked a carrier, especially since diligence in writing often wins me replies? The request of the honourable man Constantius, my brother and your devoted admirer, has joined this undertaking as its companion. He has become known to you, my lords, for his diligence, as befits an effective man, and he wishes to place that diligence under the obligation of my favours. For a man who wishes to owe what he deserves to letters of recommendation is crediting his own sweat to another's account. Still, I yielded to his entreaties. For the sake of his wish, and taking the opportunity to show my humility, I have sent this letter, asking God that with all speed you may lift me up with news of your health and prosperity. Out of regard for me, may Your Magnificence attend the man I have named with double favour, if I am not an unworthy petitioner.
IV. Ennodius to Abbot Stephen.

How sweet a business your letter is, which has brought me a spiritual gift! How welcome the need of its bearers, which in seeking a remedy for themselves has cured the longings of another! I confess that, were it not contrary to my calling, I would almost form hostile wishes to disturb the security of certain people. See, adversity grants what prosperity does not give. In quiet times, how should I, a sinner, receive letters from saints, letters that the brightness of my merits never earned? See how much help those who admit they obtained it from you have brought me. I consider that divine providence grants these things. I now believe that I have laid down much of the burden of my bad life. He who earns the conversation of saints is close to innocence. Why is it that while unclean worldly licence possessed me I never earned a letter from so great a man, and afterwards, over long intervals, never received any such blessing? Great God, what honour you grant to those who serve you, that you make those whom you have begun to regard acceptable even to your friends! Truly I have always looked up to you with singular reverence, and have always bowed my neck, weighed down with sins, before your venerable way of life. See, now I am addressed almost as an equal. My long-kept submission has raised me up. Cherish me, then, with your prayers, for your letter shows that the patronage you give is not feeble. For these men too, who brought me the blessings I rejoice in, have been taken under your protection. I return to the matter. That wretched cleric was afraid to plead the case before the bishop once he saw that I was defending those whom you commended to my service. If you so order, I suggest that one of them go to Ravenna with your letters of recommendation to your son, lord Faustus, so that no venal sentence from the judges, who abound in Milan, may be pronounced to their harm.
V. Ennodius to Maximus.

Lifted up by the words of your letter, I would let myself gape and swell with pride, if I were not conscious of what I am, and did not hold my lack of skill in check by modesty and keep the scales of judgment steady even when I am undeservedly praised. Your kindness has made you forget to be critical, while my calling compels me to live within the modest inner chamber. You exalt my writings as one who loves me, but I must fear those who look down on everything with sour neglect and condemn even what is choice. Yet I thank you for writing that lord Patricius judges me to be such as your testimony has made me out to be. This regard, then, is owed to your recommendation, not to my letter, which a rough pen set down without the gift of eloquence. In offering a greeting worthy of Your Magnificence, I thank God that he has brought you home, enriched with the success we prayed for. Because of the bond of love, my mind never feels you to be absent.
VI. Ennodius to Laurentius.

I must surrender to the command of love. Affection holds me bound, and I have given it words, so that I would not keep silent about the greeting I owe you. I could not let the chance of a household carrier be lost without sending a letter as a testimony of my devotion. So, greeting you with due reverence, I beg you to refresh me with a letter in return, for by sending this letter I promise myself an answer.
VII. Ennodius to the priest Adeodatus.

Who could forget your affection unless he were inhuman? Who would not wish to have, before God, the support of a person of complete devotion? I especially, who am weighed down by heavy burdens of sin and yet have won your favour, which promises me full absolution. So, greeting you with reverence and the respect I owe, I hope that you will make vows for me at all the holy places. Once I have obtained God's blessings, I will fulfil those vows without delay, for I know well that you deserve to be heard.
VIII. Ennodius to Avienus.

If giving offence makes Your Magnificence write twice as often, how I would wish the calm of your serene heart to be disturbed often! And were it not against my calling, I would supply you with reasons for indignation, since I have gained through faults what love does not earn. Yet I declare myself free of blame in that matter in which, while you accused me of negligence, you gave me a reward. I sent the boy while I was troubled, and through him I conveyed nothing beyond what was necessary. When the heart is free, the tongue has leisure for courtesies; a troubled mind renounces the grace of greeting. So I thank God on both counts: that I am not guilty, and that you believed me guilty. Your annoyance brought me a benefit that affection would scarcely have given. What I owe you I cannot explain: poor is the love that speech does not fail to describe. My lord, offering you the greeting I owe, I ask God that you may always write whatever you have in mind.
IX. Ennodius to Marcellianus.

I know that Your Magnificence abounds in great blessings from God and keeps faith with the constancy you promise to your friends. Your mind does not know how to make uncertain promises, and keeps its love without any lessening. So, next to God, I hand myself over to you with confidence, I commend myself into your hands, and I do not doubt that in all my affairs God's blessings will come to me through you. My lord, paying you the honour of a greeting as above, I ask you to refresh me with frequent letters. For God grants me the greatest of gifts if I am allowed to rejoice in the well-being of one whom faith and integrity make acceptable to all who fear God.
X. Ennodius to Luminosus.

The sacred bond of friendship, and the full-grown plant of affection between us, could suffer no harm from our living in different regions, if what is denied to the eyes were made up for by letters. Then, though divided by the sluggish weight of our bodies, we would be joined in mind through that part of us which we received from heaven. The tongue would set down the wishes of our hearts as a sign of pure affection, if the office of speech served the fullness of our desire and the inner chamber of the mind were opened and kept in letters. Then love would not grow old through any neglect; then the care of our mutual bond, polished by use, would shine, and the memory of me would not be harmed by rusty sluggishness. But what am I to do, when the clouds of my deserts cast a shadow over the serenity of a good friend, and my sins win me forgetfulness? Far be it from my purpose to imitate what I grieve to see done, and to take revenge for your silence by being silent myself. So I have given way to words under a double spur: I could not refuse an exchange of letters that both business and affection demanded. You know very well what your holy father, the lord bishop, asked of you, both through me and in person: that the expense he incurred at Ravenna for the needs of the lord pope should be made good by repayment. For the Lord knows that he paid out more than four hundred gold solidi to certain powerful men whose names it is not safe to put in writing, and he granted this on the strength of my pledge. I cannot face him freely until, as I trust, the promise is fulfilled through you. For this reason I have sent the bearer of this letter, a man of piety and good faith, so that you may relieve me of this obligation and injury I have described. Therefore, paying you the honour of a greeting with all humility, I beg you, appealing to him who looked kindly on the vows we made together for the holy pope, to arrange how I may be freed from this kind of trouble. But if you do not think it shameful, tell me, and I will repay from my own means whatever the holy bishop is known to have spent on my guarantee. For I have letters of the holy pope in which he ordered that whatever was necessary should be carried out on my guarantee. If I deserve to be put to this trouble, it will be for your foresight to consider it.
XI. Ennodius to Senarius.

If your mind had not shed the memory of your devotion to me, and if Your Sublimity did not force it to pass judgment after showing favour, you would send me frequent letters. But what am I to do, since love not earned does not rest on strong roots, and whatever the breeze of favour has snatched up is quickly brought back to be examined? I know that I alone ought to have been loved before being tested: the only fruit of affection I possessed was what I took by forethought while still unknown. But it would have been fitting for you not to withdraw quickly from one on whom you bestowed the name of friend, so that the failure to keep the affection promised me might not always be laid to my fault. For a conscience bound by friendship is usually a stranger to strict scrutiny, and a faithful heart must keep forever whatever it has once received. So, offering the greeting I owe, I hope that you will despise the sour disdain of the powerful and exalt your honour, and the power God has given you, with the fasces of humility. Let the tongue, interpreter of minds, confirm the pledge of this, and let love shown in letters bring faithful testimony to our minds.
XII. Ennodius to Abbot Stephen.

God's gifts are doubled for those who hope, and the heavenly gift overflows with twofold grace in its kindness. The flood of heavenly gifts runs out in broad channels; the streams of gifts that come from Christ exceed the capacity of the one who draws from them. It is the only spring that knows no shrinking and refuses to fail, supplying its currents with as much as the heart of the thirsty deserves to receive. Notice what hidden savour it pours in, when the water kindles a burning, and the moisture of the living river produces dryness on the lips while the soul is aflame. Such is the nature of your letters. They bring as much increase to desire as they bring satisfaction. Their depth is both drunk and longed for, and they enrich with so pure a stream that the inmost parts are suffused by them with a hidden fire. In them I see flames and drink akin to one another, and different natures joined in an unaccustomed harmony. My lord, by the gift of our God, long give the world the example of a most blessed life, and through the philosophy of holy religion show by your contempt for the present world that hope is not to be placed in this life alone.
XIII. Ennodius to Apollinaris.

Considering how much my care, which serves your affection because of our kinship, prompts me day by day, I would have let no traveller's opportunity go to waste [?], if I could hasten to that one solace of the absent which heavenly providence found in letters. But what am I to do, when there is such confusion among those coming and going that one does not know whom best to choose, to whom letters for delivery to Your Holy Conscience may be entrusted? For baser men turn whatever we offer to affection into an opportunity for their own gain, and it is grievous that what the force of love demands should serve greed. That is why I held back from writing until I had the opportunity of a household carrier. I did not want the duty of devotion, scattered among unworthy carriers, to go stale through others' importunity, and the blame to come back to me for something that did not begin with me. Having briefly explained why I was obliged to keep silent, I return to the practice of writing letters, in which the words I have awaited grant me the presence of Your Magnificence, by the secret paths of the mind. Farewell, then, my lord, and with the serenity you owe to your family cherish one who loves you with frequent letters. For nothing is so precious a gift to an anxious man as often to find you reporting your own health and asking after mine.
XIV. Ennodius to Euprepia.

A heart bound by duty would offer frequent letters to both kinship and love, if the thought of the lands that separate us, for which there is no remedy, did not take away from our longings their own remedies. For whatever is joined by love, whatever is linked by the chain of blood, can scarcely breathe when it is torn apart by the distances between regions. What help can there be for one to whom even the frequent chance of a written conversation is denied? By what witness can silent devotion between people who are apart be made known? For either the awaited chance of travellers is withheld, or such people are found that letters meant for loved ones cannot be entrusted to them. Still, for a long time I held my anxious wishes in suspense until I had a household carrier. Through him, offering you the honour of a greeting, I can make known to you the signs of my prosperity that you have longed for, and promise myself a reply by the sending of this letter. If your health is in safe harbour, let that be revealed to me in a welcome letter.
XV. Ennodius to Euprepia.

It is rare for love, upheld by kinship, to bow its neck to necessity. Affection is always the commander and rules by its own right, so it hardly ever becomes a servant. What obstacle has ever stood in the way of love's royal name? To what service is free charity ever enslaved? No one pleads fear of something as an excuse except someone who has cast off the bonds of attachment. A mind that serves family devotion is not afraid, even when rulers give harsh orders. No nation's laws are so barbarous that they forbid a mother to give her son what she owes him. Nowhere among the nations of the world does anyone depart from humanity in this. Everything born into the light of this world cares for the fruit of its womb and its seed. This is the one cause and concern we share with all the animals. How savage, then, must we judge a mind that is found to care less for its offspring than the beasts without reason? These opening words concern you, my sister. You have forgotten your only child, and you have deprived him both of the pity owed to an orphan and of the happiness of a child whose mother is still alive. I will say it plainly, with the freedom of my calling: now especially, when you refuse him even letters, though peace has by God's favour taken firm root between the rulers of our regions, you have outdone a tigress in cruelty. When could anything be found that you could love more than your son, or anything you should fear more for your son's sake? Concern for property should have come second, for an inheritance is never well gained when the heir is despised. I tell you this: if God had not blocked the malicious through the care of me, his servant, your whole family line would have been cut down. Lionesses entrust their cubs to the safe recesses of forests or the wilderness, so that their young will not become the prey of men. Perhaps you will say that this reproach shows how much I resent the burden laid on me concerning the young man. The Lord knows that the only thing I find bitter is that I am deprived of your presence, and that I can see from your silence that you have entirely forgotten your affection. Yet by God's kindness our boy is not denied a father's diligent care. He has crossed the threshold of nobility to be instructed in the liberal arts. I have also sent you the very speech in which he was commended; in it you should look not for eloquence but for my hopes for him. Farewell, then, my lady, and if it can be done, come back into our sight as God disposes.
XVI. Ennodius to Laconius.

For a long time now my mind has been tormented by the very expectation that used to bring it relief. You have drawn out your silence for a long while, though no necessity compelled you. I did not imitate this neglect by holding back letters of my own. Rather, I kept quiet from day to day, deceived by the hope that a letter from you was about to arrive. But now the silence of your Eminence, which has grown long enough, has overruled my deliberation. A silence that has grown hard upon some root must be torn out. My letter, then, looks to a double gain: I commend to you its bearer, Benenatus, who is coming on account of his runaway slaves, and I no longer put off the good of my own longing. Farewell, then, my lord. Know that things are going well for me, as you would wish, and hurry to cheer me with a letter in return, so that the bearer may rejoice in your kindness and I may be comforted by your reply.
XVII. Ennodius to Bishop Stephen.

Since your merits restored you to your rank and you received the honour your life demands, I have, for my sins, received no letter from your Blessedness. The forgetfulness I meet with is foreign to your calling and to your habit toward suppliants. Let not your pontifical authority accuse me of rashness. Love scarcely stops to consider what rights it may have, and one who is spurred on by the command of charity never measures himself. There is also this: I could offer no helping hand to the bearer of this letter except to bring Benenatus, who is travelling to Gaul on certain business, to the notice of your Crown by means of my letter. Commending him with all humility, I ask that through him I may be cheered by a letter in return. My lord, as I pay the service of greeting with all devotion, I hope above all that your Serenity will not fail to mention me too in your prayers when you make supplication to God without ceasing.
XVIII. Ennodius to Bishop Eulalius.

To what height the gift of your spiritual letter has raised me, words would be too narrow to attest, even if it could be captured in speech at all. My slender mind is not equal to telling of it, and my poor tongue cannot suffice. For what else shall I take it to mean that you have remembered me, if not that my sins are being overcome? Your remembrance has already driven away everything that the foulness of my deeds could supply, and has allowed me to look up through clear skies to the gift from on high. My lord, as I fittingly offer the homage of greeting, I ask God that that [?] soul of yours, which overflows with all that God commands, may take care to keep, without any lessening, the regard it has promised to my lowliness. Let me know that this is happening as I wish by the testimony of frequent letters.
XIX. Ennodius to Faustus.

Thanks be to God, who, in keeping with my wishes, makes my letters carry business, so that I may never refrain from writing; for what the force of love demands can also serve some useful end. And so, my lord, while I send you news of my health, I believe I have found your runaway slave named Germanus, who slipped away three years ago. I have sent a memorandum about him. If he really is yours, let me know promptly what should be done.
XX. Ennodius to Faustus.

The case of my kinsman Julian, who reveres you, is suffering from the many schemes of Marcellinus. Marcellinus is ready only to complain and has no faith in an impartial judgment: he shuns the very hearing he claims to want. For after he is said to have presented some order or other at Genisa, your suppliant at once hastened to a hearing at the court of Milan, and for thirty or forty days, as was proper, presented himself publicly before the judge. He formally called upon Gevica himself, who was said to have been appointed as enforcing officer, and urged him to send the man in his charge to court. He also informed the lord Thrasamund, as you will be able to see from Thrasamund's own letter. But none of this had any effect on a man whose only remedy in a wretched case lies in hiding. On Julian's behalf I ask (though with you no entreaties are needed wherever the truth becomes known, and he has sent all the documents in this matter) that by your order he be freed from troubles of this kind. My lord, as I pay you the homage of greeting, I hope that with your usual care you will relieve the aforesaid of this harassment, and also relieve my anxiety about your well-being with a letter.
XXI. Ennodius to Faustus.

Few words are needed to recommend a man who is commended both by long acquaintance and by the voice of good repute. One who is helped before your Magnificence by his own gifts has no need of long speeches. This letter speaks of the exalted Vitalis, whom your [?] has brought to rejoice in membership of the sacred body. Should a man then be fortified with letters from outsiders when, thanks to your speech, he enters the senate house as no stranger? And will the secrets of your heart be closed to one for whom you opened the inner chambers of freedom? For my part, I am glad to write often, because even if I give the bearer little, I suffer no loss to my own longing. My lord, as I render the greeting I owe, I pray that the favour of your Highness may show itself still more closely toward the aforesaid, and that it may provide for me by restoring our correspondence.
XXII. Ennodius to Faustus.

The hope that keeps demanding frequent letters is mocking me, for, relying on it, I feed my mind on fruitless correspondence. For a long time now I have been sending letters without pause, and the silence I thought I had overcome only grows firmer. But what am I to do, when a heart besieged by devoted love can scarcely be brought back to reason? It still considers remedies, even ones it has found to be of no help. So, offering with the usual reverence the homage of greeting, I commend to you the bearer of this letter, Constantine himself, whose recommendation is his own integrity and modesty. Although I owe him a great deal out of affection, I am compelled by my judgment of him to pay him still more.
XXIII. Ennodius to Marcellianus.

Among those who love and who are powerful in office, the will to do kindnesses is close at hand, and one who is accustomed to granting favours does not cheapen a request by delay. The exalted Virgilius, distinguished as much by his blood as by his integrity, deeply laments that the illustrious Count of the Sacred Largesses is imposing on him the obligation of travelling to Ravenna. Even if his own wishes inclined to this, his age would stand in the way. He is using me as his intercessor with you, so that this burden may be lifted from him, since he has frequently informed that official by reports of what he has done. My lord, offering you the honour of greeting, I ask that, out of regard for me and as a proof of your affection, what is requested may be granted.
XXIV. Ennodius to Mascator.

The unfeigned love of your heart has adorned me with new spirit. I, whose chatter, worse than ignorance, displeases the learned, now enjoy the testimony of a pen that has been coaxed out of me. Speech that is compelled has stolen from the necessity laid on it the value it lacks in eloquence. An offence committed under orders has never deserved punishment. No one can justly condemn someone who obeys. Whoever provokes an unskilled man must blame himself for the injuries done him by rustic eloquence. It is arrogance not to obey one's betters, and greater arrogance to despise what you know came down to you from one who obeyed. Not to love what you yourself demand is thought proof of a perverse desire. He who withholds censure from one who complies is agreeing with his own judgment. Strictness that weighs the merit of the one who obeys is wrongly obstinate. A man has not driven modesty from its post if he owes what he says to a command. So whatever is shabby in my eloquence is commended by my obedience. It is for you to consider what sort of thing you ordered to be offered; for my part, I think you have earned, without any loss to my modesty, what you wished to receive. Among all this I pass over what ought to have been said first: that churchly humility has renounced whatever could please; that one who loves prayer has not pursued the pomp of orations; that, mindful of my calling, I flee even what leads to glory, avoid as a vice whatever exalts, and count as a fault whatever raises up or lifts on high; and that one who courts favour loses the merit of just praise. I will not put forward the truth as an excuse, coloured with a painter's brush, by recalling that I have now left behind whatever the pursuit of liberal studies once gave me, and that in the bed of what was once a full river barely a drop of parched eloquence now flows. I say nothing of how the tongue that practice had made nimble has been dulled by another practice, so that silence now takes the place of eloquence, and I love lowliness instead of the tragic buskin. I return to this point: since I was not permitted to hide within a modest retreat or to cover the weakness of my talent with the cloak of silence, I shall count what I have offered as a complete defence. But, roused by love, I have overstepped the limits of a letter with thoughtless talkativeness. Farewell, my lord. As I offer you the honour of greeting, I shall learn what you think of my letter either from your silence or from a long reply.
XXV. Ennodius to Eugenes.

Only someone lame in faith could suppose that favour is not steadfast with you. Still, I want frequent letters to continue as a proof of affection, so that a mind anxious about a loved one's welfare may not be tossed about by suspicions even while all is well. There you have it, my lord: from this disclosure of my longing you may know the calm of my heart. Play your part, and just as the privilege of the duty you laid on me raises me up, so may the grace of the letter you send raise you up. So, rendering the greeting I owe, I ask you to make clear to me, under the cover of whatever hint you like, what your goodwill is accomplishing on my behalf. Farewell.
XXVI. Ennodius to Avienus.

Your Magnificence plays its part and proves the splendour of its blood by the testimony of its purity. Devout hearts do not know how to abandon love, and a noble mind keeps faith with a religious affection. So I have received a letter shining with a double light, since what a holy heart conceived a serene hand set down. I pray God that, if he loves Rome, he will preserve this devout nature in you for ever, and multiply such kindness toward me with the care you have promised. Farewell.
XXVII. Ennodius to Avienus.

I do not know whether frequent letters please your Magnificence; but I shall always give what I expect from those who love me. I allow others to follow a different practice; I must live by my own habit, so that the fullness of love may be unlocked with the key of speech. I cannot bear that a decaying silence should creep into affection as the habit of writing slips away. Now if your Highness cares as much as I do, let it be shown by constant correspondence and made plain by frequent letters. But if you have so far been taken up with other pursuits and now yield to my view at love's command, then however much of your right you give up, that much of my service you will possess. So farewell, my lord, and accept this small gift, valuing it not by its cheapness but by the regard of the one who sends it. Farewell.
XXVIII. Ennodius to Euprepia.

I received from your Charity a letter that went through no more than the formal courtesies and suited neither affection nor kinship. Even so, the situation required me to answer with a letter in return, my affection grown as distant as your style, lest withholding a reply should reveal, not that your cunning had become known to me, but that I lacked the words. I do not want you, sister Euprepia, to blame anything [?] on the troubles of the provinces or, as you put it, on people's instigation. Wherever you go, as experience shows, you do not leave behind your mistrustful mind: we do not escape our faults by changing places. Toward your relatives your practice has been neither to weigh their kindnesses with a fair interpretation nor to correct their excesses with no more than the reproof they deserved. But why should a letter of grief be made any longer? No flood of eloquence will be able to change your character. As for the rest, farewell, my lady, and order your life and your soul as is best for you. Know, however, that I shall spend on Lupicinus not what I owe you but what befits my own soul. For the only affection that earns a greater reward from God is the one that is given without being prompted by any human gifts.
XXIX. Ennodius to Eugenes.

Whenever words serve as pledges of the feelings, speech paints on the page, as if in a mirror, the image of a friend. It converses with that image as though face to face, and delights in a sweet likeness that answers to its longings. No fluency of the tongue can express what a heart bound in friendship conceives. And although words come more easily than kindnesses, and there is nothing that cannot be enlarged by ambitious speech, I confess that my tongue is dry and halting when I try to set out my affection for you. Yet I charge your Kindred Spirit with silence, because, though you have been given two letters, you have given no thought to a reply. See, I am sending you another letter, knowing that I am giving what I expect to receive. Farewell, my lord. Address one who loves you with the brilliance for which you are famous, and cherish him with the integrity in which you excel.
XXX. Ennodius to Avienus.

I am surprised that something unpleasant should be joined to your Magnificence's [?], and that the calm of your conscience should be stained by harsh words, when you write that I command letters rather than earn them by an affection that demands them. Do you think any kind of rule is more exalted than the one by which love makes us subjects? No heights, my lord Avienus, are exempt from the yoke of charity. Whatever freedom there is in the world is not withdrawn from such servitude. See, I, lowly in station and unknown to honours, shall thus give orders to your fasces, content to be subject in equal measure. Now farewell. However much you feel I have given you, pay back that much to me, as one who faithfully returns affection.
XXXI. Ennodius to Avienus.

Letters take their character from the talents of their writers. They often serve mere formality, and only sometimes bear the marks of affection. Sometimes sincerity dictates them, but more often they are artful compositions, like cosmetic paint. Such a letter feigns the brightness of love but is found out by the very polish that covers it, when, stripped of its contrived coverings, it is laid bare beneath the veil. Even so, I consider letters a mirror of the conscience, though absence scarcely dares to judge friendship by them. Yet it is clear what plain speech conveys in them and what artful speech conveys. The mind, interpreter of what is written, cuts through the clouds of eloquence; it quickly reaches understanding, having cleared a path through the words with its own sickles. So I take great delight in those letters in which sincerity lies open and no safe opportunity for deceit slips in. I am glad, though, whenever reasons for writing or bearers come my way, so that by writing often I may satisfy my wish and lay a burden on your sense of honour, unless what you have received is returned. Greetings, my lord; yield to my view at love's command. Farewell.
XXXII. Ennodius to Passivus.

If speech were sufficient to express love, if my halting tongue could set out all my affection, to whom more than to you would I send frequent letters? And if the worth of my feeling did not constrain it, the service of speech would wait upon no one more fittingly. Others profess with their lips an affection their minds know nothing of, and paint their passing moods in an alluring exchange of letters. Their inner chambers are on holiday, and all their love is on the tongue; nothing reaches the heart beyond what is set down in writing. But my mind toward you has fallen silent, pressed by the leanness of my eloquence and by the abundance of my friendship. For I fear that beggarly conversation might set a limit to our affection, and that the measure of my speech might be taken for the measure of our bond. It is better to leave more to your estimation through silence than to show the shortcomings of my love through letters. There, I have stated the reasons why I write so rarely, trusting that with you eloquence counts for less than the sincerity that is owed. As for the rest, greetings, my lords. Enjoy God's blessings, and as your life goes on, long fulfil the commands of heaven. For with you, kindness finds increase even when it begins from abundance. Farewell.
XXXIII. Ennodius to Faustus.

Letters that offer a recommendation for the afflicted are in keeping with my calling. For in them the integrity of religion shines clearly, since they present the tears of the lowly without flattering the powerful with any cosmetic paint. But more of this another time. When you see the bearer, you will recognise the wish of the one who writes. May he win his case with your Magnificence with the same success in entreaty by which he obtained this letter from me. My letter introduces a poor religious woman who is confident in the justice of her case. Judge for yourself whether words should have been withheld from frailty and from justice, and whether it would have been right for me to fail either my office or my character. See, as I offer you the reverence of greeting, I have shown what I owed on my part. Consider what remains for you: just as the petition looks to me for the wish of the woman mentioned above, so its success looks to you. Farewell.
XXXIV. Ennodius to Senarius.

There is nothing, of course, that ambitious eloquence does not raise aloft beyond the truth. But in my affection for you I suffer from a poverty of speech. The tongue has never been equal to love; the service of the lips has always fallen short of the good in the heart. For this reason I use the freedom of one who admonishes. I did not believe your Eminence would forget me for so long that you would refrain even from formal letters, so that even those courtesies that usually feign affection with a counterfeit face would be refused between persons bound by the chains of friendship. If I were able to put these things into words, I could have endured them. See, I am writing again, and by my example I bear witness to what I assert in words ought to be followed. It is for you to consider what it means to neglect honourable wishes from now on; for my part, trained by long practice, I meet my grief with patience. Farewell.
BOOK FOUR
I. Ennodius to Pope Symmachus.

It is the mark of a good commander to encourage a soldier's courage once it has been proved in battle, so that his valour, fed on praise, may in later engagements unlearn its love of life. Whose strength is not nourished by the praise of his general? From what conflicts would even the weaker limbs of a recruit hold back, when he sees from his commander's testimony that what he has done will not be lost? There is only one way for eagerness to fight to grow: when good deeds are not erased by forgetfulness. Would that God, moved by your prayers, might put an end to this devilish struggle! Would that he might show my devotion in peace, so that concord might commend the service of one whose zeal adversity has revealed! Your brother sent a delegation, with instructions, to Bishop Marcellianus; but he himself has written back to tell you what it achieved. As for the rest, offering you the duties of greeting, I pray that you will heal whatever is sick with your healing prayer, and that among the hidden secrets of concealed diseases you will cut away with the spiritual knife the error that is being kept alive for the destruction of all. Farewell.
II. Ennodius to Alico.

In demanding that I write to you, the venerable priest Amantius has turned what was a matter of my devotion into a matter of his command. Happy is the compulsion that serves my wishes, and free is the order of a superior that serves affection. The man who compelled me owes me for what I gave to my own wish. This letter is fortunate, for it bears witness to love twice over: it draws a new friend into the bond of affection, and it puts the heart of an older friend in my debt. As a faithful herald of your greatness, he caused you to be chosen before you were known, on the strength of his endorsement. Affection has rarely come before acquaintance. Who has ever had the luck to please before being seen? Note how much weight the bearer carries with me, for my judgments bend at his nod. We have seen the man he came to know, and we embrace the one he praises. A mind that stands on firm ground will often yield its own judgment to a friend's assessment, so we rightly look up to those whom a proven man extols. If my thin wit could unfold the richness of your kindness, if my halting speech did not tire as it approached the fountain of our bond, and if the nature of a letter, which reins in even the eloquent, allowed me to go on at length, I would declare how much your nobility owes me, since I was the first to begin our exchange of letters and the one who unlocked the door of affection with the key of speech. I do ask, however, that the bearer be loved in return for what he has given. I commend to you the affairs of the church, because whatever is spent on my hope grows into merit for you. My lord, as I offer the gift of a most heartfelt greeting, I beg that, if you are pleased to accept my offering poured out in love, you will show the devotion of a friendly heart in a letter. Farewell.
3. ENNODIUS TO BISHOP EULALIUS

Thanks be to the Trinity, our God, who supports the load of sins that weighs me down through the eagerness of a man who is strong in his sight. He sets the memory of me within that temple of your holy heart in which Christ, its skilful builder, delights, so that the bright serenity of your conscience may wipe away what I have darkened with the cloud of my own way of life. Now I know that the laments of sinners are not poured out in vain. Above all, my prayer and my tears have won me this: you have risen up as a strong intercessor for me, and you have put a right hand armed with heavenly help under my tottering shoulders. It is true that, before God, only despair destroys the one who strays. See, our darnel, thorns and thistles already promise barley, wheat and vineyards.
