Come then, chosen one of God, carry on what you have begun for my lowly self and do your part, while your persistent prayers for me wash away what I have gathered through an abundance of faults. Feed the one you have taken up with frequent letters too, so that with the salt of admonition you may strengthen a heart that is tasteless and propped up by no steadiness of virtue. I return to the courtesies of greeting, and though I have overstepped the bounds of a letter, I add one more thing, like a chatterer but importunate out of need: help me with your prayers as unceasingly as you strengthen me with your letters. Farewell.
4. COPY OF A LETTER THAT HE COMPOSED HIMSELF: A SISTER TO HER BROTHER

Some people owe favour, in short, even to children who are poor in affection, and what is given to one's offspring is thought to be a debt and not a kindness. A malicious interpreter subjects the heart's judgment to the commands of nature, and stripping love of its savour, thinks that something can be demanded on the sole plea of having given birth. In that view the name of son is believed to count for more than dutiful conduct, and nobody asks what you place on the scale of love, only what title you can set against the prejudgment of the one weighing it. Among the prudent, however, we call someone our offspring in vain unless he shows himself to be what he is called. Whoever neglects discernment regarding his children shows that conception pleases him more than merit. Far be it from us to consider in our descendants only what gave us pleasure. For unless the fruit of the womb answers with honourable conduct, it seems to have come about as a witness to lust rather than to grace. It is right that the ever-faithful fellowship of brother and sister be preferred even to children, and one may regard the sharer of one's origin in such a way that the bond of blood is not neglected and a judgment based on merit is commended. And so, lest my words proceed at length through winding preambles, and what is slight in substance swell in expression, I give and confer upon you, my brother, and transfer to your ownership freely and for ever, the slave so-and-so, who is mine by right, etc. Farewell.
5. ENNODIUS TO FAUSTUS

The illustrious Dalmatius is no diminished but a whole portion of my soul, and to the privilege of kinship he adds the splendour of his character. He believed it would help his business to be supported by a letter from me to your eminence. Since I know his affairs, I did not think I should refuse, and so as a courtesy to the man I grant what I know you owe to justice. An estate of his in Sicily, held until now by good right, is reported to have been seized by his co-owners. Whatever I achieve by pleading now goes to support civil order. My lord, as I pay the courtesies of greeting in full humility, I beg that in the interests of this noble man you protect decency, the laws and the other ornaments of the state that stand firm through your conscience. Farewell.
6. ENNODIUS TO AGAPITUS

Your greatness has been devoted to the common good and your leisure has passed into glory. Busy with your watches at Ravenna, you neglect your own quiet and make ours wholly secure, and your private talent has gone to adorn the kingdom. The brilliance of the palace has added to itself a new light drawn from a private home, and the lord of affairs rightly judged that the splendour of his reign was narrower while it lacked you. After all this, I believed that, since our regions are close together, I would be cheered by frequent letters. But my sins have mocked my hope and made my plans fail: your serene mind sends no letters to bear witness to your affection. It is grave if I did not deserve your love, and graver if I have perhaps disturbed a love I had already won. I know, however, that such things should be veiled in excuses that fit the truth: the exchange of letters belongs to private men, and it is not right to demand it of busy ones. But I also know that a heart firm in affection, though distracted by any burdens and troubles, does not deny friendship what it owes. Now I do not wish to be lavish with complaints. As I pay the respect of greeting, I beg that you bring to the desired result the request that the bearer of this letter puts before you. Farewell.
7. ENNODIUS TO JULIAN, THE ILLUSTRIOUS COUNT OF THE PATRIMONY

I have received your letter, radiant with a twofold splendour, whose worth grew because the purple of its writer was joined to your graciousness. I give thanks to almighty God, who exceeds the meagreness of our wishes with the abundance of his kindness and does not restrain the riches of his lavish generosity, even when we are conscious of our merits and confine our desires to narrow limits. I thought it would be enough if you honoured me with a very full letter. But you were not content to grant only what a beggarly request asks for. You sent pages that were apt in language and rich in praise, like a great river that is invited out of its bed into side channels to relieve the dryness nearby: it pours itself wholly into the slender stream that was wished for and floods the parched, deeply squalid land with the drenching of its saving water. Yet keep the custom of strong persons, and let your greatness not abandon what it has begun so well toward my littleness, so that the care of writing letters may serve as a witness of affection and the charms of conversation may confirm a pure love. Let the affection you promised before your rise to high office know no setting. Let your kindness toward me grow as much as the summits of rank have been added to you, lest power be thought to have renounced a friendship that a middling station fostered. For whoever curbs arrogance in high station shows that he deserved what he attained. Prove by the uprightness of your heart that good fortune can be made subject to the commands of love. While you set an example, bend those free necks of the nobles to affection. Let people learn from you that the greatest man keeps in fellowship one whom he gained when he was less. Fortune makes sport of those whom it lifts to the heights by making them show that they have forgotten their own. With one who knows the world, recounting good qualities is no necessity of admonition but an occasion for praise. I know the tranquillity of your mind, fashioned for good pursuits, and I mention it particularly to show that where affection is solid, honours have no power over it. But I have overstepped the bounds of a letter by dwelling at length on my own commendation. I return to the duties of written address, and as I report that I am well, I ask at once for news of your prosperity.
8. ENNODIUS TO POPE SYMMACHUS

Your apostolic graciousness has advanced me to the point of rashness: the confidence you granted has become the mother of boldness. But anyone who thinks I know nothing of humility will find me obedient if he considers the commands I was given. It is presumption when servants do not follow up their lords' kindnesses, and I think that what I do in obedience should be counted as deference. There, I have stated my reason for writing: I feared that, after being told to take up my pen, I would be rejecting your instructions by keeping silent. To this is added the case of Marius of venerable memory. While I was in the City, you gave my prayers hope regarding his business, which was settled with your holy church by a lawful agreement. But his heirs lament that for many years the revenues due to them have been withheld. I come to plead for them because I know you. One whose custom is always to do what is holy will not scorn what is just, and one who gives away his own will not take what belongs to others. Whoever believes that a heart close to God can be enticed by gain is mistaken: for a holy will, the loss is to withhold a kindness. You count as gains only those that arise for you from generosity, for you receive riches when you give them. The stewardship of the saints is greedy in its own way: by keeping nothing back, it turns everything into merit of its own. No profits are better than those that come to you from generosity. So I confidently promised the heirs mentioned above, out of regard for you, that the loss from their labour would be made good. Fulfil my promise by a kind arrangement: relieve them with the result, and me with a letter.
9. ENNODIUS TO FAUSTUS

When a letter is carried away by favour, it usually has no love for judgment and bestows its kindness all the more lavishly by exalting the undeserving. The man who obtains through the writer's support what his own character does not earn owes more to the one who vouches for him, because he is helped by no endowments of his own conscience and rightly credits his advocate with whatever he gains. It is one thing to graft goods that are foreign to the person commended onto him with words, like a noble shoot, and another to make known the goods that are innate in him. It is as if you were to claim that a rustic flock wears Tyrian purple of its own accord, and to say that the fields spread abroad the noble dye that the fleece never soaked up in the drenching vat. Some dye with the murex of the tongue what no dye fit for royal use ever produced, and wool unknown to the shellfish of a distant sea drinks in only the light of eloquence: whatever the words of those who report on it have coloured, though the gift itself is cheap, is made worthy of imperial garments. But both my strength and my wishes keep me from such urbanity. No threads of brighter dye will glow with splendour through me, and no one will find anything said by me about someone that he does not recognize in that person's actions. So I lend a hand to my modesty or to my principle, since I go ahead with the service of my words for one who comes to your notice through deeds well done. I mean that the most distinguished Venantius has obtained a letter from me so that he may draw the eyes of your greatness to himself and not happen to go unnoticed amid your mass of cares. He has his own recommendations, by which he may deserve to be enrolled among your protégés. He has shown you modesty, piety and innocence, companions with which he might enter the inner chambers of your serene mind. Believe me, the distinctions you cherish abound in him: you will soon find that I was not his eulogist but his witness. You, my lord, grant your favour to the bearer above all, so that a good man is not troubled by being a newcomer. He will plainly do his part, and with the riches of his life he will make up for the poverty of my words.
10. ENNODIUS TO TRASIMUND, VIR ILLUSTRIS

It is not rashness that has led me to write, since a scion of royal stock invites his subject to every kind of fellowship. This brilliance is ingrained in the birth of lords: they raise their own heights higher by condescension. You wish to treat your servants as equals, so that through love they may owe you more than their station alone requires. So, most pious lord, offering the homage I must pay together with everyone else, I inform you that I have sent the bearer of this letter to put certain matters before you. Reward your suppliant with results, because I come as a petitioner sustained by hope.
11. ENNODIUS TO LUMINOSUS

Whoever reveals a friendly heart by clear signs takes away rest from the friends he has honoured with his favour. The mouth of one who is used to being heard is hardly ever idle, for it is a great loss of decency to withhold the benefit of words, so that in sparing the tongue our face labours under shame, careless of honour. You have made me a chatterer, since you are accustomed to grant my requests. But lest I talk around what is to be granted and delay what is to be obtained with a long letter, I return to the matter. The illustrious Laurentius states that the revenues owed to him, which the Roman church promised by an agreement made with his ancestor, are being refused him by the lord pope on some objection or other. In this business he begs through me for the favour of your protection, so that what you owe to the laws you may appear to grant out of affection, and what cannot be denied to justice may be increased for friendship's sake. Grant this as I wish, so that whatever advantage this man gains I may count as a gift received by me. In sending my greetings, then, I hope that where the duties of letters are concerned, neither your sincere love will take a holiday nor your eloquence, celebrated by the testimony of the whole world, will fall silent.
12. ENNODIUS TO JOHN

Nature has ordained that whenever what we long for is granted, care turns into joy and complaint into praise. I was uncertain what your eminence's long silence meant, but now that I have been given what I wished for, I myself look for an honourable kind of excuse on your behalf. See what the serene workings of affection achieve: as if everything had turned out to my liking, I have been appeased by a single gift and pardoned your errors. Here you have a pattern of devoted love to adopt and examples of constancy in friendship to borrow. If you follow me, no further offences will draw you away from our bond, and a single good deed will absolve your companion's faults. Do you accuse me, brother, of silence and forgetfulness? Where was this spirit when my letters received no reply and you did not take the lead in urging the care of the pen? Where was that lavishness with letters, which you did not keep toward everyone in Liguria? By sending letters, as a solace for my grief, to many who were strangers to your affection, you kept up your silence toward me and gave conversation to them against my wishes. Yet this is the rule of human affairs: close kinship always produces equal zeal. Forgetting this order, you wanted to join certain unlettered people to letters, thinking that things wholly distant could come together in affection. What did your persuasive speech achieve, composed with carefully wrought phrases, when it addressed people ignorant of the liberal arts and passed over the one who loves you? But more of this another time. I do not want to rehearse the multitude of your lapses, since a brief satisfaction has soothed me. Indeed I would have been sparing in mentioning them, did I not believe you know that of offences what is concealed remains, while what breaks out into speech is removed. My lord, I pray that from now on you will not approach what you have learned is taken badly like one who despises correction, but will often send me sweet letters, so that your gift of eloquence may grow while you keep the sacred bonds of concord.
13. ENNODIUS TO CONSTANTIUS, VIR ILLUSTRIS

Your greatness keeps toward its friends and admirers the conduct that brings it glory: when you consider them worthy of remembrance, you prove your own worth. For a long time now I have received your letters as a consolation, while I sigh over the losses of your absence. What an ingenious skill, established by heavenly gifts! So that a long separation may not be allowed to pluck anything away from affection, you send letters that present a sacred image of yourself. God, who examines our feelings, knows that I waste away with longing for your eminence and find no relief while the best of men is far away. Yet I pay the courtesy of greeting by the care of a letter, and as I thank your graciousness, I acknowledge that my brother John too has been restored to me through you. Until now his silence made plain enough what it meant by forgetting me; now, won back to me by your affection, he has returned to the care of the pen he had forsworn. I ask you, however, to hasten your return, or, if a happy delay detains you, to show your love in a letter.
14. ENNODIUS TO FAUSTUS

Words are often spent cheaply as mere courtesies, but whenever they are offered on behalf of those close to us, whatever has served favour should be credited to sincere affection. A man does not feign love with painted words when he entrusts to a dear bearer a letter to be delivered to his lords. In commending my illustrious and magnificent Panfronius, it is my heart that dictates this letter while my tongue rests. I do not know to what height I should raise the merits of the man I have named, for my meagre tongue cannot express what my heart owes him. But I ought to renounce the allure of eloquence even if it were available to me, because plain speech more truly confesses rich affection; and if we extol with lavish pages those whom our hearts do not know, it is right that a letter written for those we love should be kept short. Having stated the reason for my brief words, I commend my sworn brother in however few words, yet with many marks of deference, so that with the help of your greatness he may at last be seen to have overcome, in his business, the schemes of those who clamour around him. For the rest, I offer a servant's greeting and report that I am well, provided that heavenly providence grants me sure news of your prosperity.
15. ENNODIUS TO FAUSTUS

The road to success is easier whenever a humble suppliant asks something of a devout man. Whoever is moved by a suppliant's miseries is compelled to show affection, and one whose principle bids him listen to the afflicted cannot raise his hands against them. The bearer of this letter laments that he has been driven from his ancestral land, and he places what is left of his hope in your judgment, so that the power of his adversary may not gloat over its gain and security. The sacred bonds of the laws and the defence of the lowly look to you; I have done my part by commending him. Increase your venerable name, then, with kindnesses, since in granting what is just you do not neglect what belongs to mercy. My lord, receive the respect of my greeting and grant my prayers their effect in such a way that your own desire may be fulfilled while what is honourable is upheld.
16. ENNODIUS TO AGAPITUS

I would rightly demand a reply with many letters if your greatness's silence did not testify that my pages had been unwelcome. Your silence proclaims that a chatterer displeases you, and when it sees that its silence has achieved nothing, it seeks, I think, a new kind of revenge. By refraining from writing, you aim to stop the unskilled from sending letters to you, yet the result has escaped you. Consider what would serve your purpose: being scorned has made me write more often. But one who has suffered a great grief should keep his words brief. The care of a letter accompanies to your eminence your admirer, my brother Panfronius. Whatever favour is granted to him will bind me too with the chains of the kindnesses bestowed. I have also entrusted him with certain matters to put before you concerning the office of the vicariate. Bring my petition to a successful end, for I stand by my part whenever I am obliged to bear witness before the most upright of men, since I present only men of proven worth.
17. ENNODIUS TO DECORATUS

The tongue is rightly believed to proclaim what lies within, since by speech it calls the secrets of the hidden soul into the light. The love in our hearts would remain unknown if speech did not betray and reveal it. The wisdom of the ancients rightly used letters like keys and through them made public the affection stored within. A mind that has attested its affection is drawn into the witness of writing, and it may not change the love that it once promised in longing through the mediation of a letter. I have bound myself to this custom, or rather law, declaring on the faith of a letter the feelings toward your greatness that have grown in my heart. If you join me with equal care in this bond, and if friendship, a faithful interpreter weighing itself, sees the wish of the other, let a letter bringing your reply say so. As I offer the gifts of greeting, I have not concealed my intention like one who is stingy with words.
18. ENNODIUS TO FAUSTUS

In pressing a request that has the full support of honour, I do not use many words, lest a long speech should seem to have won the favour from someone inclined to refuse; for you are accustomed to grant what is to be asked before the asking. The relatives of the illustrious and magnificent Opilio who live in Africa have sent him a certain person, prompted by affection. As this person is returning to his native land, Opilio has given me the task of obtaining from you a letter to the magnificent Agnellus commending his family. This, most upright of men, you will not refuse, for you are not content that only those living in Italy have known your kindness. Now, as I render my respects by letter, I have stated my reason for writing in few words. Grant much to one who says little.
19. ENNODIUS TO APOLLINARIS

By keeping your silence for so long toward one who loves you, you have carried your mind away into the same absence as your body. By holding back letters you have made the separation, which until now had no power, grow beyond measure. Through this lack of letters things have come to such a pass that the foresight of an earlier age gives love no help at all. Affection goes stale when a man too stingy with words will not air it. Regard is left untended when letters do not put it to use. Frequent writing feeds the friendship planted in our hearts with living nourishment. It would have been easier on my longings, brother, if you had never granted what they wanted than to withdraw what you have often granted, for hearts that you, a skilful shepherd, have whetted with sweet food cannot be at rest. For some time, by writing without a break, you had made me forget that we were apart, as you set your venerable likeness into your gentle words. But now, empty-handed myself, I search the empty hands of travellers. Yet I do not want my own error to make another's fault my own, and so be convicted of committing what I grieve has been done. Receive, then, most faultless of men, the comfort for longing that heavenly grace grants to those who are apart. If you remember me, help the bearers, so that they may not feel the hardships of travel, since a friendly recommendation will have given these named men a homeland. When they return, relieve me with news of your health.
XX. Ennodius to Julian, V.L.

The good of affection is exercised by frequent writing, for what the tongue discloses lays open the secrets of the mind. A man who exchanges idleness for love takes care to write constantly. These are the duties by which unspoken affection becomes known. Had our familiar bearer not received a letter to deliver to your Eminence, he would testify that I had forgotten the reverence I owe. For I do not know how to neglect affection, nor how to drive away, for the sake of my own ease, a favour won by toil. I owe our bond many words, but a letter forces me to be brief. Farewell, my lord. Accept the honour of my greeting, and keep toward me the regard that has grown to maturity. So may you, called forward for the good of the commonwealth, rejoice in the long continuance of your happiness.
XXI. Ennodius to Bishop Constantius.

Your subdeacon Vigilius wanted to test how much affection you would return to me. Using his advancement as the occasion, he has tried to bring our bond into play. While he is being raised in honours he wants to measure the state of friendship between us, so that the fruit we stored up from the harvest of affection may come back to him. If I deserve it, bring him to the sacred office of the diaconate, so that his rank may help me toward the hope of asking for greater things. And so that a refusal may not frustrate my petition, may you hold the place granted to your merits for long spans of time.
XXII. Ennodius to Pope Symmachus.

The eminent Laurentius has his own integrity to support him in commending his children, and a father's prudence is pursuing his offspring's cause. Yet a parent's concern pushes on to greater things and can scarcely believe that his own merit is enough for his sons. He seeks a letter as a helper in backing his offspring, and with anxious care he strives to share his fatherly ardour with everyone. Consider whether so excellent a man could be denied what he wants when his request is both pious and just. May God grant his prayers and deign to win your Beatitude's affection for those named here, so that the compassion of your Crown, once implored, may raise up the little ones and surpass the hopes of their anxious father. My lord, I hope that the kindness you promised long ago will bear witness in this matter, if the one who makes his request through me sees that a double favour has been bestowed on those mentioned above.
XXIII. Ennodius to Dominator.

Your wishes, which our brother Agnellus made known, ought properly to have been disclosed by a letter, and your speaking first ought to have provided the pattern for drawing out a correspondence. Then what you will owe could have been repaid to you, and once you had spoken I could have offered no pretext for abstaining from letters. It was in your power to turn my tongue's holiday into exercise and to remove the rust from my rustic eloquence with a craftsman's study. For just as it harms affection not to be the first to address one who longs for it, so neither the memory of friendship nor a sense of shame counsels answering a letter once sent with silence. Still, it has added to my pleasure that you have commanded me to write, even if this deprives me of the proof that in love I never weigh my strength. Let generous minds never believe that a burden laid on them by a friend is unbearable. Only embrace what you have demanded, and while you correct with your censure, put aside the stale disdain of critics. Far be it from you not to cherish one who has obeyed. Whoever has rendered you the service of speech you imposed is drawn into the hope of greater merit, even if he comes from common coinage. Farewell, then, my lord, for I do not want a conversation that is not built true to the plumb line to run long. Like rich soil, return the harvest of favour, as I trust you will. From now on it will be your choice: if you want to receive my letters often, invite me with services like these.
XXIV. Ennodius to Faustus.

A sick mind cannot bear silence, yet it forswears any lengthy narrative. Neither silence nor long conversation suits the testimony of grief, and a letter is cramped when words come to it only amid groans. But why do I assert my tongue's holiday by saying more, and promise with chatter a letter confined to necessary limits? I pray God to relieve my anxiety with clear evidence of your

prosperity. May he accept my tears, he to whom closed lips speak, for whom a shower from the eyes flowing out of compunction is a complete embassy. I see that not only my peace but my very well-being has been shaken by the strength of my enemies and the storms of rumour. God has power to remove the uncertainties of a great tempest with the blessing of calm. If I deserve it of God, fare well, and by sending letters take thought for the mind of one who loves you [?] the watches at Ravenna.
XXV. Ennodius to Bassus.

My relatives stored up rich fruits from the harvest of favour in their regard for your Eminence. If that old regard were kept toward me, out of faithful remembrance, frequent letters would show it, and words that witness to the heart would reveal an affection still unburied. But now I feel that you have forgotten me and keep none of the concord of a better time, since no letters are sent to reveal your concern. Yet I have turned the impatience of my longing into words. I know that a new friendship is sweet only if the old one is kept, and that what our forebears tested is purer in affection. I know too that if you keep Camillus in mind, you will not neglect Ennodius. So, paying the tribute of greeting by the care of a letter, I pray that you will deign to receive kindly my cleric, the bearer of this letter, whom both his own interests and my command have brought to Gaul. When he returns, set down your good fortune in writing, so that the care shown in letters may make good whatever loss forgetfulness has caused to love.
XXVI. Ennodius to Eugenes, V.I.

May a fortunate omen arriving from heaven strengthen your auspices, and may divine counsels fortify the first steps of your venerable office. Through you may heavenly favour guide the lord of liberty, so that what the shower from on high has poured into you may flow down from the fountain of your breast to the ears of the prince. See, I have set out the prayers I owed for your beginnings, though in words pressed into a narrow space. Remember the love and the pact you promised, so that the quaestorship may pay me what is owed without any loss from the change. Keep toward me the mind of your predecessor. Let the promise of your office not be broken, my lord, now that its holder has changed. Fare well, as your suppliant desires, and amid your great outpouring of benefits accept this sparing conversation. For such is the way of the fortunate and the nature of the better sort, that they outdo the abundance of words with deeds and favours granted.
XXVII. Ennodius to Senarius.

The bearer's haste has squeezed this letter and made a grieving man dictate few words about great matters. Yet this is no burden to one who can interpret the meaning amid the narrowness of words. I am tormented over the delay of the lord Faustus and the conflicting reports. After God, relieve my anxiety with a swift reply, for it is worse to waste away in uncertain hope than to learn of plain despair from the report of one who loves me. Farewell, my lord, and, seeing what I desire, send me letters, whether welcome or necessary.
XXVIII. Ennodius to Agapitus.

If my days flowed as I wished, I would devote my effort to letters of courtesy rather than of business, and I would not transfer the gift of affection to duties that are not its own. But I have been compelled to exchange a matter of regard for one of necessity. A sublime and magnificent man is struggling against the deceitful plots of his enemies, and through me he implores the protection of your justice. He asks that a wicked fabrication not be allowed to assail his reputation, and that a manufactured rumour not perhaps carry the day. My lord, offering you the most ample greeting, I pray that the vigour known to be in you may rise up, and that what is asked of you through the service of my words may be brought to a fitting fulfilment.
XXIX. Ennodius to the Pope.

Heaven's care arranges what benefits its followers. Unlooked-for gifts are bestowed on those who deserve well of God, and the divine dispensation confers even what humankind does not presume to pray for. The adversaries of your see have learned by whose championship they are defeated, as our Redeemer recently revealed in the case of the bishop of Aquileia. And so, among the excellence of the divine gifts, I ask that your Crown not refuse to remember me. For one who loves a servant even when he is far away invites many to serve him. Farewell.
XXX. Ennodius to Eugenes, V.I.

Now that our first exchange of letters has fulfilled my hope, I have loosed lips long idle to the use of speech. Success puts life even into a man who knows he lacks Latin learning. When study has lapsed, joy has often made men eloquent. If cheerfulness drives off the clouds of grief, words soon run gleaming through a clear sky. So gladness shows us as perfect, or adversity makes us infants who cannot speak. This, my lord, I can confirm from my own experience. And so, embracing this time of prosperity, I render the affectionate greeting I owe. I hope that the noble promise made to me, which began from the fullness of favour, may be doubled, as though it still needed increase. Farewell.
XXXI. Ennodius to Avitus.

Your Magnificence's letter brought us much occasion for joy amid our lament, since words announcing a death had served the cause of cheer. Yet the pleasure did not equal the tears, and the serenity of your words did not wholly drive away the turmoil of grief. Even after the conversation we longed for, the mind still feels the affliction of so great a bishop's passing, because it is the nature of things that any gladness is outweighed when set against even a little anguish. But why do we stir up, by mentioning them anew, the things that have till now subdued the mind with their hidden tossing? With God's help I promise to be a companion to your wishes, provided that, without prejudice to our lord the pope, I learn that you have chosen a man whom he who has the care of souls would not be ashamed to praise. It is wrong to provoke a believer toward crooked ways, and to lead through uncertain paths one whom you have bound to you by affection. Farewell.
XXXII. Ennodius to Eugenes.

I do not think that courtesy can go stale through frequency, or that the cultivation of regard can be blamed as the fault of garrulity. Those occupied with duties of public service may perhaps have an excuse for abstaining from letters. But a man who is free does not deserve pardon if he holds back from constant writing. Whoever could send letters, in which affection finds its food, and does not, plainly confesses that he neglects love. It is the fault of the idle if a mind well proven is weakened by the tongue's holiday, unfed by the conversation it longs for. Just as it befits us, who owe nothing to worldly cares, to foster the religion of friendship, so, unless your Magnificence does your part by sending a reply, your silence condemns what was rightly done. For if virtue is robbed of its rewards, who would not be ashamed to have laboured? There, I have briefly set out, as I judge, what each of us ought to do. I confess that my mind is ill at ease, because when Montanarius returned I received no letter, though I had given him one. I demand that what is owed be repaid by right, and doubled out of shame. Farewell now, my lord. Asking after your health and reporting my own, I pray God that, if he remembers me, he may multiply your prosperity.
XXXIII. Ennodius to Senarius.

If love gave way to shame, if the impatience of affection were bound by the law of modesty, I would hold back from writing letters and, imitating you, take up the pattern of silence. I would not be a careless judge if I inferred that those to whom you give no return are not loved, and that nothing urges an end to letters more easily than silence, since men in the service of the court proclaim by the holiday of their tongues what they reject. But your Magnificence is not so squared off by a builder's lines that you can escape a lover's eyes under any covering, for a friend's mind sees into the inner chambers with no garment in the way. Let no one think that the polish forged in the furnaces of the palace can hide the inner workings of a secret plan from those dear to him. Yet I believe you will set against my complaints the kind of excuse suited to your rank: that the duties of the idle are not rightly demanded of the busy, and that those who attend on the prince can scarcely stoop to such duties. I have often heard such things, but I confess I have not accepted them. Desire often rises above necessity, and fear always yields to affection. The fault lies with a will that defends itself with a contrived excuse. See, my lord, how great my grief is, now that I have declared it along with the duty of greeting. I commend to you the bearer [?] for his loyalty and his nobility, so that by the kindness of your Eminence the insolence of his enemies may lie crushed beneath their own tricks. Farewell.
XXXIV. Ennodius to Hormisdas.

Your welcome errand, by bringing you near, had begun to promise that my longing would be fulfilled. But then your mind passed on to more distant things, and now that you can almost touch Liguria with your hand, you have sent your tongue on holiday. Absence had less power while long stretches of road kept your Holiness away. Conversation made up for the loss of seeing you, and as a remedy, care provided an exchange of letters, through which affection lost nothing between those who lived apart. But I believe you choose to give your friends the harder things, and do not think it a kindness to feed me with conversation when we are so near. Turning the matter around, I sigh over my lot and fear that your Beatitude has now weighed up what you once showed with blandishments, and ascribes what went before to circumstance rather than to love. Let a painted face have no place in our purpose in friendship. No file of earlier study has shaped us for that craft. We know how to bring bare concord to a bond, and among those dear to us we spurn courtly polish like poison. So, my lord, as you receive my greeting, follow one who loves you in this above all: cultivate our faithfulness by frequent speech, and grant unpainted words from the secret of your heart to one who waits for them. Farewell.
XXXV. Ennodius to Apronianus, V.I.

Men who shine with the brightness of good character are accustomed to nourish the religion of friendship by cultivating conversation. In this way, while the seeds of favour are quickened by the warmth of talk, the bond of alliance comes to harvest. Through these services the foresight of older times meant absence to have no power. The lord Faustus, most faultless of men, rightly bears singular witness about you. It is plain, without a cloud, that there need be no doubt about one whom a proven man exalts. But now, bringing myself back to the narrow bounds of a letter, I shut the praise you are owed in the secret inner chambers of my heart, lest what ought to be done among strangers go stale with you through importunity. Farewell, my lord. Receive my most humble greeting. I pray God that he may prolong your prosperity and promise me too an increase through the successes of my friends. Farewell.
BOOK FIVE
I. Ennodius to Liberius the Patrician.

Out of your venerable conscience you have written about the election of the bishop of Aquileia, and your tongue, initiated into divine worship, is serving in the consecration. Meanwhile the care of your words has bound us in favour of a man unknown to us, for nothing is left for others to judge whenever a proven man has extolled someone. What would he leave to the opinion of his followers, when he obeys justice and his decision is not open to examination? For the good of your conscience you do what your command would scarcely be refused. You, the greatest of men, more exalted still in humility, sat as a colleague among the judges of the venerable Marcellinus. And lest crooked interpreters attribute his approval to the favour of power, you added to the worth of the man you praised what you drew from your own character [?]. You played the part of an ordinary man, so that the commendation of an exalted one would not be suspect. Those at the summit hold themselves in check so that the testimony of the most illustrious may carry weight. Happy the priesthood before which a mind full of light has carried the torch! Blessed the life that was brought into question only so that it might prevail with so great a man supporting it, a life that would not have tasted victory had it not first been exposed to uncertainty. Adversity has always brought glory to the innocent, and a modest attack gives them the strongest defenders. But why have I stretched the limits of a letter with loquacity, overstepping in a human composition pages bound by rule? I too, most eminent sir, in the measure of my small capacity, join my consent to your side, with heaven complying with you. And, what is held a marvel among men, from regard for you I am drawn to love him. An affection inspired in me through another pleases me, while the love remains rooted deep in my heart though its object is far away. May heavenly grace join itself as companion to your desires, and as your wishes are fulfilled, may it either find the good of the episcopate in him or create it. Farewell, my lord, and relieve one who loves you with frequent conversation, so that even if business does not call for frequent letters, they may be granted to affection.
II. Ennodius to Marcianus.

While my mind was tossed in anxious uncertainty between hope and fear on your account, you revealed in the honey of your words solid proof of your progress, for as heir to a faithful teaching you follow the eloquence native to your family. The vein, I see, does not degenerate. Skill in speech and learning passes down by the same right as an inheritance... I used to think that the gifts of learning were a matter only of talent, not of family, and that what continual labour and tireless sweat acquire was not handed down through pedigrees. But, as it seems, eloquence keeps its lines of descent, and the splendour of speech that overflowed in the ancestors passes on to their descendants. The course of learning is like that of rivers: the stream of eloquence too glides along its accustomed channels. Learning comes to you along with your father's estate, and through the blessing of offspring the tomb gives back Asterius. I confess I have till now envied the older generation and sighed for the age to which he was granted. I was a careless judge of heaven's benefits, for I could despair of the fruits of the toga while the root itself remained. But to lend charm to its benefits, divine providence makes its gifts unexpected, and by going beyond what is familiar it displays its power through its generosity. Liguria is not barren of good offspring. It nurtures shoots for the forum that the senate-house too would gladly embrace. Advocate and senator are joined by a well-known closeness, and the consul's embroidered robe beckons, ready to receive into its open folds those who have used the toga well. Farewell, dearest one, and give yourself wholly to these honours. Let honourable studies take up all of you. Hasten to come into your father's harvest, cleansing your tongue with the hoe of reading and your character by imitating the good.
III. Ennodius to Opilio, V.I.

I owe a reply to your earlier letter, and in keeping with my purpose, or with modesty, I should repay what I received twice over, unless a rustic letter displeases you. I would not want my superior's condescension to turn into regret at having laid aside his disdain. For through our fault those at the summit do not forget their haughtiness if they suspect that the humble too pursue that kind of evil. Since self-restraint exalts the most eminent, and the fullness of worldly honours grows by this device alone, one must consider what harm a lowly station does to the humble when they do not take their own measure. Let it be enough for your Magnificence, then, that after your second letter I see what error I fell into by my silence. But I confess I was afraid that fleeing from fault might lead me into vice, and that words meant to win favour might give offence, since no file of skill had polished them. I shrank from the dread that seizes the unskilled when given the chance to obey. See, I have declared that I had both the mind of one who admits holding a deposit and, when it comes to repaying it, the modesty of one who knows his strength well. It remains, most faultless of men, for me to learn, once you have examined my plea, that you too are pleased that I have not until now repaid what I received. Considering our own capacity is a faithful guide. As it is foremost in all things, so, when kept, it protects one's reputation where speech is thin. For if the endowment of the eloquent grows through modesty, the name of prudence is easily won when, through modesty, the inarticulate keep silent. Yet in the matter you entrusted to me I am losing face, and in carrying out your orders I am putting my reputation at hazard. Agnellus is toying with me over the houses with all manner of promises, wanting us to name the price. But you know that a bad man's greed burns insatiably and can be cured only by contempt for money. My lord, I greet you and ask that the religion of devoted love and of our pact toward me be kept.
IV. Ennodius to Helisea.

What I had long and eagerly sought has come about. Favours are granted after long waiting so that they may carry their full charm. Kinship lives on in whatever part of the earth we are. The chain of blood is not broken when bodies are separated. Across distant regions love suffers no loss, since among those who live apart affection takes the place of presence. I give thanks to almighty God, who has made you mindful of family duty and led you to remember your lineage on a religious occasion. God is my witness: after the lady Cynegia told me of the merit of your way of life, I longed with special ardour to see you, if only a welcome opportunity had made my wishes possible. My lady, as I offer you my respectful greeting, I pledge my devoted service in the matter set out in your letter, for as much is given to the soul as is shown to holy endeavours. I tell you truly that I never liked the man you detest, and I was afraid that your consent too might lean toward the advancement of that dreadful man. May God help us, so that no one who was never shaped on the anvil of good training may attain ecclesiastical rank.
V. ENNODIUS TO AVITUS.

I would wish this business drawn out, if I were not burdening your purpose, for through it I have earned frequent letters from one who loves me. While you send pages about business, you also serve affection. But among the wise, and those who know each other's minds, brief conversations are enough. I do not know how to be smooth in promises, or how to flatter with a painted face those to whom I owe my soul. You need only press on with what you have begun and, obeying heaven's commands, turn the bad man you speak of away from his ambitions. It is fitting for me to show more by deeds than to promise in words, for what I give I expect without hesitation to receive back. My lord, as I send you my fullest greeting, I ask you to thank the lady Helisea, our common mother, on my behalf, for she was kind enough to show the bonds of kinship in her letter
VI. ENNODIUS TO ABBOT LEONTIUS.

The heavenly kindness shown to me has grown beyond anything I deserve, for I who am worthy of punishment rejoice at having gained the rewards of the just. Despair, the mother of peril, drives sinners headlong to extremes, and it does so in vain. Let those caught in the gravest error be restored to firm hope by my example. I do not know by what deed or what innocence of mine the fruit of your letters came to me, filling a soul rich in sin with the honey of heavenly good. Perhaps the reason is this: He who took our wounds upon himself and suffered for us reverses the terms of desert. He chastises with gifts those he sees deserving of the scourge, and, turning things about, he improves the souls of the guilty through shame while filling them with good fortune. So it is by the condescension of a heavenly mystery that I have drawn forth the fruits of your conversation. He who made you anxious for my bodily health is the same who, through spiritual physicians, compels the care of my soul to return to the state of health granted to it. With religious solicitude you inquire into the condition of my limbs. Their state neglects the soul's share and is weighed down by the whole dominion of this world. Bring it about by prayer that I become such as your kind words claim I am, for the brightness of your calling knows no pretence, and when it proclaims someone good it announces ahead of time an innocence soon to come. To my brothers and fellow servants whom you sent, I did not refuse whatever comfort I could give, though I was equal to it more in wish than in fact. It remains for you to accept my respects and, together with the whole community over which you preside, bound as one by the mercy of almighty God, to persist in prayer to God for my lowliness. My own actions give me no confidence of good things, so may your intercession win them for me.
VII. ENNODIUS TO EUPREPIA.

You have often seen how thin my talent is, yet with a hasty command you chose to put to the test the poverty of a tongue whose quality was proved long ago. But I do not refuse to obey one who loves me, so that, if eloquence lacks merit, the grace of obedience may come to its aid. The kinds of heavenly gifts are many, though they come from a single author. Perfection commends one person; another wins favour because he is willing to obey without any delay. I composed the epitaph of my lady Cynegia at unpolished speed, with scarcely an hour to work on it. Consider the constraint: I had to set forth a woman of such great merits in hurried leaps of words. May her venerable soul pardon my barrenness, accepting the writer's cloudless devotion in place of a fine figure of speech. You, my lady, embrace this letter in place of my presence, and pray that her spirit may in no way be offended by my rough tribute.
EPITAPH.
Neither her sex nor the tomb does her harm, nor the Sisters' final threads
that they thin out with a treacherous thumb:
joined to God, this woman lives on after death through her deeds,
bearing a man's achievements along a woman's path.
Blood, honour, spirit, uprightness, a steadfast countenance
have overcome destruction with such great worth.
By her conduct she upheld the lineage of great parents,
she whose noble mind was the proof of her descent.
She trained her children to keep a serene life,
teaching them by example always to love God.
VIII. ENNODIUS TO PETER.

After the venerable justice of the prince tested the character of your Greatness and gave you the first bud of office as a harvest for your virtues, you gave your tongue a holiday and fostered an irreverent silence. In this you have sinned both against your eloquence and against my love. Eloquence grows, strengthened by its natural dignity, whenever it serves to announce good fortune. A richer eloquence serves the increase of honours, and the learned proclaim their promotions with speech equal to their success. See how this unlovely silence has robbed you of the delight of speaking and begrudged me the fulfilment of my joy. Perhaps you will reply: “You could blame me, my friend, for your ignorance, if rumour, entrusted to random messengers, had kept from you any news of my high office.” But I cannot bear to learn of the elevation of those dear to me by rumour, or to gather the evidence of my joy from the fickleness of report. I knew what hope of close attachment the sincere assurance of a learned man had given me long ago. I believed it would be vain to commit my mind to fair breezes in any matter about which you had not bidden me be glad. I thought that rumour, though built with the oarage of a thousand wings, could be outrun by the feet of your letter, so that no one else might snatch the fruit from you by bringing the longed-for good news to one who loves you. Now, my lord, as you receive the honour of my greeting and know the causes of my pain, do not deny me a speedy remedy. As I presume, neither faithfulness in affection nor speech polished to perfection ever fails you when you speak. Yet, not content to displease in only one kind of writing, I have added a poem. After the feasts of the Antenorean waters, the baths of Aponus punish them by forcing the flesh into narrow bounds, as water pares away what the offspring of the waters have swollen. So I too, who have never touched the streams of Helicon, may join in as a new poet. Accept, then, poems that will raise a laugh, and, content that you alone have recognized your [?], shield me from public severity. If anything happens to please, your verdict is enough for me. If anything deserves a bite, I count whatever you learn of a friend's faults as a secret. You will also pardon me because, oppressed by pain in my eyes, I may have composed limping verses. The footsteps of verse cannot be firm when they lack the service of sight. Read, then, about the hot springs you are visiting.

The land rises, resting on a sloping swell,
propped on a gently lifted brow.
It lifts no proud head toward any summits,
nor does it seek the depths like low-pressed valleys.
Here smoking Aponus flows on every side from wide veins,
and a peaceful fire breathes out in mingled waters.
The water keeps the hearths alight; the flame does not drink up the stream;
so the sacred spring crackles from the pyre poured into it.
Here a drunken heat offers healing to all,
drying bodies with vapour-laden dew.
Here the pyre surges with floods, the water with sparks;
they live by a friendship of mutual death.
Lest he perish, Vulcan plunges into those nymphs:
a warring concord has broken nature's treaties.
IX. ENNODIUS TO FAUSTUS.

May God prosper honourable desires. May good studies not be denied a happy beginning. May noble aims grow strong with the fruits of success. Whoever aspires to liberal studies with heaven's favour has handed honour a hostage for his vows. Love of the good arts scorns a savage nature, and only those trained in good character strive for the ornaments of eloquence. Spurred by these goads, our Parthenius, my sister's son, hastens to visit Rome, the natural home of learning, and I have promised him the fatherly support of your Greatness. The suppliant gives your Highness a certain grace when we beg in prayer for what custom requires anyway. It is as if someone believed he earned the sunrise or the course of a river by prayer. There is no favour where the usual order is kept, for what binds everyone simply follows custom. Yet I come to you expecting to receive something beyond that course, from which you never depart. I have sent a person by whom the standing of my merits may be judged. Others, perhaps, may be helped by a recommendation they have not earned, but for one's kin, whatever we cannot surpass is too little. My lord, I offer you the service of my greeting and have described the bearer and his business in a few words. It remains for me to learn what the person, the cause and our kinship deserve.
X. ENNODIUS TO POPE SYMMACHUS.

While your Crown's care governs the apostolic see and you rule the summit of heavenly dominion, what is held as promised to my services smiles on the advancement of my kin. One who has served a steadfast man faithfully holds a hope without flaw. A giver's splendour is great whenever what one person has earned is repaid to many. Those through whom a family receives what one individual has laid up are following the ordinances of heaven. So it was that punishment did not touch the sins of the people of Israel for David's sake. Their forefather's integrity helped the nation, and one man's faith either rescued the people from error or aided them in grace. With this confidence in his heart, then, Parthenius, the bearer of this letter and my sister's son, has been sent to your Crown. Concern for a liberal education has driven him to seek out Rome. The study of letters is holy, for in it vices are unlearned before skill increases. By this path grey-haired counsel usually comes to boyish years, since training can supply what youth shrinks from. Cherish him, then, whose reasons for coming you have learned now that his kinship has been disclosed. You hold a hostage in whom the measure of my merits with you may be plainly seen. My lord, as above, I repay the reverence of my greeting with devoted service. I beg that the bearer of this letter, your servant, may by happy fortune be received among you under the name of a stranger, for whatever is granted to my prayers adorns your office beyond its own endowments.
XI. ENNODIUS TO LUMINOSUS.

Let others see to the matter, those before whom a young man stirred by concern for a liberal education must be supported with many words. A common cause has won him you as patrons. You receive strangers as one who knows what that is, and you encourage those who must be taught as one who has been taught. Those who have known hardship often lend a hand, and you invite those who falter toward the palm of eloquence with festive speech. A man who has risen from stranger to man of power, and from beginner to master, encourages by his example. Both apply to Parthenius, my sister's son. As he goes to Rome for the venerable disciplines, he needs nothing more than to see you in place of iron spurs. If he is not at odds with human nature, he will keep your Sublimity before his eyes and be stirred to virtue by deeds rather than by admonitions. Ambition for praise teaches toil, especially when it abounds in one you remember was once in a similar position. But if I am dear to you, show yourself [?] a father to the young man I have named. Then our mutual love may rejoice in this exchange of services, and whatever labour I once spent on your Greatness may be repaid to me through another. My lord, as above, paying the respects of my greeting, I thought it was recommendation enough if you knew who the bearer was. Someone who doubts he will obtain what he asks uses long prayers, and asking at length is proof that one deserves nothing. Far be it from your character to lose the charm of kindness by drawing out in long supplication one who ought to be relieved by a swift result.
XII. ENNODIUS TO FAUSTUS THE YOUNGER.

First I give thanks to God, who has wiped away the clouds over my eyes that an inexplicable pain had produced. I rightly credit his kindness to him, for he gave me my sight and has given it back. Only now, after countless days, am I breathing again, heartened by confidence in my recovery. This also has to do with the long absence of your Highness: one whose good spirit had left his side was bound to see nothing. But he who took away the mists from my body has the power to change sadness into fair weather. Having spoken of my trouble, I return to the business that forced me to write. You will love the bearer, I hope, for his reason for coming commends him. Parthenius, my sister's son, wishes to show himself well-born through the disciplines of liberal study. Unless I am mistaken, he hopes to be acknowledged as one of your own. May your Greatness, then, which holds fast to the past, is mindful of the present and is prudent about the future, receive the bearer on my recommendation. Through seeing you he will be happier than the one who writes; do not let him feel the hardships of living abroad. My lord, rendering the service I owe, I ask that through this opportunity at least, since Parthenius will be able to send letters from there once he has received them, the conversation I long for may be multiplied.
XIII. ENNODIUS TO HORMISDAS.

We know that the sacred vows of the religious calling are set apart from the sin-bound multitude by innocence and faith, and that the titles of a venerable office distinguish character rather than bodies. Who would look for a good conscience among men if worldly compulsion must be applied to the decisions of bishops, and if the promises of priests can be secured only by wary safeguards? He never had constancy of heart who was not free to act otherwise than he had promised. Worldly life is held in check by fear of the laws, but it befits God's servants to do what is good out of love, not fear. Some time ago, when fear pressed upon us and we hung in doubt on the clemency of the pious king, uncertain how our merits would be judged, we handed over our camels, [?] in number, to be given to the lord pope. We did so through your Reverence on this condition: if we did not need the animals themselves, a fair price would be sent for them. Your Holiness knows very well that, while we could, we supported the interests of the holy Roman church through your mediation. Now, in return, make a kindness out of what is simply just. With our greeting already given, we also ask you to tell us what you have decided on this point. We believe that neither the aforesaid bishop of the apostolic see nor you, who act as mediators, intend anything other than what undoubtedly accords with both your calling and justice.
XIV. ENNODIUS TO SERVILIO.

Pupils are confident of their accomplishment whenever they look forward to their teachers' presence. When a pupil invites his teacher to enjoy his own handiwork, it plainly shows that he has hope in his learning. Bright are the minds driven by longing for their instructors, and those who have learned with good fortune seek out their mentor. So I, possessed by affection for your Holiness, though I dare not boast of my skill, still look forward to seeing my teacher's face. I do not want you to think that you entrusted the seed of the Church to an unworthy son. My memory may not be able to rise to a hundredfold harvest, but it knows how to return the seed to the sower multiplied. Come, then, so that you may be present and look over your crop like a good farmer. May God keep envy far away! Under your ploughshares the plant of the Church's fruitfulness has grown so strong that no blast of a raging storm can overturn it. I do not wish to burden your Holiness's judgement with praise in advance; you will examine for yourself what the evidence of learning declares. With my greeting given, it remains for you to hasten now to your joys, for divine favours always come by steps, and to those on whom they bestow good things they promise better.
XV. ENNODIUS TO SENARIUS.

Prayer poured out before God is never stripped of its hoped-for result, for with him tears win gladness and grief passes into joy. Divine help has come to my desires and, with mercy as its guide, has called you back from the far-off ends of the nations, you who are the greater part of my soul. Truly I cannot spread this letter out into many words, hindered as I am by tears that joys heaped high have brought forth. My lord, do not let the fullness of heaven's gift be lost to my lowliness. Let us both have one lodging, and let no worry arise from narrow walls, since a single heart offers our souls a dwelling large enough.
XVI. ENNODIUS TO PAMFRONIUS.

The commands of joy are great. Gladness knows no restraint and longs to burst out into speech. The day I longed for has come. Your Greatness has received that splendour which I asked for, never on the strength of my merits but always from heaven's goodness. High office has been restored to your lineage and your character, and through it the integrity of a faithful conscience need not fear to come into the light. Good God, guard what you have granted, increase with success what you have given, and for your servant make the highest rank only the first step. I anticipate in hope the things I pray for, since gifts bestowed by heaven do not linger at the threshold. One always rises step by step to the summit when heaven's favour provides the beginning. In human life, even among those who keep their conduct unsoiled by any cloud, who could rejoice that so much befell him in a single day? You have entered upon the first auspices of honours, and my sweet Senarius has been restored from the farthest parts of the earth. Only a brief span of hours lay between your birth into the palace and his return. I speak the truth, and, secure in God's mercy, I promise myself that heaven is willing to grant protection to my frailty. What has been granted to you is pledged to me as well. My lord, as you receive the respects of my greeting, I ask that, if you have any regard for my love, you do not fail to entreat Senarius, the lord of my soul, with all your power to stay with me. If you do not obtain this, you will have taken much from the heap of my joy.
XVII. ENNODIUS TO AVIENUS.

Your Greatness does well. In paying due regard to your birth and character, you join correction to error without delay, and what you wisely recognize as a fault you turn aside before anyone else points it out. Who would believe that a man so swift to correct himself has done wrong at all? He can hardly be called a follower of excess who raises his hand to block faults as they creep in. My lord, with your kindness as my guide, this is my answer to what you were good enough to write. For the rest, the weight of my affairs has made me humbler than my calling, and in my misery I have scarcely remained able to answer letters. My lord, presenting the respects of my greeting, I pray God to reward your Highness for the consideration with which you do not despise a lowly man.
XVIII. ENNODIUS TO FAUSTUS.

A man intent on happy things can hardly foresee adversity. If his mind glimpses ahead of time anything harsh in the future, he rejects it as an ill omen. He shudders at the very thought of troubles, lest bitter things should mix themselves in at the wrong time. I used to think that Ravenna, now so unlovely, was no distance away while it was full of my treasures. No spring drew me so when I was thirsty, no breeze when I was sweltering, no rest when I was weary, as she drew me to herself. But now I think Rome itself has been moved farther off because of the burden of my sins. Where is that frequency of letters which once seemed too rare? Where are the frequent visits? Where are all the comforts of affection? I speak truly for my own part: I loathe this life, which not even those in distress hate. Perhaps your Highness will say that what you desired has come to you by heaven's dispensation. But happiness is not complete when one of your own is afflicted with the miseries of a hard separation. Believe me before God, what I lament is not feigned, and neither a letter's elegance nor the narrow bounds of speech can unfold the tragedy of my heart. Christ, judge of all things, come to the aid of my need, so that human frailty, unequal to the burden of boundless grief, may not be crushed and give way. My lord, paying the service of my greeting, I ask you to keep up your care for me in letters, so that by this remedy at least my mind, caught amid these troubles, may breathe again.
XIX. ENNODIUS TO PARTHENIUS.

I am not surprised that you refrain from writing, for one who has stored up little brings forth nothing. Do you think that this way the substance of your progress stays hidden? Silence betrays a lack of skill, and unpolished conversation reveals childishness. Before, at least, you were not without grace, and you knew what affection and a loving person's concern required. You have become ignorant of good things since we sent you away to obtain what are thought the highest. For the rest, farewell. Take to heart the words of one who advises you, and make your improvement known by writing diligently.
XX. ENNODIUS TO AVITUS.

When affection looks for its own remedies and longs to have the fever of anxiety relieved by the medicine of conversation, the mind is set ablaze by the very help it receives: from the very thing that is thought to quench it, the fire of love rises doubled. Often, while I was searching for a supply of letter-carriers, I happened to grow sick from the very thing I expected to do me good. See, my longings are now healed by one who has hurried to you for the sake of his own family: what he undertook for his own need becomes a help to someone else's. I shall see what my recommendation may achieve for Boniface; meanwhile, what he obtained from me by long entreaties serves my own eagerness. His mind, a witness to his blood, shows that he was born of good family. He states that his brother is a captive in the neighbourhood of the city of Aquileia, and he begs that you help him. The custom of your holy house is widely known: you have already given such a life of good deeds as a hostage that anyone weighed down by calamity may claim help from it as if it were a debt. My lord, as you receive the homage of a full greeting, be prevailed upon to do what you are accustomed to do of your own accord, so that one who is a suppliant to your house need not be a suppliant to anyone else.
XXI. ENNODIUS TO AVITUS.

Your Magnificence asks me so pleadingly to become a supporter of your good name, as though I were still freshly forged on the anvil of friendship, or as though a man who changes his purpose of love on any occasion whatever did not cheat his own nature. Let fickle judgement about one who loves be far from Christian conduct: whoever has dedicated the service of his mouth to praises is not free to abandon what he has begun, lest he spoil the honey of his earlier praise by the cheapness of what follows. Let others look to it who think it noble to chase novelty: as I am slow to choose friends, so I persevere in them unchangeably. I serve my own interest whenever I raise your reputation to the stars, because among those to whom we are unknown our character is judged by our companions. I confess truly that I poured out the splendour of your conscience abundantly, in place of rumour: before Your Highness arrived, it became known in Liguria through the service of my speech how great you are. Thanks be to God, who made the general opinion agree with mine. Would that poverty of eloquence did not humble me! My prayers hold more of your merits than my tongue can utter in praise; lacking eloquence though I am, amid whatever clamour I have not kept silent about whatever could befit your glory. The light of your character has become the proof of my judgement. May God forbid that frailty, the enemy of illustrious character, should ever steal my testimony away. In what you have so richly woven in yourself there is no cause of offence that I could recall; and even if one had arisen through my own deserts, it would be laid to sleep by the memory of past kindnesses. For the rest, farewell, my lord; follow my journey with the kindness of your prayers, and make up for the loss of my absence by remembering our love.
XXII. ENNODIUS TO VENANTIUS.

If nearness of blood invites minds to love, then, obeying the commands of devoted affection, I am glad to have sent my words ahead and, by beginning the correspondence, to have opened the way to conversations we should embrace. For a long time indeed I was worn down by vain expectation and sent no letter while I waited for one; but affection dug its spurs into my mind and made it come first to the task of writing. If I judge rightly, I have the privilege of the one who loves more, since I speak even after your long and studied silence, and my own silence I may put down to modesty. Now, however, lest the composition of a letter overstep its limit and disfigure its author, I pay the service of greeting and, if I deserve it, come forward to be won into your favour, since the loftiness of the great is doubled by fellowship, and kindness shown to inferiors carries a torch before even the most eminent.
XXIII. ENNODIUS TO CONSTANTIUS.

If it were permitted to contend with Your Magnificence on equal terms, if the honours, age and merit that have carried a torch before you did not drive me into the shade, I would rather be the one rightly to blame Your Highness for refraining from letters, since after you set out for the city of Rome you have not relieved me with any fruit of remembrance. But see, by the providence of things, how cautious the management of elders is, and how full of contrived words: innocence is forestalled by complaints and, lest it bring its grievance into the light, it is accused; it is made the defendant so that it may not bring the charge. So is this what you promised me when you left? Was it with this assurance that you kissed me and raised me up, that I should believe you would forget me? Or are letters given us for any other purpose than to reveal the secrets of the heart by the key of the mouth? But I refrain from a long letter, lest a prolonged conversation breed greater resentment. I return to the duty of greeting, asking that you pour out prayers for me before the apostles of God, so that by their favours the foulness of our mortal straits may be overcome and the mind, serene, may rejoice on the pure path of the heavenly commandments.
XXIIII. ENNODIUS TO LACONIUS.

Heaven's dispensation has granted fulfilment to good desires, and by renewing brotherly affection on the occasion of a conversation about business, it has made what was thought merely necessary into something to be wished for. Thus heavenly care ordered a suitor not wholly a stranger to our blood to approach my niece, so that, while the need for consultation pressed, nourishment might be given to holy love. I confess I could hardly bear the long pursuit of a deliberate silence, but, as a gentler interpreter, I thought that what was withheld from affection should be put down to timidity. Thanks be to God, who has brought Your Fraternity back to the use of the pen and to friendship. Know without any doubt, however, that by the divine laws kinship of the degree set out in the memorandum is permitted to be joined in marriage. But I am at once sending my men to the city of Rome to obtain a reply on this point from the venerable pope, so that the authority of a higher ruling may strengthen your mind. My lord, as you receive, as above, a most full greeting, know also that our holy common father is of the same opinion; if divine favour allows, I will send you his letter through my man, together with the writings of the Apostolic See.
XXV. ENNODIUS TO AVITUS.

How often other people's sins weigh us down, and what does not arise from us is charged to our account as a fault! From my own case I have learned that the faith of the ancients does not perish, since the hoary sayings of the poets are renewed by fresh events. I think it was said of me: "He fell, unhappy, by another's wound." This whole affair concerns the son of Sabinus, a man of revered memory, who until now has been held back by the obstacles of illness and so broke what had been agreed through no fault of his own. I confess that the forceful charge of Your Magnificence had almost made my mind guilty, and I believed the fault to be my own, though my conscience did not hold it. See, as soon as he was restored to good health, he travelled to Milan in the greatest haste. The rest I did not think needed to be pleaded before you, because whoever commends justice to great men seems to imply that they have forgotten fairness. My lord, I present the gift of a most full greeting, and for the rest I ask that the state of your favour towards me, though it is already most full, may yet be compelled to receive increase.
XXVI. ENNODIUS TO AGAPITUS.

Sins stand in the way of desires, and so that offenders may learn the state of their deserts, the things they long for are snatched away from the very edge of their lips. Things offered hurt more sharply when they are lost: thirst is greater when a taste of water sharpens it. Benefits refused at the outset do not burn the memory; but who could calmly bear to lose a sweetness set before his eyes? Yet these things are rightly referred to the providence above, by which the heavenly dispensation of mystery sets its hand against human arrangements precisely in order to grant the fulfilment of prayers. Your holy father had promised that he would gladly obey Your Magnificence's command about my coming to you, but plans that arose later carried his mind in another direction, for the benefit, as he says, of the church, as his letter sent to you has explained. He awaits, however, a second conversation with Your Magnificence about the business in question, so that it may be shown more clearly that I am needed for the benefit of your brother Faustus the patrician, to whose favour he thinks himself free to refuse nothing. For the rest, receiving the humble homage of my service, I pray that the Maker of heaven, who has deigned to fill Your Highness with care for my littleness, may himself arrange through you what is to follow.
XXVII. ENNODIUS TO EUGENES.

The tireless pursuit of a deliberate silence troubles me beyond measure, and although my mind is firmly at anchor, I am saddened by the withholding of speech, which reveals the secret of the heart in living images by the key of the mouth. I do allow that love is sometimes feigned in the sending of letters, yet I never believe that those who love refrain from this service. Perhaps Your Magnificence will reply that the care of public business has left no room for private letters. But the situation was the same in former times, when Your Highness provided frequent conversation and was not so burdened by duty at court as to lose the memory of the love you had promised. What secret whisperer has mixed poison with the honeycomb, mud with the springs? Or have you perhaps now brought to judgement what had been won from you by stealth through affection? But I do not delay to keep you busy with letters, so that, since the spurs of your promised favour have ceased, you may at least be provoked by the fruit of my chatter to return to your old habit. My lord, paying the homage of greeting with full humility, I let you know that I am eager to present myself before your eyes, if indeed, having weighed the matters which I do not doubt are dear to you, you write back that it should be done.
BOOK SIX
I. ENNODIUS TO PARTHENIUS.

If I did not love you desperately, and if the solidity of devoted love did not stand on an unchanging root, I might, provoked by the pain of your insults—whether when you are angry like a boy or when you plead arrogantly—be moved to [?]; for I find nothing prouder than contrived humility. I prefer insults to the flatteries of a painted face: feigned sweetness outdoes bitterness. There is no need for entreaties, if you understand what chain binds you. Let those who are free to disobey ask pardon for their excesses. The splendour of heavenly judgement has so assigned servants to us that wherever the mind turns, their necessity must bend that way. It is the one who could refuse a strict command if he wished who waits for clemency. The power given me by God will scarcely let me stray far from this order. You should rather hope that a just consideration of your deserts does not spoil the mildness you proclaim in me, and that a multitude of faults does not cheapen the path of kindness. Although, unless I am mistaken, punishment is a merciful companion to one who goes astray, and no patience is better than that which does not open the door to vices, yet let my indignation be far from you, because your wrongdoing will be chastised not by pent-up resentment kept behind a deceptive show of favour, but by the rod. Now there is only one way you will manage to bring to a scar the wounds dealt by your intemperate words: if learning shows you to be a gentleman through the heights of liberal study. You will not obtain pardon unless skill speaks for you: I will change the law of leniency for which I am known and keep up severity towards the idle for ever. For the rest, I pray God that you may be well and, attended by heavenly favour, increase the hope you have given by your verses.
II. ENNODIUS TO FAUSTUS.

The height of joy is the opportunity offered by a letter-carrier who, as servant of affection, through his own needs serves the desires of others. Honesty commends this man, and a modesty foreign to the merchant's trade recommends him. Add to this that his acquaintance with Your Highness has strengthened confidence in his integrity, for it was through his coming that I was filled with the fruits of your venerable writing. Bound by the law of duty, therefore, I return the deposit, and him whom I received in Liguria as well as my modest means allowed I send on, with a letter to accompany him, to your most powerful patronage. For the rest, I offer Your Reverence whatever the humility of devotion possesses, entreating that I may now earn your letters, if only through the constancy of mine.
III. ENNODIUS TO EUPREPIA.

The course of all things consists in the obedience of the body and the command of the soul: the one is ennobled by its kinship with heaven, the other is brought low by its earthly abjectness.
