Nor is what has been taken from the lowest things free not to follow wherever the mind, bestowed by God as its parent, has turned; nor may a soldier raise a hand against the decrees of his emperor. Hence Crispus asserted that one part of us we share with the gods, the other with the beasts. By the logic of this secret we travel abroad with those who are absent, and while our own limbs are healthy we burn with the fevers of those we love; by these bonds we are separated by no intervening distance, and though divided in our dwellings, we come together as one in our affections. You know, venerable sister, you who surpass every sweetness for me, what occasion called for this preface. Now I will meet you with an open face and without reserve. I could hardly bear the endearments you had sent before; after my admonition you poured double honey into your letters, enough to shake all the secrets of my heart and carry my captive soul, leaving the seat of the body, over into longing for you. How I fear that affection may again be cast back into uncertainty, and that when my whole mind has let out the sails of love, the anchorage may be withdrawn and it may suffer shipwreck! You know that my mind is ignorant of pretence and could not adopt the detestable polite games of lovers. Your sex and nature, on the other hand, promise something different, as the most wise Solomon says: "The soul that is full scorns the honeycomb." He who is the witness and judge of my words knows that I have resolved—unless perhaps I am deceived by a treacherous taste of favour, and you withdraw the cup once offered to one thirsting for the love he has tasted—to fulfil not the image but the very reality of a spiritual marriage, and, so long as one will and one refusal hold between us, to display it before the eyes and minds of all, whether to spur the good to imitation or to vex the wicked. Only do you, with God as mediator, promise that a firm and unchanging constancy will be kept against every assault born of envy. Farewell, then, my lady, and be content with a brief admonition about the greatest matters, since neither does the form of a letter allow more nor does reason allow inner matters to be committed to paper. If you answer what has been set out here with desire and faith, pledge it by the testimony of your own writing.
IIII. ENNODIUS TO FAUSTUS.

I have not written to burden you with the bitter news of my illness, but to appeal to your solicitude, so that it may persevere in prayer. The labour laid upon my eyes before my health was firmly restored has done them harm: all light left me when you did. It is enough to have let you know what I suffer. It is your part to demand my recovery from God, whom you appease by your prayers, and to help me, who open the doors of correspondence, with frequent conversation. My lord, I ask God to cause you to send me news that I will be glad to learn.
V. ENNODIUS TO AURELIANUS.

My confidence has not been stripped of the successes it foresaw. He is strong in affection whom I, with just judgement, assured my mind would remember our love. Thanks be to you, heavenly dispensation, who grant human affairs the fruit of prosperity from the occasion of adversity and do not let sorrows remain as they are. I do not know what hostile malice has plucked from the abundance of Your Magnificence's patrimony; yet on this account you have won a very rich favour with our most invincible lord. A loss of property is good if through the expense one finds acquaintance with an illustrious prince; a decrease of means is not to be feared if through it one gains the love of the supreme lord, which surpasses all riches. Add to this that the loss itself, since it became the mother of gain and the road to honours, could not keep the substance of the humiliation inflicted. What the enemy snatched away has been so restored that you still await a heap of joys. Further things remain to be hoped for, even though Your Highness has already attained the greatest. With these benefits conferred by heaven, let us join the blessings of our acquaintance and fellowship. When would I have had the chance to come to know so great a man, except through the events I have mentioned? But may heaven increase what it grants, and may divine care bring us to what our desires reach out for. For the rest, farewell, my lord, and cherish one who loves you with frequent letters, for if the form of a letter did not keep to the limit prescribed by its law, my joy would pour me out into many words.
VI. ENNODIUS TO BOETHIUS.

It would indeed have been fitting to answer Your Magnificence's single letter simply, and that one who was indebted once should not double the correspondence; but I have been led to this by caution, not ignorance. For of the two letters, one pays the debt and the other is offered to affection. Believe me, I thought it wrong not to repay with interest what your venerable mind first bestowed. The kindnesses of love are sweeter when they come before any example, and the one who enters the path of friendship second has not as much strength or grace: in short, one who is shown the pattern in love cannot claim the credit for himself; yet it is shameless not to respond to love when a thing well begun displays virtue. I wrote this quickly because the carrier was in a hurry; hereafter I will pour out my words more freely and, with your merits before me, will not look at the leanness of my talent—provided you indulge my desires with frequent letters. My lord, paying the service of a most abundant greeting, I ask that conversations sent without interruption may show that you remember our kinship.
VII. ENNODIUS TO AVIENUS.

For a long time now, held in suspense by sincere longing, I have fed only on the service of letters: for while I address Your Magnificence, I feel I am not deprived of the sight I long for. But the mind of the afflicted grows sick on its own remedies, and what serves as food for love torments all the more the one who goes hungry for love's fruit. Truly, my lord—so may God keep you safe, my light—if either the strength of my body or my lord's haste had allowed it, I would have made for Ravenna with all the force of my resolve. But if God wills, and my lord your father and my lady your mother are spared, I will come after Easter with heaven's help, so that, having seen you, I may revive to the hope of life. My lord, sending a most abundant greeting, I pray that you see to it that all the saints pray for me most earnestly.
VIII. ENNODIUS TO SENARIUS.

Although, because of my sins, even the comfort of your letters is withdrawn from me, I nevertheless, mindful of the debt by which you, as men mindful of God, have bound me through your kindness, do not omit to write, hoping, lord Senarius, that you will always keep your eyes on God, whom you have considered in me, and will often grant me the gift of your letters. My lord, I greet you warmly with my customary reverence, and I implore you not to cease asking God, in all the basilicas of the saints, on behalf of my affliction.
VIIII. ENNODIUS TO FAUSTUS.

Although the innocence of his office stands beside the bishop as his companion and protector, and one who by his profession has risen above humanity has no need of human support, yet almighty God knows that I have written this letter at the command of the holy bishop who bears it. For I resisted for a long time, lest it seem arrogant for a minister to speak up for a prelate, and for someone scarcely middling to vouch for so eminent a man before a most holy conscience. But perfect obedience means refusing nothing a superior demands. And therefore, having first offered the homage of due
greeting, I pray that you bring help to comfort a man weighed down by many assaults, so that, doing a deed of singular goodness, you do not allow a blameless bishop to lie under prolonged sorrow.
X. ENNODIUS TO FAUSTUS.

May God, who has planted in your mind the love of good works, himself protect you, his obedient servant, in great happiness and to a long age; for although the innocence you cherish keeps unceasing watch on your behalf, those bound by your kindnesses cannot hold back the prayers they owe God for you, since even God, made flesh, abhorred the failure to give thanks for favours received. Would that I were able to render as much in words for your deeds as I feel I owe! Yet to these I do not fail to add suggestions that may bring you further reward: that you order the deed you drew up in the case of Laurentius, the registrar of Como, to be sent to me completed; and that, for that blind woman whom Martin, the lessee from Monza, is oppressing, you obtain letters from the count of the patrimony ordering him to restore without delay the slave he took from her, because, with rustic insolence, he scorns to carry out what he has just now received in his instructions.
XI. ENNODIUS TO AVIENUS.

Now that our common lord has left the city of Milan, the only comfort left to me is the solace of letters, because while my words are directed to you, some image of your presence soothes my longing. I ask you too, my lords, to do this often, bearing in mind that your absence can be endured only through such constancy. Let the most fortunate enjoy the presence they long for; for me, as I reflect on my sins, the care of letters will suffice. My lord, sending a most abundant greeting, I pray that you never cease to pour out prayers for me through the saints of God, and to give thanks to the Lord, whose blessings towards me are granted even beyond hope.
XII. TO LIBERIUS, EUGENES, AGAPITUS, SENARIUS AND ALBINUS.

Fuller pages are needed when the bearer's reliability is lame. With Stephen the deacon, who loves me and is devoted to you, a sparing conversation is enough: he passes over letters spread out into many words and prefers what is necessary to what is plentiful, while in the summary of a faithful confidence he does not hold back what must be reported. For the rest, I let you know that I am well, by God's favour, and I ask after the blessings of your prosperity. I pay you the full homage of greeting and pray that the unspoiled integrity of your regard may not leave my confidence exposed.
13. Ennodius to Avitus.

Another man's need makes me importunate, because I owe words on behalf of one who pleads. The law of my calling rejects stinginess in intercession, and it adds to the burden on my conscience if I turn a suppliant away. The son of Sabinus, of respected memory, came on the appointed day to await the judgement. But for practical reasons he was forced to go back to his little estate, because both the guarantor and the officer charged with carrying out the judgement failed to appear on the set day. I had sworn not to cheapen myself any further over this man's business, but the bearer pressed me to send messengers to him so that he might appear again, and I let you know that I have done so. Now, as I offer you the homage of my greeting, it lies in the power of your Eminence to show in this man's case what is deserved by the justice you cherish and by the confidence you have given.
14. Ennodius to Avitus.

I know that with you my silences cry out, and that nothing happens which is not grasped by some hidden interpretation. Yet I have not stopped writing, nor have I used any contrived cleverness to withdraw the son of Sabinus, a man of exalted memory, from judgement. He suffered violence on his little estate and is said to have been busy until now with the barbarians. Believe me, he will present himself at the hearing without anxiety and will come before your tribunal without any fear. My lord, as I offer the reverence of greeting, I pray that you will think my person worth supporting, in memory of the affection long since planted between us.
15. Ennodius to Faustus.

Providence on high arranges things well: while favours are being asked of me, my concern for you finds welcome letter-carriers. Far be it from me to deny others what I allow myself, or in squalid greed to hold back what brings relief to the giver. Simplicianus, the bearer of this letter, a young man of the highest birth, is setting out for Rome, the native seat of learning, and he believed it would be a singular advantage to him to come to the notice of your Eminence with a letter as his guide. I had no wish at all to deny him what he wanted, knowing that it is your habit to do what others do only when entreated. Now, my lord, as you receive the service of my greeting, see to it that the hardships of travel do not weigh on him. And through the frequent carriers now obtained, do not stop relieving me with frequent letters of your own.
16. Ennodius to Luminosus.

Conversations that love has found as a remedy for itself ought not to be about business, and the wages of devotion ought not to call us to necessary dealings. How sweet it would be if the duty of letters served concord alone and did not turn affection into the hunt for gain! But things have come to this: unless the old love between us, which began at the very threshold of life and through the growing strength of our progress brought the harvest of grace to the threshing floor, is now driven by the goad of this letter to rise up on my behalf, I shall be struck by a heavy barrenness of ill will and losses. Your Amplitude remembers what you discussed with him about the expenses my bishop had incurred at Ravenna for the benefit of the apostolic see, when I promised him repayment, and you had promised that their restitution would be swiftly carried out. But for my sins some mishap or other has stood in the way. Because of this the said bishop has turned his attention to me, so that he scarcely granted me a respite to send to the most sacred city. Now, after God, the matter rests with you, for you can rescue my person both from the pontiff's displeasure and from losses, so that my duty of good faith may not seem to have brought misfortune on me alone. My lord, as I pay you the gifts of greeting, I pray God to move your mind without delay to consider my interest. I could find nothing more to do than to send you a trustworthy bearer with a clear statement of the case.
17. Ennodius to Bishop Marcellinus.

The graciousness of the magnificent lord Stephanio, your son, brings me before your Beatitude to be read. Through his kindness love does not suffer the losses of distance, and what presence cannot do it makes up for by speech. With these words, then, I present the service due to your apostleship and ask you to support me with the aid of your prayers, so that, placed in your venerable mind, I may deserve to rejoice in every fruit of your graciousness; for I do not doubt that your Crown will answer my confidence.
18. Ennodius to Dominica.

Your Magnitude has done what it owes both to its holy character and to its blood, in not letting the memory of kinship languish in the torpor of silence. In whatever part of the world kinship lives, those bound together by its chain are not separated by regions. Believe me, holy love does not perish, nor does nature suffer any loss from the distances between us. For know that your son-in-law spends so much affection on me that no repayment could be enough in return. For the rest, my lady, as you receive the affection of a due greeting, I pray God that he may grant, for the good of our mutual happiness, an opportunity of seeing you, so that our pious longings may be relieved by the conversation we desire.
19. Ennodius to Faustus.

Since the chance of seeing you has slipped away from my longings, my mind turns back to letters. It is forced to ask for the help of pages it had renounced, and to feed and sustain a soul used to richer fare on what amounts to a trade in cheaper food. Oh, how heavy it is whenever a fleeting freedom carries a man who must obey various necessities over into a new way of life! Hard things are broken by persistence; habit cuts away much of a burden's weight; a lamentable condition leads on to hopes that will not last; lighter is the lot of one who is busy with constant cares. I am the more unhappy under the bundle of my sins in this, that I have tasted the flavour of good things. But more of this another time. What cannot find a remedy in human counsel must be left to God. Meanwhile, as I pay you the reverence of greeting, I have not failed to give you news of my return, and I hope to be relieved by an equally cheerful letter from you.
20. Ennodius to Faustus.

The flavour of good things goes unrecognized in prosperity. The quality of heaven-sent blessings is hardly perceived while we hold them; once they have gone, they grow sweet. We do not know the worth of what we long for while it lies in our hands. I truly confess that as long as Ravenna had you, I thought it an evil omen even to think of what I now suffer, and amid good fortune I did not, like a spiteful interpreter of my own happiness, sigh over what your absence might bring. Had I not been separated from you, I would not have had to recognize what I deserve, or to understand that what flatters one who follows sin is fleeting. But why does this letter go beyond the bounds of disciplined speech? May he whose command all things obey bring a remedy to these matters. For my part, to come to the reason pages were granted, I am well in body, and through this exchange, with God's help, I wait for news of your prosperity. Accept, then, my homage, and if a favourable outcome has come about in the matters you have learned are going on with me, tell me without hiding anything.
21. Ennodius to Faustus.

I seized on a household carrier as an opportunity to pay my humble respects. What you arranged for the efficient conduct of other business will serve my desires. I confess, I thought it hard to deny you letters now that I am nearer, when I could never refrain from conversing with you while I was far away. For, occupied with the watches at Ravenna, I seemed to myself to have touched your Magnitude with a kind of right hand of the mind. So I have extended this letter to relieve my longing, so that by reading I might make up for what was taken from living speech. Showing you, then, the honour of greeting, I ask you to relieve me with remedies of this kind whenever opportunity offers, for in them, by divine provision, absence has its only help. You know the cure for one who languishes with affection: it is for you not to deny healing to sick souls.
22. Ennodius to Eugenes.
Devotion is the cause of many letters. It is owing to your reverence that I do not refrain from writing. My voice, the witness of my joy,
does not fail, because I have joyfully received news of the state of your health. Farewell.
23. Ennodius to Parthenius.

With God's favour may the beginnings of your affection grow strong; may he through whom studies gain their strength be present to the desires we share. By the brilliance of your writing you have shown that you are already at home in a city friendly to liberal studies. At the very threshold you have put forward something that surpasses the eager hopes of your parents. I am not a harsh judge of your style, nor do I reject the slightness of the present, which holds the promise of what is to follow. Whenever we write on the earth with ploughshares, the mind is lifted by hope of the coming harvest. The lover of ploughing always discerns in the green blades the wealth of the ears to come, and the careful farmer, while the fruit trees are still white with blossom, already reckons up the multitude of their fruit. May adversity be gone and whatever sins bring forth depart! The flow of your little speech, though it does not yet hold steady in the brilliance of eloquence, has nonetheless shone with the flavour of the Latin vein. The language ran without discord, though it needs to be enriched by reading. But why should I pass judgement after so great a judge, to whose ears, as you indicated, the composition of your work was pleasing? It would be like a goose cackling after swans. Whoever has pleased him enters any examination without fear; eloquence that he has praised is strong enough to win favour even from enemies. Work, then, so that a happy outcome may crown what has begun well. Devote yourself unceasingly to the company of honourable men. Those who defile you by their fellowship you must flee like a cup of poison, out of the respect you owe to my warnings. Always report your progress by letter to one who longs to know it. For the rest, farewell, and with the help of every heavenly favour repay your family with the harvest of learning.
24. Ennodius to Archotamia.

The claim of affection, bound by the law of kinship, does not perish through long distances, nor is the chain of family that links souls broken by the separation of lands. Yet love feeds on seeing the one you love or addressing them in speech: the secrets of minds would be unknown were they not disclosed by tongues. Antiquity brought this into use so that what is shut up in hearts might not lie hidden. Even if I do not see Gaul with my eyes, which claims me wholly for itself on your account, I do not desert it in affection. But thanks are due to the bearer of this letter, who, on the occasion of his own need, did my longings the service they desired, at a time when my agitated mind lacked a carrier. Greeting you, then, with due service, I pray that the carrier may receive a return for his kindness, and that he who helped bring me joy may believe that through me his wishes have been fulfilled in turn.
25. Ennodius to Faustus.

Your Magnitude knows with what presumption the followers of liberal studies honour me, asking for letters of recommendation from me as though they were their due. The custom is that you confer benefits and I confer words, and that the greatness of what is granted surpasses the petitioner's desire. If I held back from these duties, then for all the genius of your gifts I would be failing to show the goodwill of a well-wisher. The bearer of this letter, Pertinax, will make himself known to you by the honourable witness of his birth, and in support of his lineage he will make good use of modesty. Through him I give you news of my health, as you wish, and I pray that he may reap a rich fruit of his confidence from the harvest of your graciousness. And whenever a welcome traveller is going my way, send me, to relieve me, letters such as you yourself receive as a solace of love.
26. Ennodius to Euprepia.

Silence is owed to necessity, but letters are owed to devotion. Fear demands that we refrain from letters, but sometimes it yields to affection. The mind of one who loves hardly gives way to any obstacles; it burns all the more to repay the wages of kindness when it is forbidden. There, having said first what cause kept me from these duties, I leave it to your conscience to judge what makes me dutiful. Having prayed to God, I tell you that I and our Lupicinus are in good health, and I hope to learn the same of you, as I have reported of myself. But I do not want you to weigh down your care with the burden of the child you have left behind. Believe my conscience: I owe him more out of devotion than you yourself could give him by nature. May heavenly blessings improve his talent! I tell you truly, now that you have gone further away, the care of both parents falls on me, a care we could have eagerly shared when we were together. My lady, as I give you the fullest greeting, I pray that you grant me as much love and as much support of prayer as you have found me to give in carrying out your wishes.
27. Ennodius to Senarius.

May rich recompense attend your conscience by the dispensation of heaven. May the Most High repay what he knows you have conferred on my littleness, you who have always been faithful to those who love you. To have found the devotion of your heart is to have found a sure harbour; such is your character that you outdo the hopes of your friends by the benefits you confer. I await a second reminder to set out on the journey you enjoined. Give my humility a lucky right hand and share your good fortune with me. My lord, as I present the homage of greeting, I ask you to let me know whether the lord of affairs will happily be staying at Ravenna, so that I may carry out your instructions without uncertainty.
28. Ennodius to Gudilevus.

Those to whom happiness and power are granted by God's ordering usually console the humble with the office of letters and share their prosperity by sending them pages. I waited a long time to be relieved by such services, but since you held back, I thought it necessary not to stay silent, so that, as the Gospel reading says, importunity might obtain what love does not demand. My lord, as I give you the fullest greeting, I ask you to cherish me, your old devotee, with the affection you once promised, and to let me know of your prosperity by sending me letters.
29. Ennodius to Faustus.

I had already safely entrusted the duty of carrying letters to Sabinus, an exalted man endowed with every integrity, who is hurrying to Rome, so that he might faithfully report what was to be made known by letter. Yet my anxiety required me to inform your Magnitude by a double notice, so that the bearer, made secure by the letter, may take up the beginning of his account. Let this foretaste in writing suffice; I return to the reason letters are sent. I report that I am well in body, and I pray God that he may restore the state of my soul through your prosperity.
30. Ennodius to Faustus.

My halting tongue cannot express the greatness of the grief that has come to me because you refrained from writing by the bearers of this letter when they were sent to Liguria. I do not believe you were unaware of their journey, and I recognized your Magnitude's presence from the nature of the request; for it is granted [?] that a negotiator be found by those who have been appointed [?]. Yet this holiday from letters burns me, a holiday which even when you were most busy you used to drive away to relieve my sorrow. Now I return to my prayers. Farewell, my lord, and reveal in many a conversation the heavenly grace that surrounds you. For your deeds have earned you the right, in a time of quiet, to rejoice in the harvest of innocence sown amid labours.
31. Ennodius to the Lord Pope.

The ever-watchful care of your Beatitude attends to its devoted servants wherever they may be, as though they stood before you, and, never resting, it both gives the support of grace to those who have known it and draws in outsiders. For many reap the fruit of watching another's labour, since a man learns to exert himself when he sees the rewards of sweat and faithfulness being paid before his eyes. Would that the result matched my wishes, and that I were granted to fulfil what I have learned to desire for the sake of religion! My lord, showing you the humility of my service, and content with few words on matters of the greatest weight, I leave it to the letter of the lord bishop, your brother, to make known what he thought about the embassy that was sent.
32. Ennodius to Avienus.

An exchange of letters between those who love each other is always delightful; long joys come from it even when Spartan brevity is used, and such services are a remedy for the absent and a welcome gift to the anxious. Yet a sick mind is tossed about over the welfare of those on whom it depends, and it breathes again only through this cure. When someone who is shaken by no uncertainty denies that cure to the anxious, he reveals that he is not held by affection. For a long time the letters your Magnitude sent fed my mind and provided nourishment fit for cheerfulness. Now their absence brings not sadness but ruin. What once served affection could have given help to my health; the duty of love has been forsworn when words that would benefit my health are refused. You see what your silences have done; remedy them by amendment. For if forgetfulness of me does not rule in you, they can be changed by writing. My lord, as I return a most generous greeting, I pray God that the dispensation of heavenly favour may come to meet my fevers and move you, as a solace for my griefs, to send me news that will be a delight to hear.
33. Ennodius to Hormisdas and Dioscorus.

I know that a religious conscience counts it a great gain when an opportunity arises to do a service, above all to those it remembers to have been devoted. So, although reverence for you is the first reason for sending this letter, and the statement of my own interest ought to come second to affection, yet an anxious mind often puts necessity before affection. Your Fraternity remembers that the lord pope promised restitution of the expense my bishop had incurred at Ravenna for his benefit, on my guarantee. But it has come about that my bishop scarcely gave me respite to send to you, and he declares that he must be repaid out of my own property. Now, since the sum demanded is not large, and it would be the greatest kindness to rescue me from his displeasure, which seems justified, arrange what the recompense of heaven will repay you for. My lords, as I return a most abundant greeting, I ask God to inspire your minds with what may relieve me. For my part I have done what I could: with a declaration of my grief set out in this letter, I have sent a most faithful bearer to receive what is to be brought to us, without any reduction.
34. Ennodius to Faustus Albus.

By a long silence your Magnitude has shown that you have forgotten me, and in refraining from the duty of letters you have cast aside the memory of your servant. Yet the providence of heaven does not allow your prosperity to be hidden from my longing, and by various signs it reveals the success I wished for you. Now, however, my devotion has brought my mind to the point of sending my own bearer to you, so that, having fed on the living sight of you, he may bring clear news of your good fortune back to me. Believe me, my lord, I am bound to you by a great obligation, and my heart is given no respite in which I do not seek with full intent to see you. It remains that, once concord has been restored in the Roman church, an opportunity may come of meeting you. My lord, as I offer your reverence the fullest greeting, I pray that you will give a favourable hearing to what the carrier, my man, has to put before you, and that by a message in return you will inform us about your happiness and the state of your whole household.
35. Ennodius to Domnina.

Amid the cares and troubles to which I am subjected under the burden of my sins, I have chosen a singular source of help: to send a letter to you, my ladies, so that by your prayers all things might go well for me, and the clouds of distress might be laid aside and I be restored to the serenity of joy. For the first cause of my grief is that, while you live far away, I can scarcely learn of your welfare, and from this springs all the adversity that besets me. Come, then, to the help of a suppliant with your prayers, so that through the intercession of God's saints healing may be given to a sick mind. My lady, offering the service of greeting, I beg you, and I adjure you by the God whom you worship, to commend me to the Lord with continual petitions and with the tears by which the kingdom of heaven suffers violence. For I count this a special gift and place it before every advantage.
36. Ennodius to the Priest Adeodatus.

The dispensation of heaven never denies fulfilment to religious desires, for what we long for piously it grants with timely zeal. I wanted to ask by letter for the support of your prayers, and my wishes produced a household carrier, so that, roused by the goad of this letter, you may pray for the soul of one you have taken into your care; for the teacher of the Gentiles cries out: "Pray for one another." There is nothing that one who loves God cannot obtain, even for sinners. Labour, then, with the patronage you promised long ago, and win joys for me through your tears; may the fruit of innocence, unknown to my own merits, come to me. These are the things of which I have presumed to remind a saint of God. For I am afraid of long conversations, because a necessary thing should be asked for in few words. Now farewell in Christ, my lord, and show me by good fortune that I am feeling the gifts of your intercession.
37. Ennodius to John.

Is it, then, a false belief that love is repaid for devotion, that souls question one another in silent conversations, and that the senses bear witness to the faith of minds, so that what we spend is owed back to us in return? The hidden places of the mountains give back a voice, and mute things speak in obedience to humankind. Yet it has befallen your greatness, in contempt of me, to return silence for writing, and, in keeping with an artful disposition, to hold back from letters and so suppress the persistence of garrulity, trampling on the law of nature. Far be it from my character to follow what I grieve to see committed, or to make faults lighter by imitating them. See, once again I address one who indulges a holiday of the tongue, and I pursue him at greater length, mindful of the affection he promised. My lord, offering as before a most abundant greeting, I ask that my importunity may at least now exact the debt of your favour, while I look to you to satisfy the ardour of my longing with lengthy letters.
38. Ennodius to Firmina.

Whenever something we have wished for comes suddenly, it gains value from the very shortness of the time. For heaven, to increase the charm of its benefit, makes its gifts sudden, so that long waiting on the part of those who hope may not spoil the mercy of the giver. Who, receiving suddenly the object of his desire, would not prize all the more eagerly what he has obtained? So, thirsting for it, I received your greatness's letter at the moment of my departure. I was grieving, I confess, and deeply distressed, since there was no one to carry my respects to you, nor was I to learn before I left the good news of your health. See, good fortune has granted both: I have received at once the longed-for tidings, to which I now reply, and at one and the same time I let you know that I have returned from the Cottian Alps and am about to set out on the road to Ravenna. Pray that, tossed as I am by the various hardships of my labours, the gift of heavenly blessing may pour patience into me. As for me, since the splendour of your eminence urges me to guard your favour, I believe it easier for the courses of rivers to be turned back the other way, and for fish to leave the nourishment of the streams and seek the empty air, than for any faults to make me forgetful of such great kindnesses. For the rest, farewell, my lady, and pray unceasingly to our Redeemer for the one you have taken under your care.
BOOK SEVEN
1. Ennodius to Julian.

We have discharged the service we owed to the instructions of your greatness, for whoever complies with the admonitions of a just man comes close to equity. The nature of cases entrusted to a friend of truth for examination arms the mind of an upright judge with caution. Regard for your greatness would have filled us with goodwill, had our own devotion not already supplied it. In the case, then, which is in dispute between Bauto, lessee of the royal household estate, and Epiphanius the archivist, the outcome of our hearing hung in doubt and the parties clashed with opposing claims. Bauto asserted that he could not pay the sixty-four public solidi which, by issuing a written bond, he had acknowledged he owed from the arrears of that indiction, because he had paid forty solidi to Epiphanius through the hands of the sublime Projectus as a fee for patronage, and no benefit was shown to have followed from it. Epiphanius replied that if he had received anything he had earned it by his labour, that nothing had been paid him by Bauto in vain, and he kept extolling the credibility of the witness he had produced. We therefore decided that the noble Projectus, named above, should declare to me under oath both the kind of benefit that had been hoped for and, if it was so, affirm that it had not come about; and that, when this had been
done, Epiphanius should refund the amount of money he had received. It is now in the power of your eminence, if you please, to confirm our decision with your authority.
2. Ennodius to Faustus.

How much an interrupted affliction adds to the weight of grief, when adversity, to burn the more sharply, flatters us with a turn to good fortune! Has any burden ever fallen more harshly than one that returns after the load of continual calamity has been thrown off? How well long use had fitted me to bear your absence, while my prayers had learned not even to presume on what happiness did not possess! See, a fresh suffering tears at me again on top of old griefs, and a sharper blow reopens the healed-over scar. As you departed I had begged you for this mercy, that what I lost of our conversation face to face might be made up by letters; and, starved in all my desires, I have not earned even this fruit. I, not neglecting my custom, compose these lines amid tears, and in them I have thought it better to say nothing about my affliction, content with the report of the illustrious lord Pamfronius. Now, my lord, graciously accept the respects of your servant, and grant the customary remedies to a soul in distress.
3. Ennodius to Avienus.

With what entreaties I implored your greatness as you departed I might rightly recount again, were I not careful to avoid insulting your memory. For whoever reminds a loving friend of what has recently been done

importunely charges him with a forgetfulness that good men should shun, since it is the special mark of those bound together that, by a kind of foreknowledge, each supplies the other's wishes, and that, for the substance of love, by effective arrangement they bring about in deed, before it is asked, what would otherwise have to be requested in prayers. Heaven's ordering suggests what should be done, if you inquire what love desires. To this is added that, when you set out on your journey, you came to the aid of my troubled soul with many promises, saying that I, deprived of my light by your absence, was to be sustained by letters. See, the promise limps in its faithfulness, and, provoked by hope, I burn. The confidence that came from counting on a remedy has made hardships harder to bear. But now, my lord, receive the honour of my greeting, and since I have told you what ails my mind, let a speedy cure come to my aid, so that the state of your health and of the prince's favour may be disclosed to me in the letters I await.
4. Ennodius to Agnellus.

Pages that have always served devotion are now demanded by grief to betray itself; it has drawn these ministers of joy into giving voice to an injury, and, not content with the paint of urbane dissimulation, it has neither clothed the secrets of the heart in silence nor turned them elsewhere with flattery. I know such contrivances, indeed, but I shun them, and, content with simplicity, I meet my friends with an untroubled brow. Where in the world was the bond we promised each other under oath before God, that on setting out you should leave me ungreeted, as if I were a stranger, and that I, remaining behind, should not have the chance to suggest what was needful? I suppose you arranged it so that one weak in his eyes

should lose all his light along with you, and that I should not, with my eyes closed, behold my daylight in the presence of a friend. If these things happened through negligence, you will leave it to others to judge what place I hold with you; they are to be borne more bitterly if they are understood to have come about on purpose. Now farewell, my lord, and invite my mind, which innocence [?] urges to stand firm at its post, to the better share of your favour, since it has lain open to you in sincerity.
5. Ennodius to Senarius.

Although the prince's concern binds you, my lord, to himself through proofs of unblemished loyalty, and the distinction of your character so involves you in public affairs that it shuts you off from the taste of welcome quiet, I do not believe that the sacred duty of friendship is so far set aside that, while satisfying the commands of him who reigns with God's help, you fail to pay affection its dues. You know what the court demands and what friendship demands, and at one and the same time you fail neither the master of affairs nor love, since the integrity of a Christian mind, divided among these parts, is made only firmer. By these pursuits, then, in which a venerable custom is preserved, I believe my anxiety is relieved. It remains only that your greatness, aided by the consolations of our God, may have cause to rejoice. My lord, presenting the respects of my greeting, I hope it may be my lot to be gladdened about your condition, or that of your friend lord Faustus, by the longed-for news of a letter.
6. Ennodius to Florus and Decoratus.

Until now I have allowed your greatness to attack the fickleness of the Ligurians with the polish of urbane argument, because my origin made me a stranger to them, and your promised constancy had set you apart from their faults. But since by one and the same lot I have departed from your eyes and from your mind, I declare with a herald's voice that no one can condemn what he himself follows, nor, while sinning, pass sentence on excesses without loss of shame. It is right for those free from guilt to detest vices: who would calmly bear an admonisher who does not avoid in deeds what he demolishes with words? It is the teaching of the Gospel that whoever does and teaches thus can be judged worthy of God's grace. You have abundant speech whenever error is to be rebuked, and a purity of words to be embraced, while your conduct is neglectful. You have lost all memory of my tears, which the blow of a twofold grief poured out as you departed. See how many days have passed in which, amid so great a throng of travellers, I receive no letters either from my lord your friend or from you, to bring me the news I long for about him. By imitating the guilty you have acquitted them—not because the Ligurians have, as you say, given up their purpose of faithlessness, but because they have happened to find companions in what ought to be avoided. Yet, having paid the service of my greeting, I beg that at last, like good lords mindful of my prayers, you will make known to me in the service of a letter your prosperity, or that of my lord who loves you.
7. Ennodius to Helpidius the deacon.

Perfect love suffers no loss from bodily absence, nor is the serene union of minds penalized by the separation of travel: those whose souls come together as Christ joins them in love can be separated by no intervening lands. In this hope, or rather confidence, secure as I am about your heart, I address one who loves me as if he were held in my embrace. Cherish, lord Helpidius, the one you have received with God as mediator. Let the world have its cunning, and let the damnable call the skill of deceiving 'urbanity': as for you, mix nothing into that sweetness which I have tested, except what may lead us by good steps to perfect love. My lord, as before, returning a very full greeting, I ask that you let me know of your prosperity and that of those who love us in frequent letters.
8. Ennodius to Euprepia.

How well habit had fitted my mind to bear the separation of your absence, while long silences were by their very nature breeding indifference to that sweetness! The scar that had been healing under the medicine of devoted love has been torn open. I confess, venerable sister, your letter, seasoned with a flavour all too familiar, has called me back to my old longing. See with what art you contend with me, allowing neither satiety from your presence nor forgetfulness from your silence to come to my aid. The most high searcher of minds knows that, on reading your letter, my soul could not remain within its inner chambers, but, driven by the honey of your affection, flew off to your presence. The dwelling at Arles held me while I was enclosed by the walls of Milan; and while the freedom of my mind ran off to its sweet abode, the captivity of my body shut me up within Italy. O, if only I had abundance of speech to set out what my mind desires, or if shame did not snatch away what my tongue is able to say! Small is the love that can be adequately disclosed by the witness of the mouth; it is an admission of lukewarm love whenever eloquence does not fail before it. For the rest, I pray God that you may be well and be kept, for the blessing of our mutual prosperity, to relieve my grief, which you have doubled with your all too skilful writing.
9. Ennodius to Avienus.

The pomp you avoid in your letters you nonetheless possess, and your speaking is nothing other than preserving the distinctive marks of declamation: nature has heaped this up in you, and so has unfailing devotion to reading, the mother of skill. But no consolation can reach my miseries, since what I have deserved is set before my eyes, and the more unworthy the man preferred to me has proved, the more openly are the sins of the one passed over exposed. Why do you try to raise my spirits, most illustrious of men? What can be held in store for my tribulations in a life full of grief? As the boon of heaven's dispensation I have fixed on an end, if only with my life. Yet I return you thanks, though inadequate, for keeping toward me a devotion greater than which you would not show even to the most worthy. My lord, paying the reverence of my greeting, I hope that you will not cease to pray for me, and that letters bringing help may be sent to comfort me in my calamities.
10. Ennodius to Florus and Decoratus.

Acting as debt-collector, I have with difficulty compelled the advocate to make good his promise and pay what he owed to advocates. A hard sort of profession—let me anticipate what you would say: as a cleric, I bent him to a sense of shame. Judge for yourselves what kind of thing it is by which the most obstinate are softened, and what it means for someone to despoil robbers. The pound of silver that brother Epiphanius gave I have handed to brother Gaianus to be brought to you, though the agreements I received are still kept with me. It remains for you to indicate whether I should hand them over. My lords, saying a very full greeting, I ask first that you deign to pray for me through the saints, and then that you render my respects to the lords who love you, with that humility with which you know I wish it done.
11. Ennodius to Agnellus.

It grieves my mind that your abundance has given me nothing of the gifts of its eloquence, and broods so over the riches of its speech that sharing any of them is reckoned sacrilege. Avarice in all things is indeed shameful; yet it proves more shameful if it is words that you withhold. It often happens, too, that those who write frequently love less; but it has never happened that one who persists in perpetual silence keeps anything in reserve for love. Ambiguity can arise from the flatteries of letters; but it is a sure conviction that one is not loved by him who keeps silent. This is what I have written hastily, in the bearer's hurry, spurred by two goads, the haste of the courier and my grief. Apply remedies, then, without delay to the weariness of my mind, so that, although affection has hitherto lacked its fodder, the love you promised may yet be shown to stand firm. My lord, saying a very full greeting, I beg that what is easy enough for a most skilled speaker may not be denied to my expectation.
12. Ennodius to Hormisdas the deacon.

No room for pardon would be left to the unskilled if they spoke at greater length: brevity alone commends the unlearned. A rustic's lengthy narrative is worse than a mere fault: when something to be read at length has been extorted from an ignorant man, the one who demanded it has only himself to blame for his irritation. Does anyone wish tedious things to go on at length, and things seasoned with no flavour to have no short limits? You have demanded this, brother, with Roman and all too artful subtlety; but simplicity tinged with no tricks protects us against contrivances. For although you have drawn me out with the soothing words of your letter, you have not made me forget myself. I know how to keep a page short whose worth I, as its author, understand. Know, however, that I do not fail in my part, though one who is both urbane and a cleric calls me into the open. But why do I lengthen a page whose brevity I promised above? This is my contest with one who loves me; such is the fruit of letters. My lord, saying a most abundant greeting, I pray that, by the mercy of our Christ, you will often report your health to me in welcome letters while you ask after mine.
13. Ennodius to Boethius.

If it were permitted to put off commands, I would still be allowed not to lose the ornaments of silence: for it is the gift of my taciturnity that you believed me able to speak not uncouthly. See how much a restrained voice has added to the reputation of the tongue. But it is the mark of an empty mind not to hold on to remedies that have been proven. Concern for speech brings it about that the speaker's ignorance is not hidden, since the labour of breaking one's leisure cuts off glory. See, I, who was praised before being tested, submit to examination and break my holiday of silence, lest I seem worthy of the praise. For when humility renders obedience, we lose what silence had won for us. You deign to proclaim virtues in me, most faultless of men—you whom diligence has made venerable in your boyhood years without the prejudice of age; who through application fulfil all that is required; for whom, at the very beginning of life, constant reading is play and other men's sweat a delight; in whose hands, with doubled

fire, glows the torch by which the ancients shone. For what scarcely came to our elders toward the end of life is yours in abundance at its threshold. Truly you have given a reward to my loquacity, approaching first one who longed for conversation. A new thing has happened to a chatterer: that he should be held back until a letter demanded a reply. Thanks be to God, who by hidden paths has reminded you of the affection due to a kinsman. See, you now have two grounds for complaint: for after making myself known as a rustic, I presume to call myself your relative. My lord, rendering the duty of greeting, I hope you will grant frequency in the service of letters, a work in which both one who loves and one who is eloquent show diligence.
14. Ennodius to Archotamia.

You have advanced so far beyond the brilliance of your birth by the light of your character that the goodness of your deeds brings under your sway even those whom kinship does not bind to you. For who would not be ready to pay perfect reverence to a soul exalted in the worship of God? For he makes himself a stranger to the Redeemer's grace who does not [?] those who obey God. It is a sign of excellent conduct to love the worshippers of our Christ: he who loves those already proven is near to the most faultless; you give sure testimony of good merits if you are eager to follow the perfect with praise, continually and as is due; he who proclaims holiness in the saints without pretence becomes near to the saints; whomever you have set above others at the prompting of affection, it is a loss of shame if you do not follow. Who, without loss of shame, walking among thorns, would praise a cleared path, and, looking upon the way of salvation, choose the tracks of the wicked? It is a profession of blindness to reject the goods set before one's eyes as an example, and not to keep hold of that by imitating which one may advance. These things, my lady, report has announced of you by no uncertain signs; nor has the chattering crowd tossed them about with mouths ignorant of judgment—a crowd whose habit concerning human actions is to fan sparks into pyres while extinguishing the growing flames of the faithful. This has spread through the report of our relatives, and especially through the account of my lady and sister Euprepia: not only that you are worthy of praise, but that you have established what deserves to be celebrated, bringing to your venerable son, along with the radiance of his lineage, the torch of a holy life. The dweller at Lérins, so I have learned, has something to learn from his holy mother, even though she has not left her home in the city. If your piety believes me, it is a greater thing to have conquered the world in battle than to have avoided it: flight from the contest betrays fear, and there is no hope of virtue when the adversary is avoided before the encounter; a consciousness of one's own strength rarely consents to hiding; to choose seclusion is to have shown fear. I do not write this to accuse my lord the priest, the radiance of our family, who I believe does not lack, even there, assaults to overcome, in the very place where he seemed to have declined the conflict. For he trampled on all the allurements of the world at the moment when the chain of youth, wealth and birth could not hold back his departure. But to you, the weaker your sex, the greater the praise owed for winning the palm. It is almost as though you were the guardian even of his calling, you who, bearing the evils of widowhood and bereavement, allow nothing of your venerable son's merits to be lost for the sake of your own comfort. See how a woman, forgetting her frailty, like a fortress shields both a man and a youth from the enemy's assault. May you remain the glorious leader in this deed and continue in the world until the time when, if the matter so requires, the field of this world receives him in his maturity. I should like, I confess, if the composition of a letter allowed it, to draw out my words at length and with abundant speech to recount a few of the ornaments of your deeds. But let these be kept for writing to others. It is enough for you to know that, although I have never seen you, you are known to me, and, set among the memorials worthy of veneration, you are already held fast by the root of my heart. It is written, you remember: 'Let your neighbours praise you.' Truly, I would wish there were cause for me to go to Gaul, if only so that, together with my lord the priest, both of us kissing your hands and eyes, we might make you happy in whatever affliction of the times. My lady, as to the reason letters are sent: I let you know that I am well in body and ask after the state of your prosperity, beseeching and adjuring you by God never to deny me the help of your prayers.
15. Ennodius to Agnellus.

Thanks be to God, who, though he has deferred what was desired for your greatness, has not refused it. For desires are deferred lest the faith of the suppliant falter, since a swift granting spoils the charm of the joy to come. And it is clear that you have deserved honours rather than wished for them. But the earlier arrangement voices the prayers of those who love you. The Almighty knows that, moved by the luster of your family and encouraged by confidence in the favour you promised, I ran ahead, in wishing for your success, of all that you hold back by discipline or reason. Let a brief conversation at the doorway suffice: reply about your prosperity to one who is anxious, though not doubtful of your love. My lord, paying the respects of a very full greeting, I commend the bearer of this letter, whom I have found faithful and honourable, wishing that all should know how much of your esteem I enjoy, so that those who hope may be fed from the harvest of our shared favour.
16. Ennodius to Agnellus.

The cheerful festivity of speech usually spreads the news of good fortune, as whatever good comes to the eloquent runs through the peoples in a voice akin to their joy. It is easier to smother with the tongue a fire blazing on a pyre than to keep silent amid what one has longed for. It is a law of humanity and a command of nature that gladness of mind should overflow through the resources of writing; for good fortune leaks out even when it is shut up in closed rooms. But in your Greatness, just as your youth is already white-haired, ripening with the dowry of modesty and knowledge, so you hold your joy in check with the reins of moderation. Yet should discipline run on to the detriment of friendship, and should the devotion of friends be diminished by what is added to the adornments of your character? Though you hold the mint of Latin eloquence, you still cannot find a way to claim that you acted rightly in giving no words to me while I wait. Is it fitting, then, that heavenly blessings should be announced to those who love you only by rumour, and that one who already shares the joy should be left anxious whether his congratulations stand on solid ground? Driven by this need, I have sent a servant, not to ask for a letter but to demand one. You know the confidence of those who love sincerely, especially of those whose hope you hold, confirmed by the promise of your favour. My lord, offering my fullest greetings, I beg you to send letters that are both frequent and not cramped into a narrow space. See how sure of myself I am: I, who have so far received none, ask for long pages.
XVII. Ennodius to Avienus.

If you had any concern for my humble self, so long a silence would not continue, especially since the illness of my lady, your mother, afflicts me in my absence through various rumours with nothing to relieve it. For I know that the holy woman is weighed down by this burden alone: that she shows boundless kindness to one who does not deserve it. But why do I draw out words bound in the chains of sadness? If heavenly favour has restored her good health, send me word quickly by letter. For I expect good fortune to be reconciled with me only when I learn that it is with her. You have learned the cause of my grief; after God, give me some remedy without delay. My lord, presenting the respects of my greeting, offer fitting respects to my lord on behalf of me, your suppliant.
XVIII. Ennodius to Avienus.

If a judge suffers wrongs at the hands of worthless persons, I do not know whether he can relieve others of a burden under which he himself is collapsing. A healing hand must be applied to grave wounds, lest the disease grow through impunity. His Sublimity the vicar has wrung this address from me, although it was owed anyway out of regard for justice; let him himself make known what he has endured. One thing I know: unless you come to his aid, the evil to which he, the very guardian of discipline, has been exposed will become general. It is not foreign to Christian profession that I report this, since it is wicked that the order of things should be thrown into confusion by such disorder. My lord, with the honour of my greeting set first, kindly receive the voice of a suppliant, so that he who has taken up the burden of so great a task may gain strength through its success.
XIX. Ennodius to Simplicianus.

May the first beginnings of your youth be made firm by the help of divine favour; may he who gave adornment to your beginnings grant success to your harvest, so that what you promised in white blossom you may not withhold when the fruit is ripe. It is the first concern of my calling that, anxious for the good name of a beginner, I should send prayers to God, so that what has been anticipated in the training of a fine nature may ripen through help from above. May he bring the crop of your talent to the granaries who drew forth from the turf the grass that nourishes mankind; may he shape into wheat the form pressed out from the milk of the earth, he by whose rain the face of the soil is wedded and made fruitful. To you, learned boy, I give thanks that, although you have shone with brilliance of speech and are praised in that city with the assent of literary learning, you also desire the support of my commendation. The fruit of my devotion is yours, even though the testimony of a countryman confers no adornment. I gladly proclaim your words together with the most eloquent, and I join my judgment to theirs so as to grow rich in the company of good men. It follows closely that those who agree in any judgment are not divided in merit: he is one with them—nor does he stray far from the citadel of the lofty—who agrees with equal admiration in what they pronounce. But I return to the honey of your letter and

your style: its preface is so charming on account of your present tender age that strength and genius are not withheld from the age to come. Latin diction has settled into its hollowed channels, as the stream of Roman eloquence glides along its own bed: how far he will reach, judgment can hardly grasp, who appears so great at the very threshold. In the light of morning you have glowed with the brilliance of noon. May heavenly grace watch over its gift in you, and may Christ our salvation inspire you to honour one who loves you with frequent services of letters.
XX. Ennodius to Maximus.

While the servants of the presses were gathering in autumn's dowry and bursting the tender skins of the grapes with hurrying heels, I turned my eyes and my words back to a man of the highest rank, my kinsman and brother, judging it right that, while the vineyards yield their abundant liquor, I should address a sober person with pleasant merriment. So break your Pythagorean silence and share with me the riches of your skill and eloquence: let there be conversation between us in place of a happy vintage; let the sweet new wine of words flow. You have matters, most holy man, to share with a deacon about the principles of conduct, with your well-known richness of speech. For those who, like you, stand firm in the uprightness of the Church do right to shun silence. Write by what strictness golden chastity is maintained, by what path foul avarice is escaped, by what means the shameful darkness of deceit is avoided; in short, teach without pretence what you practise. Above all, graciously instruct one who is eager to know by what religious strictness the charms of a bride, or of the world, are rejected. My lord, presenting the gifts of greeting as above, I pray that you will gladly accept what this playful intrusion, not to be spurned, demands should be done amid the heaps of your cares.
XXI. Ennodius to Maximus.

Where is the proven good faith of your shining conscience, which white-haired reverence did not abandon even in your boyhood years, which the observance of honour lights up with the dignity of old age, which, ripening in deeds in the time of youth, entered upon infancy and outran it? Was it fair that a loving friend's pages should be answered with nothing but messages? Is a servant's word as trustworthy as a freely written letter? Did you consider it worthy of your proven character not to follow one who challenged you to religious duties, or did you think it wrong to answer letters which, amid your lapses, you happened not to have begun? Is this, then, your discipline? That is not how the uprightness you once displayed makes you known. Yet I, with the loquacity for which I am known, strive to break your hardened silence. Is your tongue unequal to your birth? Do you not proclaim the testimony of your lineage in the flower of your speech? Does the fruitful eloquence of your heart abandon the purple of speech? He reveals nothing but ill will who, though able, gives no words to one who longs for them. See, amid belches owed to Lyaeus, I compose words like a second Silenus. Know that your name is to be written in the purple of my talent and inserted in my own little books, so that, even if you give no reply, I may still hold the high ground, since I send to learned men, without any trepidation, something to be read. My lord, receive the respects of my greeting and pay what you owe in letters.

So may your virginity stand firm through enduring ages,
And may nothing perish that a blessed life has given;
So may no swarthy girls defile your limbs,
Nor may you lie abed for the sake of a Tartarean face:
As you refresh one who longs for it with holy words in writing,
And let a stream flow from your fountains to your brother.
XXII. Ennodius to Maximus.

The broken ridges of mountains or the hidden places of the forests receive a voice more faithfully than your Sublimity does: by nature's ordinance even mute things give men an answer; the echo of a noisy solitude comes back to mortals; the favour that tongues, or even wild haunts, have received is not lost. Why, then, in your Greatness is this counted a kind of praise and philosophy, to say nothing and to keep the caution of silence amid the uncertainties of those who declaim? You, a man whom nature did not bring forth barren, nor learning leave unshaped! But, I suppose, you disdain to address me, unwilling to give precious words to a boorish judgment. What of the fact that it is the mark of a man rich in eloquence not to withhold the words they desire even from the unlearned? That course of rivers is beggarly which is thought to quench only the thirst of the noblest; abundant rain drenches even rocks that will bear nothing. It is plain reasoning that he who fears losses reveals his poverty: whatever does not flow out is meagre. Still, I have sent you a singular gift of birds, which the hawk caught. For when we went out to Bromius and the rites of Bacchus, we waged war among the birds: the allied contest of feathers profited our gain. Remember that we sent a single duck, knowing that the god delights in an odd number. Our gifts are instruction: if you love me, take as doctrine what we say in jest. Make my merriment bear fruit. If it imposes on you the care of perpetual chastity, the tongue now exercised in admonitions will labour in your praises. Farewell, my lord, and, if I deserve it, answer one who loves you as a learned man should, setting aside all pretence.
XXIII. Ennodius to Maximus.

Your Greatness is drawing out the wedding festivities for a long time: while you pursue at such length a thing to which you were compelled, your necessity has suddenly become your desire. Should anyone devote himself perpetually to a business he entered unwillingly? You have withdrawn from the care of the blessed state you once guarded as though you had spent long years learning how a husband is made. Thirty days have happily gone by, and you still keep yourself away from the city and from my eyes, wearing me down with long waiting. Truly, do whatever you like: if I live, I will not keep silent what I have composed to say to you. Yet, having received the honour of my greeting, accept this taste of a few little drops sent to you, as befits a brother from a brother. Blush, for you neither ask after a sick man nor send him anything from the wedding delicacies that might relieve his lack of appetite.
XXIV. Ennodius to Stephanus.

The urging of our common son Marcellus—given to you by nature, to me by affection—requires of me that I take the lead in the duties of writing and, overcome by love, bestow the comfort of letters, through which antiquity willed that absence should have no power. You already owe me double thanks, even if you send back a reply, because I

began first. He opens the door of love who sets the example in conversation; those who answer letters keep to the pattern set before them. So, with God's help, I send you a letter announcing my good fortune. And I add this for your joy, so that your fatherly heart may exult: your son already holds, in the liberal studies, the testimony of his noble nature, and shows himself such in this pursuit that he surpasses even the greedy hopes of his family. An honourable beginning in a young man is the hope of perfection, and he who gains the glory of a good undertaking at its outset is not far from being learned. So, greeting you with the affection I owe, I hope that when the opportunity comes again you will let me be lifted up by good news of your prosperity.
XXV. Ennodius to Symmachus.

A law written for desires is scarcely obeyed: affection, impatient of stricter precept, is not always made blameworthy by being free. It often becomes more lovable through its fault, when its very lack of restraint gives it a greater gift for pleasing; for it commends its offence with a certain honey of its own boldness. I defend myself with this preface, since I am the first to venture upon letters. It remains in the power of your Highness, if you choose to put up with a chatterer, not to keep silent, and to nourish me with the milk of the original Symmachian fountain. Farewell in our Christ, nobility of the Roman people, and deign now to regard me as your client and servant, as befits the light of your character and nature.
XXVI. Ennodius to Agnellus.

As I wished, you have produced a letter, though in clearing yourself you clear matters darkened by no cloud. It is the happiest lot in pleading a defence when we stand by innocence, and it is always a favourable omen when we lend the use of our voice to things that shine of themselves. You easily vouch for the light of one who shines, nor are words lacking to serve those already acquitted. You have come forward with such words about the promised horse, as though you had ever had a vile inclination to lie. Truly, by my soul, I would more easily believe that holy bishops could fall into that pit. Vices do not know mature men unless they have imbued them in their youth; bad faith does not sprout anew in men; whatever is in our character both follows and has gone before. So farewell, purple of Latin eloquence, and repay me in love, seeing to it that, as compensation for the delay, a horse worthy of your gift comes to my aid.
XXVII. Ennodius to Probus.

I choose to give up my modesty rather than incur the disgrace of seeming not to love, knowing that damage to one's face is more easily repaired than damage to one's loyalty. To be unlearned is a misfortune; to hate the virtues of your family is a crime. We could lack the liberal disciplines without sin, but nothing will make up for it when one has cast off good character. Should I not honour in a letter the good things heaped together in your Eminence? Should I not look up to that light of your family, enlarged by learning and integrity? It seems to me that he who cherishes upright men does not stray far from virtue, since anyone is believed capable of following what he loves. So farewell by the grace of God, and, approving my zeal, enrich one who loves you with the gift of letters.
XXVIII. Ennodius to Adeodatus the Priest.

The opportunity that serves to carry my writing to you answers my wish. For a letter charms in place of presence and promises itself, from the dispatch of its pages, the same as it offers, since the most upright men, just as they think it detracts from their virtues that others should have gone before them in giving proof of affection, so they consider it a disgrace to neglect an example. Among holy men this fellowship has always lived: that, through the care of the inner man, earthly separation should do no harm. It is fitting, my lord, that you follow both my wish and my pattern. So, greeting you first of all, I beg you to remember me, so that what is withheld from me through my negligence may be conferred by divine grace through your intercession. I tell you, then, without lying, that on the third night after my departure, at the very break of day, my holy lady Cynegia appeared to me, displeased with me, and that I was much blamed by her for the haste of my journey. She complained, in no gentle words, that her tomb had not been honoured even with any verses. I did not take this as having the semblance of prophetic truth, nor did I offer the sweat of my labour to what may have been illusions of the night. But because those who love are easily persuaded, she who admonished me had no trouble exacting the work that was owed. The reverence due to the lady is preserved. I adjure you by the day of judgment to have the verses I have sent written soon on the wall above, at her feet. Know that this will be pleasing to your son as well: for he wishes her merits to be celebrated by the mouths of many, but in the manner in which you find them here. Greet my lady Stephania and my lady Sabiana, and also my lady Fadilla, for me. When the verses have been inscribed, write back at once. Be so kind as to tell my lord the pope to arrange something in my affair through the holy deacon Dioscorus. I have written as much as I could in the haste of the courier. Give my warmest greetings to my lord and brother Hormisdas, and tell him to send that key.
XXIX. Ennodius to Beatus.

I do not confine my letter within narrow bounds, mindful of Spartan concision, nor do I mock your youth by studied compression of speech: far be it from me to say little to the little. Let it be the way of sophisticated people to withhold long writing from the young and, without any need, to shape their pages to the measure of the persons addressed. Whatever you may think subtle in me in what I have said by way of preface, haste, not always a friend of art, and chance produced it. It is a great thing for me if accident has given you something to admire. So I make known the reason for my writing, which, with my greeting set first, I commend to you. When I had gone far from the city, an admonition from my lady Cynegia came to me, asking why I had not honoured her tomb with praise drawn out into verse. Although I would have done this out of reverence for her husband himself, I considered it further, because what shines with the light of merits ought to be celebrated with a rich pen. For God does not reject the service of the unskilled, and, content with what he himself has given, does not require diadems of words from rustics. So I have sent the epitaph to be inscribed in these verses. As to what is thought of it—so may your father live, and so may Rome not make you her own in the things for which she is blamed—tell me simply and honestly, and do not flatter my ears or my feelings with the paint of false favour. Do not blush to read my page over to others too, but especially, and deservedly, to my lady Barbara, since you are lodged with her. I hope, though, that my little tablet may have as much flavour as your promise, which in its white blossom surpasses both my hopes and those of your parents, greedy as they may be. Greet my lord Cethegus and my lady Blesilla, his sister, for me. Greet Fidelis, Marcellus, Georgius, Solatius and Simplicianus for me. And tell them: if the discipline of my lady Barbara is dear to you, frequent the company of her lord, or of her fathers or brothers, because hers is a chaste house, free from luxury; whoever does otherwise need not hope to return to me.

The reward of my best prayers, by the gift of Christ:
The cross has given to this tomb the one who was my life,
Loosing my offspring from the flesh [?] without wound to the mind,
Because I die, happy, before Faustus my husband.
The healing of the heart has scattered tears.
Let the matron who by her merits keeps a faithful bed
Long for a like lot.
XXX. Ennodius to Faustus.

The hope of young men is sound when the care of great men attends it; if that care ceases, a rich crop of wheat turns into tares. Parthenius, my sister's son, had long been drawn to diligence in letters by fear of your Eminence, as his father's report has disclosed. But now, released by your absence from the law of reverent fear, he is undertaking shameful things: that age, too friendly to sin, finds many guides to error. His father implores the faithfulness of my calling and mourns his living son as though he were dead. So do those act whose confidence in the progress of their children has met with no return. Overcome by his entreaties, I had nothing left to apply by way of remedy except to inform your Eminence promptly of the excesses of the aforesaid young man. Lend your healing hand, lend your accustomed help, lest the growth of vices cut down everything in him that could have borne some good. Entrust to your friends what should be done; inform his teacher, and grant whatever can help; for these are the things which, with the respects of greeting already offered, I, mindful of my profession, can provide for a kinsman without pretence.
XXXI. Ennodius to Parthenius.

It would indeed have been fair to set taciturnity in return against an ignoble silence, and for retribution to go out by the same path by which the fault had come. Is it right that in your excesses it should be a voice, and not mute pain, that shows how you have offended? Believe me, the cure is near once indignation has been expressed. Pent-up feeling ought to have been striking you for a long time, if indeed you have not departed entirely from human feeling. What wrong had I done, after you had asked pardon in your first letter with contrived humility? Is this the faithful promise of amendment—that once you have wrung away the anger I had conceived by soothing speech, you should blush to have sinned so little? As far as I can see, after professing your shame, you avoid only the narrow straits of error, thinking it wrong not to raise your brow toward your parent and foster-father as high as you ought to have lowered it, in fellowship, for so many kindnesses. Or do you perhaps think that boyish anger troubles me, or that any compulsion could overthrow a mature affection? Are not the blows of children welcome to a father? Are not the parents of crawling infants soothed even by their injuries? Those think nothing bitter in whom, amid their desires, something has boiled up that partly opposes their wishes. We find thorns and tares among the fields of wheat, and while we gather the fruitful plant, barren ones spring up alongside. Should the care of cultivation therefore be rejected, or should the ploughshares cease, if the earth has not wholly satisfied the farmer? I pray God to shut out from you what I detest; yet I, believe me, will never abandon the duty of one who admonishes. I have heard from your father's report that you have already grown slack in your studies, and that, as though you had reached the citadel of knowledge, you are not at all concerned with instruction in reading. You know, my son, that the sum of this matter is held only by the greatest perseverance. It has profited no one in this work to have laboured at some time, if he has given up the effort of labour: knowledge flees the negligent on swift wings, and whatever was won by time and sweat is carried off in a moment. I greet you and want you watchful, so that you may bind the harvest of your progress with the chains of daily reading. Write back to me, even now, if you consider what befits you; for, believe me, you will never find in any part of the world such a supporter of your compositions.
BOOK EIGHT
I. Ennodius to Boethius.

Full of the best hope for one I wish every good fortune, I take up the task of writing a letter. It is fitting that your fasces be honored with this preface, and that amid the purple robes, which grow brighter in the light of their wearer, I should not hold back from some conversation, of whatever kind. Is love recognized only by the gifts of learning? Must we believe it wrong for the wishes of a rustic to come out in public? Wishes become known more simply when no sleight of skill veils them. So we are in speech what we are in heart. We cannot disguise bitter feelings with soothing words, and he praises modestly whose mind supplies what must be said when he composes a compliment.
