Thanks, then, to almighty God, who in you guards the old goods of your family while he multiplies new ones, and, what is greater than the summit of rank itself, makes you worthy of the heights. This glory is indeed paid to your lineage, but, what is more illustrious, it is won by your personal merit. It may have been the custom among the ancients to buy the eminence of the curule chair with sweat on the battlefield, and to shine in the sun of honors through contempt for life. But another kind of virtue is sought now that Rome has become the prize of the victors. Our candidate obtains his due triumph after a plain contest, though he has never seen war. He claims his laurels by judgment, and he did not think it necessary to fight armed men. Among

the swords of Cicero and Demosthenes he shone, and he gathered the keen points of both their arts as though born in the very peace of learning. Let no one fear a discord between Attic perfection and Roman, or doubt that the chief goods of the nations can come together in partnership. You alone embrace both. What would have been enough if shared out man by man, you, a possessor greedy for the greatest things, keep within yourself. You surpass the eloquence of the ancients while you imitate it, and you give the most learned a model of speaking while you seek one. I have in my hands the venerable composition of your letter, which bears out what I say. Would that what you send were as frequent as it is sweet! Perhaps you will say: it was natural for him to praise a relative who labors for the advancement of the whole family, since what the palm-embroidered robe seems to confer on one man alone is not his own; indeed a share of the curule chair comes to me. But, believe me, I am lifted up more by the genius and studies of the man who has been raised so high. Those things sometimes come by chance; these have fallen to virtue alone. A man who boasts only of his parents is brought to the consul's ivory staff almost destitute of support. You have both in your own store: Latin learning and the purple blood. Oh, if only regard for the epistolary style, which would otherwise run on at length, did not hold back my hand! What others enrich in their accounts I would set out raw, even if in confused order. I return to the business of the letter. I report that I am well, and I beg to know whether you are, asking as the crowning kindness that you honor me with a reply. I also pray that you will grant me, on whatever terms you wish, the house in the city of Milan which your abundance and your neglect have by now almost abandoned. It is only just that your relatives should have what falls away from the mass of your inheritance. Believe me, as God is my witness: if I am found worthy to obtain this without loss to your estate, I shall repay it with greater services, as one bound by a gift. On this matter—so may everything turn out happily for us—if I am to be secure, send me the assurance of a complete deed.
II. ENNODIUS TO AVIENUS.

It would have been fitting for Your Greatness, while following the instructions of your holy father, to bring out the wealth of your talent and to air the learning you acquired with much sweat as proof of your diligence. That composition would win you double praise, since the palm of eloquence would be carried before the public while the devotion of those who received it grew: what reveals your love to us also exalts you. By one and the same act both the splendor of your speech and the splendor of your loyalty would be multiplied. Those placed at the summit are thought to bestow on those beneath them as much affection as they express in words. This, my lord, your father observes, though he is extremely busy and set in the citadel of human affairs. For a man who lives at leisure and grants no words shows contempt. I remember reading: no honor to stingy speech. Now, therefore, having paid the services of greeting, I let you know that I am well. It remains for my prompting to rejoice in the abundance of the conversation it draws out.
III. ENNODIUS TO MESSALA.

After one letter, which you sent when overcome by my frequent writing, you persist in continual silence. I believe you keep this philosophy of saying nothing out of necessity, not choice, and you do not consider that the ancients said nothing in the present so that they might speak better, and that their care for silence was the nurse of speech. You seem to me to follow the Attic disciplines faithfully in their mute part, unwilling to publish what you acquired by silence. After this holiday of your mouth, show what riches have come to you along the path of the ears. You sent me your declamations, in which, though there was not the sublimity one might wish, there was no shabby baseness to be found. I gave thanks to God that you had at last freed yourself from the chain of negligence that bound you. I promised that what followed would succeed beyond what the beginning had led me to expect. But as far as I am concerned, since you send me nothing, you have joined the beginning to the end. Lord Messala, by the dispensation of our God may it be granted you to keep daily before the eyes of your heart whose son you are. But I do not want harsh words to run long. Farewell, receive the duty of greeting, and, corrected by my frequent promptings, give yourself back to the duties of letters.
IV. ENNODIUS TO ARATOR.

Going off to distant parts, you have become forgetful of affection. Pious devotion was not allowed to leave the city walls with you. While you live in town, you keep up your crafted flatteries with no little Daedalean art; but once you decide to head for the country, you leave behind the memory of your friends like heavy baggage. You went in search of the delights of the villa, and in your mind we stayed behind among the evils of the city. That affection had no root which you cut off as if it were the torment of cares. You may ask: why so swift a reproach? It is not fair to bring out the torturer before the offense. You promised without hesitation that you would write as soon as you reached the place you longed for. Yet, as your father, always the publisher of your faults, has revealed, servants have already come from you empty of letters. I fear that this silence may grow strong with time and that shameful neglect may harden into a habit of silence. My lord, I greet you, then, and remind you that you ought to remember your promise, so that among the hoary groves you may be raised on high, crowned with ivy.
V. ENNODIUS TO FAUSTUS.

There is no need to accompany with a recommendation the craftsmen sent by the holy bishop. A thing that will please more by its own nature is spared the injury of a praiser's devotion. It is a household of servants, and when you see them you cannot doubt that they were sent by the church and have come out of its treasures and its bosom with this purpose: that, treated generously, they may earn you a reward in the exchange for the better age. Who will deny that in these servants, according to the saying of the most blessed martyr Lawrence, there are the greatest riches? For they are women who, though they have lost the eyes of the outer man, will shine with the brightness of their minds; whatever good fortune is taken from bodies grows into fruit for souls. Do not take it amiss that they will be unable to see, and that no beauty alluring with its charm will be seen—something far removed from your mature years anyway. A man who, like you, has set his life on this path of innocence is in heaven if he feeds such as these. Believe me, although that abundance of tears poured out to God will bring you joys, you will be content to keep these mourners for good. To these goods I have mentioned, which would have cost you great labor and price, I add what follows. One of them is both freeborn and childless, and I think she will not have... [?]—which is close to holy desires—for among Christian people barrenness is fruitful, and it is the greatest comfort to lack the supports of the world. But perhaps your mind, busy with public affairs, may grow weary of a long reading. Good things placed at the beginning may encourage you, and sweetness placed in the opening, as the rules of oratory direct, may wipe away any irritation. Still, so as not to keep your wishes in suspense by contrived concealment: I obtained no documents for them [?]. The bishop thinks it hard that I should make mention of the mules, and although your servant, brother Gaianus, pressed the matter effectively and his importunity weighed on us beyond measure, we achieved nothing by our joint efforts. They want only this to be inserted: that your holy father, prompted by your many kindnesses and favor, provided for you by way of a gift in return. If this kind of document pleases you, write back without delay, or tell me what form it should take. Now I, a man of tested usefulness, long proven over many years in your service, have told you in swift leaps of words what I have accomplished, which another could hardly have related at the cost of endless paper.
VI. ENNODIUS TO AVIENUS.

I believe justice requires that I should be the first to show what I expect from you. It is fitting that one who waits for good works should invite them by example. He who supplies the model of a duty spurs slowness into action. With these words, then, offering the gift of greeting, I announce that I am healthy after the illness I suffered for my sins, and I ask about the state of your prosperity, hoping that you will apply yourself fully to repaying this.
VII. ENNODIUS TO SENARIUS.

Among holy consciences, the business of the ruler's favor does not deny affection its due, nor does the palace banish the warmth of pious love. He bears witness to solid affection who does not bury it in forgetfulness amid hindrances. Commend Your Eminence to me in writing, which I, importunate in my wishes, have earned: keeping fellowship is the honor of high office. With these words, then, greeting you most dutifully, I keep my letter brief, knowing that long ones can be dreaded, and I ask you to give thanks on my behalf to the Lord, who wiped away the trouble I suffered before you could learn of it.
VIII. ENNODIUS TO HELPIDIUS THE DEACON.

By what means, by what art, shall I stir your fraternity to write, when you, a man rich in words, keep a foreign silence toward me? I have chosen to make you speak by speaking, and to draw that Attic learning of yours out into letters by my own chatter. Was it right for you to neglect your promise for so many days and not send a page to tell me how you had arrived? Or do you perhaps think you must keep up that caution of yours with me? You disdain to converse with those whose favor you sought with much sweat. Believe me, unless you pull yourself back from this vice with the same speed at which you usually walk, we shall have to transfer our patronage to others, who, being mindful, reward love with services. With these words, then, greeting a friend and physician, I tell you that I am suffering from a serious bodily illness. Unless a page dictated by you, full of jests, cures it, I shall stretch my little frog out under its torments until it matches tall men.
IX. ENNODIUS TO MESSALA.

If divine favor is now leading you away from your habit of negligence toward the studies we hope for, if you are heeding where your talent calls you and where lord Faustus calls you, do not keep silent with the letter I long for. But I fear that while I long for a dutiful correspondent I may have to put up with a rustic, and that what I wanted may begin to work against my wishes. May heavenly riches rouse that sluggishness with the goad of piety, and enrich the beggary of your mouth with help from above. Look, write, even if only because insults have provoked you. Sending greetings, then, I ask that I may learn from your letters what is happening with you.
X. ENNODIUS TO MAXIMUS, VIR SPECTABILIS.

May your wishes be well ordered by the judgment from above. May he himself come to your wedding who granted the gift of blessing to the first parent while he still rejoiced in his native immortality. May our Christ grant that you lose neither the fruit of the integrity you have kept nor the gifts of marriage. May your virginity so benefit your offspring that fruitfulness takes nothing away from your chastity, and by a wonderful secret of providence you neither perish to the world by being a father nor perish to the grace of God by being chaste. May there come upon you what Isaac, piously deceived, wished for his younger son. May your wife enter her mother-in-law's house under the same auspices with which the daughter-in-law entered the inner rooms of Tobias. Let the virginity you have kept be the cause of perfect love in your wife. Know that she alone is assigned to you, for whom you kept yourself as though you were not from the dregs of the world. See, since I could not come, I am not absent in prayer. My lord, I hope that you will receive the honor of greeting and graciously accept what I have sent.
XI. ENNODIUS TO ARATOR.

I wonder why you disfigure with shameful silence the gifts of conversation polished in you to Roman elegance, and why, shunning to spend the riches you gathered with much sweat, you waste them in taciturnity. Whatever is bestowed on the worthy

adorns its giver so long as it is put to use; he who locks away the elegance of talent diminishes it. It is one and the same error for a rustic to come forward and for one worthy of the honor of praise to hide. Did you have nothing worth recording, or did I seem to you unworthy to be honored with your eloquence? Here, surely, was a subject to be celebrated in everyone's speech and writing: a man has been brought to the marriage bond who, great though the light of his birth and the abundance of his means may be, surpasses both in discipline and modesty; who, renouncing the vices of the flesh, rejected as a base enticement whatever the laws granted as a remedy, and, unwilling to give his body over to the services of a wife, thought that he would be enslaving his free chastity if he spent any of it on the world. Even if you do not love these things, you ought still to praise them to display your talent. We can believe you are becoming good if we hear you proclaiming what is honorable. Now, sending you the fullest greetings, I urge you to write back, and do not judge me by this letter of mine, which—God is my witness—I dictated in passing as I was returning from the basilica.
XII. ENNODIUS TO FLORUS.

With what a bond I hold you, with what devotion I embrace you, you can gather from the quality of your own mind. For it hardly ever happens that people are loved unless it is clear that they love sincerely. The vigor of souls meets with its own kind and with its own pursuits [?]; it reveals itself through silent speech. And so, if you intend to repay me in kind, press our lord to order that the suburban estate be sold to me, if he deigns, at a price paid by me, so that I may happily have it while I am in Liguria, and after my death he and his heirs may possess it. Yet he will seem to me, after God, to bestow freedom and a livelihood on me if I obtain this kindness through him. But as you hope your daughter may live, as you hope to have from her such grandsons as you wish, as you hope God may make your soul equal to his saints, and as you hope your brother may live, so press him humbly and insistently until you bring my petition to fulfillment. Let him think of God, let him think of my needs, for there is nothing greater that his power and his affection toward me could grant.
XIII. ENNODIUS TO AURELIAN THE PRIEST.

I would be lying about my affection if, in leaving you, I had not stayed behind, and if I had not carried Your Beatitude with me, though you remained at your post. Since in me, as in everyone, the mind is the commander of the body, it is held captive, with all its attention, by love for you. So, paying the honor of greeting with due humility, I report that my health has lost nothing through the wear of the journey. See how I repay your concern with the care of kindly zeal. Do as it is written, returning what you have received: let me rejoice at news of your prosperity.
XIV. ENNODIUS TO FAUSTUS.

I would keep silent about my troubles if I had not understood that your concern relieves me. You do not yet know how many kinds of illness wear me down. For my sins I am frequently given over to fevers, and the strength that seemed restored is broken. So supply your usual remedies and apply the practice of your holy life, so that whatever human medicine cannot do you may obtain by prayers poured out to our God.
XV. ENNODIUS TO EDASIUS.

Before it is tested, the loyalty of friends is hidden; once it has come to light, it binds to itself the minds of those who have any discernment. Yet the service rendered to dear ones is a very free servitude. I confess to Your Greatness: until my man brought his report I did not know what discernment and grace lay hidden in Your Sublimity beneath a noble humility. I learned that you are a man who surpasses even hoary-headed blessedness in loyalty by treating the absence of friends so well. You had indeed promised much on leaving, but, true to the character of your conscience, you delivered more. My lord son, offering the gift of most abundant greeting, I give and feel thanks that fall short of what you deserve for what was granted me at the very outset of our acquaintance. As for what remains, I beg you to have those remaining slaves secured now. See the confidence that comes from earlier kindnesses: he who once feared to offer requests to a stranger now does not hesitate to give orders.
XVI. ENNODIUS TO BARBARA.

It was not from forgetfulness of my debt that I refrained from my duties, nor did I, scorning what was agreed, hold back my chatter from showing my respects. But after I returned from the city, various illnesses and everything that summons one to death at once pressed in on me. Truly, my lady—so may joys come to you and yours—our Christ, in testimony to an ancient mystery, has once again called Lazarus from the tomb, though this time a sinner, and not like him who was worthy to be called a friend. The deed is one, though the persons differ; and the greatness of the divine work is now all the greater, because what he deserved has come to me undeservedly. This is what kept me from performing my duty. But as soon as I was brought back to life, I turned at once to paying my services to you, asking God to guard you and yours with help from above. I also promise myself and my desires that some high office will call you, with happiness and joy, to attendance at court, which would satisfy my wishes. Do not, my lady, withdraw from this labor, this burden. Let the provinces see the goods of the city of Rome, and let those who can scarcely be taught by admonitions be formed by example through the goods God has granted you. Having shown you the reverence of greeting, I ask that you relieve me with the letter I so eagerly await, but do not let anyone else dictate what you write to me: so may your prayer never be turned away from obtaining what it asks.
XVII. ENNODIUS TO STEPHANIA.

I believe you came to my aid in my dangers even without knowing it—or rather, why should I suppose that those to whom it is given through God to foreknow all things know nothing? For after I returned from the city, the divine mysteries were renewed in me, and what had grown old with time rose again in new examples. Once more Lazarus was called from the tomb—not one equal in merit to him who earned the name of friend of the Redeemer, yet in the difference of the events the pattern of a single mystery holds. Led down through many illnesses to the tomb, but called back by a heavenly voice, I turned first of all to the duties I owe you, believing that it pleases God if services are rendered first to his worshippers with the tongue he himself has restored. So, offering the reverence of greeting, I beg you to take care to pray for me more earnestly, as I asked, that through your merit divine mercy may deign to confirm what it has granted, and that you will often relieve me with the kindness of your letters. I ask you not to have anyone else dictate them, by the soul of lord Asterius and by your profession: so may the glory you desire for him remain with him until the time of the consummation.
XVIII. ENNODIUS TO FAUSTUS.

The bearer of this letter has driven me back to my pursuits and, almost importunately, exacted what I wanted to do anyway. So the one who asked conferred the favor. In his affair he asks for the scrutiny of your justice, which the world has proven, and he thinks no one will discern the truth of his case if you hold back. For him I come as intercessor, asking that, while you attend to heavenly commands and seek out the truth with all your attention, you may come to the aid of an afflicted man in his need. Having rendered the service of greeting, I also hope that you will let me know of your prosperity, not neglecting the opportunities for greeting that frequently present themselves.
XIX. ENNODIUS TO FAUSTUS.

Although any number of letters seems few to the anxious, and no foresight is enough for one held in suspense by affection, still the party to whom they are sent cuts itself off from humanity if it does not reply. So, having first paid the duties of greeting, I report that, God granting, through the prayers of the saints and your own, things are now going better with me, and that the fevers and the state of despair have abated. Now, as for what remains, I hope that you will deign to receive with your usual kindness the petition I sent through my fellow servant, brother Florus. For although at present the matter seems to me one of gain, for you, who care more for the things to come, the greatest benefit comes from this side.
XX. ENNODIUS TO AGNELLUS.

If I were able to accompany you in body, I would refrain from words; but since the one fails through ill health, the other comes to its aid. The searcher of secrets knows that, though separated from your presence, I cannot be absent from you. So I relieve your concern with news of my prosperity, and, since that is why the exchange of letters was granted us, I ask after yours. Having paid you the honor of greeting, I let you know that I have sent a servant to receive the horse. Only send one such that it is plain you were the giver, and that I may rejoice to have received it as the height of honor.
XXI. ENNODIUS TO BEATUS.

If I could blot out my letter by writing, I would set about it with every effort. But since a human being cannot help erring, I, that grey-haired man, who am also your father, beg you never to remember my earlier letter. If you do, may your father and your homeland welcome you as the kind of man I declare you to be to everyone every day. I trusted what others wrote, and so I bit with the untimely haste of my pen. You had acted as a wise man does: you read my verses only to lord Probus, who holds the citadel among the learned, and that was the right thing to do. I was the untimely one. I should not have trusted anyone else, and as far as I can see I was upset for nothing. So go to lord Probus (so may your father live, and so may you hear that I, whom you have always loved, am alive), since I dictated this when I was nearly dead. Kiss his knees for me and tell him this about that last verse: Terentianus led me to it with his example, "So he speaks, weeping, and gives the fleet free rein." Still, he saw in advance everything that deserved correction. I greet him with the love I owe him. If I pull through, I will correct those verses and send them on. As for your letter, which you sent by the boy Rufinus, I received it only in July. That is why I did not know what had been done, and so I was this upset.
XXII. Ennodius to Florus.

Who has a better right to learn the signs of my good health than someone who has wished for it sincerely and without ceasing? And it would not be fitting for anyone else to hear first that another man's wishes have come true. So, having paid the service of greeting, I tell you that by heavenly kindness I was soon healed, after human treatment had stopped. What brought me back to the hope of recovery was the very fact that the physicians had given up. Now that you know of your joy, which I judge from my own, join me in praising the giver of so great a gift. If some longer delay still keeps you away, let me know by letter how well you are.
XXIII. Ennodius to Florus.

The spectabilis Eleutherius has a case which the Vicar took over from the lord prefect to hear. He hoped for a letter of recommendation from me to your greatness, believing that he could have full help, without harm to justice, if my words to you supported him. So, having paid the honour of greeting, I ask you this: if he really is struggling against unfair treatment, stretch out a healing hand to him. It is wrong for cunning to see its schemes succeed to the detriment of a good case.
XXIV. Ennodius to Faustus.

Your kindness, set above other men, keeps to its custom. The care of a most holy man truly is medicine, for a venerable conscience always makes its requests known to God. After you left, a fiercer fever burned me. The devil drove me headlong, and my sails were spread toward utter despair. The physician came to me and said there was nothing he could do. That gave me greater hope, since man had given up. At once, in tears, I turned to the help of the heavenly Physician. I armed my whole body, which was already being made ready for the tomb, against the fevers with the oil of lord Victor. My God knows that the Commander of that great soldier was soon at hand, and what I asked through His worthy witness I received without delay. Soon that heat, the agent of eternal cold, cooled. At the ninth hour, as we read, it left me at the command of my Christ. I know the hours of your prayer. I know that your many tears also helped the sufferer at that very moment. You see, I have not kept this welcome news to myself, but the scarcity of letter-carriers held back what we both wanted. Your relief does me much good, though you yourself, who have spurned pleasant things, hardly wish for it.
XXV. Ennodius to Faustus.

Heavenly grace looked on me. My soul was trembling at the nearness of heavenly judgement, and grace released it by granting me a span of life in which to become better. As soon as this happened, I told your greatness by letter about God's kindness. Truly, when the physicians gave up, I did not lack the medicine of Him who is won by innocence and tears. Believe me, if those treating me had not come to my aid by abandoning me, I would be good for nothing. I had been growing sicker through men's efforts, and I began to be healed by neglect. All this was reported in my earlier letter. But so that the opportunity should not pass, I have added this note. Having offered the service of greeting, I hope that you will lift my spirits with news of your own health, on which I depend.
XXVI. Ennodius to Avienus.

Whoever longs for your letters must not keep silent, and whoever [seeks?] conversation must not set an example of silence. Thanks to the support of your prayers, which your innocence and devotion make acceptable to our God, I already feel better. Having paid the honour of greeting, I want to know how well you are. Now that I have recovered my health, my only comfort is to be lifted up by the blessing of your well-being.
XXVII. Ennodius to Barbara.

I am still at the point of death, and because of the weight of my sins my Lord's kindnesses do not come to me, since I deserve to be worn down for a long time. Even so, my soul, hanging in the balance, has not neglected the service it owes to your reverence. It is almost being called to judgement already, and still, in this light, it looks up to those it has honoured. How true is the saying that holy affection does not perish even in death! So, my lady, I offer you the service of the greeting I owe and ask you this. Now that you know what is happening to me, I ask you to pray to my lord the apostle and to his brothers, by that standing in which you surpass everyone in the brilliance both of your birth and of your way of life. Through their entreaty, may the power of God not hold back the gifts of His mercy, which is not usually slow.
XXVIII. Ennodius to Beatus.

With what return, with what attentive service will it be repaid that I address you in frequent letters and do not shrink from coming out into public view through the service of your words? Neither your youth nor a skill equal to my own can hold me back. I choose to trust kind people rather than learned ones, since they put the goods of birth above studies. That you are faithful is a divine gift in your nature. Learning, a secondary thing, will come through God. Love of integrity must show you everything, since you already hold the marks of the first rank. So, having received the honour of greeting, you should know that, at your request, I have dictated a letter of advice to you, though in haste. I have arranged to send it to the lord patrician Symmachus, so that whatever in it deserves emendation may be corrected. But in case negligence slips in, I have also supplied you with copies of it. So keep this to yourself. When you meet that most eminent man mentioned above, take care not to reveal that it has been delivered to you, but ask for it as something new. If you learn that it has pleased his expert judgement, you will not be afraid to bring it to the notice of the wise.
XXIX. Ennodius to Beatus.

Your mistake has not made a fool of me, nor has your affection, now turned around, deceived me. You kept to the order of your age, your nature and your character. I was the one at fault, for judging you otherwise than the truth required. This is where people end up when foolish diligence holds them captive. So now I must speak without beating about the bush. What mad presumption made you so forgetful of yourself that you told the holy priest that, in those verses, some people thought the affection of married love was not expressed? Those verses were composed in a moment. Did I want to make public what I had written? Did epitaphs require this, or did reason? What ignorant person, who as senseless as you, said that a poem which lord Faustus received with the greatest favour should be damaged by the gnawing of you and your companions? Perhaps people who do not know Terentianus found something in the third phalaecian line to talk about, looking for an excuse in a single syllable. Truly I deserved what I have suffered, since it is written that pearls should not be thrown before unclean animals. I am well aware of my diction and my lack of skill, yet I had learned long ago that you know nothing and never will. Farewell, and turn to other people whom you ought to talk about.
XXX. Ennodius to Adeodatus the Priest.

I had been crushed by a bitter attack of sickness and by fevers of great violence. Christ our Lord had shown in me what He had done in Lazarus, to confirm the faith of the old testimony, and was proving the faith of the gospel by present examples. It was then that I received your letter. He who had the power arranged that, in the days when He had restored my life, He would also strengthen and support it with the words of His friends. As for the verses that monster spoke to you about, those foolish judgements made me laugh. You should know that my lord held them in the highest esteem, even though they were written in a short time while a courier was passing through. But if you have not copied them, don't. It is enough for me that in writing them I did what I wanted to do. Now I turn to what one should especially ask of holy men. Pray more earnestly for a sick man who loves you, and, if I deserve it, write to me often with instruction and consolation.
XXXI. Ennodius to Boethius.

Respect for your greatness called for an exchange of letters, but the carrier's haste has kept this letter short. I could not hold up a man in a hurry. Yet I did not send him off without this duty, because of some pressing matters. I have sent several letters about the house I asked for. If what I want can be granted, tell me now, because all the buildings are growing old through neglect. My lord, paying the service of greeting, I ask you to help a suppliant at no cost to yourself.
XXXII. Ennodius to Symmachus.

Whoever commends orphans and strangers to the father of all does something necessary. The comfort of your apostleship is the only path that brings healing to those from abroad. Far be it from me to call afflicted those who have managed to reach you. Those whom your crown has taken into its care do not look elsewhere for parents, homeland or wealth. The bearer of this letter is of noble birth and is seeking the studies of Rome, which will serve as proof of his free birth. I, your suppliant, commend him to your beatitude with my assurance. Graciously accept the service of greeting, and for my sake do twice over what you do by habit.
XXXIII. Ennodius to Hormisdas the Deacon.

What you are is adorned by mercy, and what you will be is won by piety. By these pursuits you have raised up a deacon, and your care in this promises a pontiff. The bearer of this letter is upright in character and lofty by nature. He has lost the protection of his natural support, and he has come to Rome for the honourable arts, though he will be a stranger there. Consider whether the qualities I have mentioned deserve help from a man who is devout, well born and wealthy. Now, having paid the duty of greeting, I ask this: if you love me, and if you love the good reputation you have earned, let the bearer flourish through your generous help.
XXXIV. Ennodius to Porcianus the Abbot.

Divine examples show that heavenly men do not visit us except by the grace of God. What remembrance can there be of sinners, unless heavenly favour works by hidden paths? Through a path inspired in their minds, it banishes the forgetfulness that could creep in because of sins. When the worshippers of God keep a person in mind, that is a sure sign that divine mercy has been obtained. So I give thanks to the Trinity, our God, who moved your reverence to visit me with a letter. I also accept your deference, for no small honour is owed to those who obey, since the glory of Christ awaits the one who commands. Pray for me, you who have escaped the weaknesses of human nature while still men. You have been granted release from the weight of the flesh before being parted from the body. Having received the service of greeting, grant me the fruit of grace while the cultivation of our correspondence grows.
XXXV. Ennodius to Aurelianus the Priest.

An unwelcome occasion served my wishes, and a hardly bearable necessity opened the way to what I longed for. I embraced a letter whose opening was charming, and what it went on to say dismayed me. The calamity it reported covered the sweet beginning and the honey of your serene conversation as if with the cloak of night. Truly, as you spoke, the things I read were set before my eyes. The letter of a wise man broke in on the happiness of our separation, and I was forced to see that Aetheria as all too earthly. Guided by guilt, she has been cast down from the loftiness of her name into Tartarus. I say nothing of what she owed her parents, or what she owed her modesty. I say nothing of the house the unhappy woman left to go to her crime: she abandoned the servants of God and pursued a marriage that was in effect a brothel. Believe me, she inflicted the punishment of her crime in the very act of committing it. Sunk in a disgraceful union, she found in her husband both the outrage and its penalty. By choosing an unworthy man, the woman carried within herself the roles of both defendant and judge. I would produce the letters, but I want the memory of that ill-starred woman buried in oblivion. You choose to have Gaul relieved by their expulsion; we wish Italy not to be defiled. Let them rather make for the Libyan Syrtes and be cut off from human company. If they flee lord Aurelianus there and Ennodius here, where will they turn? I have urgently passed on to the lord prefect what you asked, and he at once obtained royal orders. Through these, we believe, good men and friends have found an opportunity to help. Even so, free your mind from anxiety, since the power of heavenly judgement will be enough to punish the wicked. My lord, offering the service of greeting, I pray that you will often lift my spirits with news of your well-being, since there are travellers to carry it.
XXXVI. Ennodius to Boethius.

While you kept silent, the tongue had lost the reward of learning. As long as silence kept the beauty of your eloquence shut in, people believed that what has lately burst forth did not exist. You have brought into the light a new radiance of eloquence. While you make daylight in your letter, people think your newly won splendour is already mature. I thank you for urging me, with the flower of your letter, to guard our friendship. But if you knew how faithful I am, you would have no doubts about things that do not change. I fear that you may show the very uncertainty you suspect in me, and that while you fear a lover's lukewarmness, you yourself may grow cold in affection. My lord, paying the courtesy of greeting as above, I hope you will often send me letters in exchange. In these duties both diligence and accomplishment urge you to apply yourself often.
XXXVII. Ennodius to Boethius.

Even when a petition meets with slight success, eloquence rises, and good fortune both wins favour for eloquence and enriches it. However full of words letters may be, they go hungry if they are refused what they ask. Fortunate letters deserve more praise than learned ones. A man rightly speaks in words of lofty brilliance when the charm of his speech captivates the highest men. Ill fortune scatters any figure of oratory, for a tongue fed on kindnesses grows rich. Some time ago I sent your eminence a letter, produced with a kind of daring. You lifted it up so much by the spirit of your reply that I thought I had lost through idleness the times when I might have earned worthy favour, since a modest effort had won the judgement of one who holds the citadel. You had also promised that the house I asked for would not be refused. I was walking tall with a double success, since my reputation would grow by the approval of a perfect man and my means by the generosity of a very rich one. But I loathe the delay, which my barren sins have brought about. The man from your high office whom I was waiting for has arrived, and he said that he had been given no instructions that could serve my wishes. See what dark dealings my deserts carry on. Their efforts against me cannot break your word, but they impose delay. Far be it from my conscience to doubt your brilliance. Only a foul mind would think that you do not remember what was agreed. But I ask that, while you show the light of your intention, you overcome the obscurities surrounding what is owed to me. So pour the gift of speed into your grant. My lord, paying the honour of greeting, I add the request that I may receive the consular gift together with your answer to the petition mentioned above.
XXXVIII. Ennodius to Symmachus.

Whoever commends strangers to the father of all does not ask in vain. The nobly born are owed everyone's support, especially from those who grant kindnesses without being asked. Beatus, the bearer of this letter, is a young man of high rank. If your crown graciously receives him, it will grace a distinguished act of kindness, as befits a pontiff. He is a man who deserves your favour both by his birth and by his character. A brief commendation is enough for the worthy. Now, having paid the service of greeting, I ask you to lift the spirits of one who loves you by writing to me often.
XXXIX. Ennodius to Hormisdas the Deacon.

If the regard you promised me had lasted, your frequent letters would show it. Those whom good fortune has carried to the heights hardly look back on the humble. It is a grievous thing if the hope of prosperity cuts the bonds of charity. Fortune that smiles on one's wishes should not undermine one's attentiveness to friends. If, however, you still keep some favour toward me, if the spark of the love you promised is still alive, I commend to you Beatus, the bearer of this letter, a most noble young man. It is only right that your beatitude, out of regard for me, should be both a father and a homeland to him. Be his particular guardian, as you will soon be the guardian of all. My lord brother, having humbly paid my greeting, I ask you to let me know quickly in writing how well you are.
XL. Ennodius to Boethius.

To repeat a request accuses a good conscience of forgetfulness. But I would never goad a man who is already running, or press a steadfast man to remember his promise. I have touched briefly on what I wrote to your highness some time ago, so that I may receive the house about which you have already made your will known in writing. I have given the rest of this letter over to greeting, so that, just as my health here is stable, heavenly favour may let me learn how your highness is.
XLI. Ennodius to Agapitus.

The absence of those who love each other would be unbearable without the remedy of letters. Letters feed the hungry souls of those who long for each other with the food of conversation. Through the pen, love paints a fine likeness of the friend it loves, and with that likeness it can share the honey of speech without having to endure toil. That is why your greatness, an artist, wrote, so as not to leave our affection unfed. I owe you something in return, since I have learned that you remember me. So, having paid the honour of greeting, I ask you not to stop doing what you know is precious to dear and loving friends.
XLII. Ennodius to Avienus.

The news of your illness has added to mine. Such is always the habit, almost the nature, of an anxious man. He hardly believes that what he feared has passed. The things our Redeemer in His heavenly kindness has made past, he still sighs over, as if they were before his eyes. Lord Avienus, [?] nothing of the enjoyment of this light remains in me now except your affection, after the fear of God. Even when things go better with me, I am just as you left me in my despair. It remains for your prayers to obtain forgiveness of my sins, and, if God so wills, a swift death in place of a cure, so that what I [?] may not be more bitter than death. My lord, paying due greeting in all humility, I ask that through you I may learn what news there is from Rome about our case.
XLIII. Ennodius to Messala.

Has anyone who prayed to God with confidence ever failed to get what he asked? If the mind does not limp in faith, prayers and their abundant fulfilment go together. See, my silence has achieved with you what so long a time of talkativeness could not. As far as I can see, nothing but silence earns your letters. You write to those you think are mute, and you keep away from those believed to have a tongue. Yet you did what befitted a lord and, as you say yourself, a kinsman, in thinking me worthy of a letter when I was weighed down by a serious illness. I ask you to keep doing this. My lord, paying the respect of a greeting in return, I ask you not to stop praying for me through all the saints of God, so that, restored to life, I may rejoice in seeing you.
BOOK NINE.
I. Ennodius to Arator.

I would like you to look kindly on my effort and pardon my meagre talent. It is wrong, in matters of devotion, to scorn an endearing desire to learn, when a harsh critic empties out what a gracious man has offered. Even someone not thought to equal the eloquent in speech deserves praise for his studies. Between the kind and the learned it is uncertain which to choose. Let that pass, since each side has its value. So trust a man who cares for you, and put away bitterness from the season of lawful love. I do not want you to turn a matter of free desire into a necessity, or to turn into grief the desires through which nature brought the human race into being. A man who will not be able to keep continent is at fault unless he wishes for marriage. One who avoids the remedy of the marriage bond will choose either virtues or crimes. I beg you to take your own measure, so that you neither take up a path above human strength, full of falls, nor contemplate, beneath human dignity, things that deserve punishment. A man who does not stray from nature and the law scarcely sins. So, after the camp of the Muses and the songs that are empty in our age, change course to the task of raising children. Avoid what has become cheap, since among the armies of the unlearned it is madness to refuse to be rustic. It pleases the wise man to be what most people are. Let the stigma of philosophy be gone from our gatherings. I want to be free of cares whenever someone who leads the way follows a happy ignorance. So, accepting the honour of greeting, write back and tell me what effect my letter has had on your mind. And if you ask my own opinion, I now loathe the very names of the liberal studies.
II. Ennodius to Faustus.

Your Highness well knows what we owe to the wishes and to the family of the illustrious Faustinus. So, although he believes it is enough for you that a father has made a request for his son, his anxiety still thinks it has done too little, and he renews his entreaties through me. He hopes that through you the young man may, God willing, be raised up to mature character, and that you will give him instruction in what he should pursue and what he should avoid, and will commend him by letter to whomever you think necessary. I know that Your Highness would do this even if I kept silent, but I could not, and should not, fail to support the entreaties of so great a man. Moved by the tears of the man named above, I too weep as I beg you, by that conscience which God has granted us (so may the holy advocacy of the martyrs commend your petitions to our Saviour), that both the father pleading for his son and lord Faustinus pleading for Ambrosius may plead with you to good effect. Guide the young man I have mentioned, and pray for him, so that Rome may destroy the youth neither by vices nor by diseases. I know that you prevail in many things with men, but in greater things with God, and so I now confidently promise success to those whom I commend. Paying, then, the respect of a greeting, I have woven much into a few words. It is enough that you have been told of the devotion of a man pleasing to God. Let both the matter and the person be arranged by your care, with God's help.
III. Ennodius to Meribaudus.

Whoever commends what will please on its own merits wastes his effort on needless expense, as if he were helping the sun with torches or enriching the sea with a little water. But it is foolish to let slip the chance of doing a kindness when a strong man begs for help. A man lavish with wealth is enriched beyond his means if he trusts in the help a poor man has offered, and a gift becomes royal when the one who receives it sets a high value on it. Lord Faustinus, anxious about his son's advancement beyond what a father's care requires, believed that our Ambrosius would be strengthened by this commendation to you. He thought that the young man's blood, prudence and wealth lay hidden in the narrow confines of Liguria, and that the fame of his skill was hemmed in by obstacles, and that through another's protection his brilliance would burst forth into the light of Rome. Far be it from my pursuits to refuse a testimony that benefits its author still more, for whoever vouches for good men is himself approved. See what confidence there is in you, to whom a noble land has entrusted whatever it has of greatest excellence. I would not have him think that anything better than this family is to be found among us [?]. It is enough for those eager for honours to surpass most men in such a way that they are ranked with the very best. The well-known modesty of his birth shows the young man's integrity. May divine providence grant that his beginnings, well laid here, may be made firm through you. So receive the honour of a greeting, and answer my request with fatherly devotion, as antiquity called teachers fathers.
IV. Ennodius to Probinus.

If my humble suit had lasted in Your Eminence's memory, it would have shown itself in frequent letters, and oblivion would not have buried those in Liguria whom you once graciously called your own. But because those divided by place and by wealth are not held to the same law of attentiveness, you grant perfect love to those beneath you, if they are worthy, by addressing them. So we come together in friendship on these distinct terms: you are obliged only to regard us, and we to love you. It would be arrogance in the lowly to expect more than words from the powerful. Love commanded me to come down to complaint. You ought to have thought me worthy of a letter after the danger you had seen, or because the witness of a recent mystery commended a man coming back to life. I think that those whom the power of our Redeemer has redeemed from the tomb are worthy of the favour of honours [?]. Yet though I am lavish with boldness and talkative, and still have no confidence on my own account, I am introducing my kinsfolk. The bearer of this letter, the son of lord Faustinus, gives ample promise of good merits inherited from his father. I beg you to take him under your care, for you know well how conspicuous his father is in the light of good character, and no one armed with the authority of his life and family should hurry to anyone but you. So, my lord, paying the courtesy of a greeting, I ask that you take the trouble to make your well-being known to me by letter.
V. Ennodius to the Deacon Hormisdas.

Heavenly providence unites in love through the kindness of letters those who are joined to one another. Affection joins those whom long journeys separate and relieves their anxiety, provided they take care to write. Yet I am greatly surprised at your silence: after I had laid down the burden of my illness, you did not raise my spirits with a single word. But since by speaking we can fittingly compel you to speak, answer, even if only by imitating a chatterer. For what one desires is properly both requested and obtained by example. So, paying you the honour of a greeting, I let you know that by God's favour I am now well, and I beg that you bless me in turn with something from your pen.
VI. Ennodius to Beatus.

If you had stored in the granary of your heart the harvest of learning, to be brought out in its season, the hands of travellers would not arrive empty of your letters. But since your silence betrays your neglect and barrenness, we must once again set about the cultivation of admonition: we must sow seed on the unfruitful ridges and press them to fertility with renewed furrows. Where are the admonitions which you declared would live on with you? Where is the eagerness to converse, through which both knowledge and love are revealed? Your silence cries out that you have not attained anything that could deserve the judgment of good men. For as occasional silence betrays the learned, so constant silence betrays the unskilled. So blush, and at long last break the chains and hindrances of speech. Show what you can do, show what progress you have made, if indeed heavenly grace has not deserted you, as we pray it has not. Now receive the honour of a greeting, be content with a short letter, and know that what a long reprimand would set out has been entrusted to your father.
VII. Ennodius to Avienus.

I bless the threefold unity in majesty of our God, who in the midst of my troubles has raised my spirits by the gift of your marriage, which has served me in place of perfect health. The news reached me late indeed, but it was welcome. May our Redeemer be present and fulfil what he granted when he bent down to our prayers. My lord, paying you the respect of a greeting, I ask that, with Christ's help, you complete with your father, lord Liberius, the whole of your business concerning that suburban estate. If an exchange takes place, may he consent to accept the price, so that we may no longer waver in the uncertainty of a promise. For you know that there is nothing more you could do for your suppliant in this worldly life.
VIII. Ennodius to Victor.

While Your Sublimity protests your ignorance in advance, you have revealed the secrets of your learning. The perfection of your writing refutes what you assert. For while you modestly declare that you are unlettered, you have shown what natural vigour and the file of study have given you. Believe me, Your Sublimity: you have already enriched with your own goods the boy who is to be instructed in the liberal disciplines. If such a tongue escorts the son of brother Paul, so eloquent an endorsement both commends and teaches him. There is no need of teachers living far away when the one who sends him to a teacher speaks in a way worthy of praise. I blush that the one you have introduced has found less than he brought with him, and I pray God that I may by strength of talent live up to what your affection presumes of me. Yet do you, having received the honour of a greeting, spend the duty of writing on whomever you please, provided that frequent and careful letters answer my anxiety about your well-being.
IX. Ennodius to Camilla.

You have forestalled our plan, following someone's advice, I know not whose. For your little one, who ought to have been taken in hand for liberal studies, you have marked with the titles of religion before he reached the age of proper judgment. The form of ecclesiastical service is indeed worthy of reverence, but it does not let the mind be divided between two concerns. The road by which one goes to Christ is single and difficult, and the narrow way has never received those who are busy with many things. The Maker of salvation does not reject those who hasten to him from secular learning, but he does not allow anyone to leave his own splendour and go to it. If, then, you have withdrawn the boy from the world, do not look for the fashions of the world in him. I blush to polish one who professes the church with secular ornaments. I had agreed to what you asked through the deacon Patricius, so far as he himself reported it. Why should the boy have been sent to me in any state other than the one in which he was found in those very days? If you ask my judgment, I want those who belong to me to be holy in merit rather than in title. Truly, you have driven my mind out of its harbour of quiet into a sea of thoughts. Still, God willing, I have taken in this young servant of my own blood. Now it remains for heavenly favour to smile on my efforts and to set right the negligence of men by the abundance of its kindly moderation. My lady, as above, saying the greeting I owe you, I pray that you now take on a twofold anxiety for us both and do not fail to commend us to God with constant prayers.
X. Ennodius to Celsus.

What is shown only to those who are present is flattery, not the sacred bond of friendship. Sincere friendship does not abandon even those who are far away. Let him who obtains favours only when he stops asking understand what true faithfulness can do. I have myself to thank that you, settled beyond Gargara, have now become the object of my entreaties. By the light of your conscience you cut yourself off from friends and letters at one and the same time, seeking out places not only distant but hidden, so that no keen-nosed hunter of the good can find you anywhere. Even here you always loved lairs hidden among the hares, but often someone who tracked your footprints with his nose to the ground found your hiding place. Now, by some loftier design, I suppose to stir up grief, you have withdrawn from the company of men. So did you owe your people of Milan only your boyhood? Those who had you as a boy ought to have kept you as a man, and those whom you gladdened with your embraces you ought to have helped with your counsel. But more of this another time. You will have only yourself to thank for the joys or the tears your plans bring you. Meanwhile, having first greeted you, and mindful of my debt, I have sent the deed of gift concerning the boy. My reasoning was this: that neither should the importunate one prevail at a time when he distrusted himself, nor should the one who held back rejoice amid the evils of despair [?].
XI. Ennodius to Faustus.

I have received your letter, rich with a manifold dowry of joys, announcing God's grace toward you, which I already knew. At once, with tears prompted by gladness, I disclosed the news to the witnesses of our Christ, and giving thanks for what had been obtained through them, I proclaimed it like a ninth [?] herald. Truly, lord Faustus, it has been made plain to all in this matter what merit and what power in prayer belonged to that holy soul who has gone before us. For although our hope is still clothed in the blind light of the world, she obtained without any labour on our part what she knew to be fitting. When she took away from us the matters we had in hand, she brought forward those who were separated by a long distance, granting more happily what was needful than what was desired. So this world does have something true in it; or if it does not, what is true is not under its sway, and is soon snatched away [?]. Men lied when they swore they would receive favours if they gave them. By heavenly providence those also have been joined from whom we neither received flattery nor gave it: a sure confidence born of despair, and a cloudy settlement born of a publicized promise. Truly, if this breaking off grieved me, I would say that not even Liguria, which you call the nurse of lies, could have produced such men. What shall I charge them with first, the shame of deceit or the shame of folly? They have lost two who are joined to each other through the intercession of the saints, through whom the spark of a family long fallen and driven into the shadows could have been rekindled. You remember that lord Avienus told you in church that he did not pray to God for that girl in particular. See the offspring of holy parents advancing to the enjoyment of life. He understood that he would accomplish more by his parents' tears than by his own efforts. Thanks be to you, almighty God, thanks be to you, ruler of the faithful, who, regarding the prayers of your handmaid, have fulfilled in her the promises of the prophecy that says: "His soul shall dwell among good things, and his seed shall inherit the earth." Complete, kind judge, what remains, and look with favour on the union of your other servant [?]. If the illness that has already seized my vital strength does not leave me to see these things, may their father see good things come of them, and may he receive the name of grandfather and great-grandfather before he passes away. Yet heavenly grace has not yet deserted me, sinner though I am, for I forestall admonition by caution. Though it pains me, I have set aside my desire to receive the title of provincial envoy. I feared either that the lord of affairs might believe that what necessity compels us to request was being demanded of him at your instigation, or that I would become a burden in the office and fruitless in its business, since I would be equal neither to carrying it out nor to the tasks laid on me. I ask you to pray to God that he may keep me in the uncertainty of this world at least until the time of our shared hopes.
XII. Ennodius to Messala.

I can bear the absence of your letters, if your silence serves in this way to increase my joy. A pause in letters is no hardship if the rare conversations come with splendid writing. I accept what was to be expected concerning God's grace toward you and concerning your holy parents. Through the prayers of God's friends you have now come to know it in him who is both father and brother to you [?]. Truly, I could not reread your composition without the tears that joy gave me. I do not wish to lay out before you, with tiresome words, what I think of you. Work to set out with eloquence what you discover as the vein of your mind prompts you. You fall short in nothing of being the son of lord Faustus and of my lady your mother, except in what you yourself deliberately hold back. But may God forgive you for believing that I have forgotten you because, hindered by illness, I do not honour you with frequent letters. You ought to know that whatever wrong is done out of necessity deserves pardon. My lord, saying the fullest of greetings, I tell you that I bless God in his works for the marriage of lord Avienus, and I look to you for what his goodness promises.
XIII. Ennodius to Panfronius.

With you away, you would think I was a stranger in my native land even if I were well. But since both illness and the weakness of certain people press upon me, what am I to do between the two? Who can bear diseases and faithless men at the same time? Know that in our city neither caution nor innocence keeps what has been promised with God as witness. Everything is granted to good fortune, nothing to love; there is rarely any condescension toward the humble; the best man is the one who stands higher. But I do not sigh over these things on my own account, for nothing is left for me to hope for. It grieves me that those I love are perishing. Your man will tell you more fully about the whole affair and about the envy I have incurred because of my zeal for you. Imparting to you the honour of a greeting, I ask that you deliver my letters at once to lord Avienus and lord Liberius. And by him who may grant you our Panfronia in good health, I adjure you to let me know soon what answer they have given. For if some business prevents the king from coming, I hasten, with my God's help, to come to you, however frail my limbs may be.
XIV. Ennodius to the Deacon Helpidius.

May God attend your holiness with the marks of his mercy and grace, for you treat my humble affairs as a friend's, deign to concern yourself with them, and promise to cherish me and mine with special affection. I know that God in his kindness has granted you the favour of the invincible prince in such a way that the lowliness of the church should not perish. Truly, lord Helpidius, if the pious king deigns to concern himself with his servant, it is your doing, and none of your friends will ever be able to repay your kindness in kind. Know, however, that I am afflicted daily with various kinds of illness, so that I despair of my life. Still, having received the honour of a greeting, I ask that, mindful of your own soul, you sincerely love lord Faustus and his sons, and that you never cease to pray for my soul as much as you can, since nothing is left for me to hope for in this life. I also ask that you deign to write to me often, and that you take care to let me know if our lord is to come to Liguria.
XV. Ennodius to Stephania.

It does my spirit good that you have remembered me, weighed down as I am by the burden of sin, and that, as your letters to lord Avienus make clear, my person is not lost to oblivion amid the cares of your holy heart. I give thanks to God, who with his accustomed mercy helps sinners by a clemency they do not deserve, sustaining them through the intercession of holy souls. I do not believe that one whom you ennoble by your notice is abandoned in your prayers. So I greet you with fitting humility, and I ask that you give the constant support of your prayers to the one whom you nourish with such abundant remembrance.
XVI. Ennodius to Adeodatus.

I would long ago have answered your beatitude's letter if it had been easy to learn when people were travelling to Rome. The powerful of the world pass by the lowliness of the church as something foreign to them. But as soon as lord Dioscorus returned from Rome, having discharged his duty of pious labour, I looked up to your reverence and set about repaying my debt. You want your sons, lord Faustus and his holy children, to return to Rome; we want them to stay. Our differing views come back without straying to a single path of affection. Yet may God, the best of disposers, arrange what he knows to be suited to his happiness. The prosperity of lord Faustus and his family consoles me in place of his presence. My lord, discharging the courtesy of a greeting with full love, I am sending back the codex you gave me by your son, the lord prefect, on his return. Please send me mine, or the one you promised, if you wish. Above all, grant me this: never strip me of the defence of your prayers, for no wall could be stronger for me against the battering ram of sin than their protection.
XVII. Ennodius to Apodemia.

The ancient belief holds that closeness of kinship is not cheated by distance of place, and trust in it does not limp. The bonds of families stay firm on their hinges, and those divided in their dwellings are not separated in their souls. A heavenly vigour runs through wherever kinship of the flesh extends, and that heavenly portion is not confined within the narrow bounds of a single homeland. So you, my lady, have sought out Ennodius, who lives far from you in body, by bringing forth a noble gift for eyes that longed for it. I have received a cowl, such as a most holy woman ought to send to one professing religion. Pray that your gifts, even if they did not find me worthy of the garments of the humble, may yet make me so by the nobility of their own merit. My lady, saying the most abundant greeting, I ask that you often cheer me with your venerable letters. Please send me quickly a cloak and some wraps, in whatever colour you like, red or dark.
XVIII. Ennodius to Stephania.

The merit of the bearer would indeed be enough for an exchange of letters, since his own talent supplies what needs to be said, and so does his pure affection toward me. But my spirit hastens to a double service. Not content with the simple humility your reverence requires, it adds a letter to lord Avienus, whom both his life and his speech show to be of your stock. Yet I take it hard that you describe your words as rustic in a style far too urbane and subtle. Heavenly grace has not shown itself in your family in such a way that anyone in it may differ from his ancestors in speech or conduct, except perhaps that you surpass them. The brilliance of holy widowhood in you outshines the renown of your elders. You are, after all, the sister of that lord Faustus in whose prefecture something is found that might train monks, and who is more venerable for his conduct than for his title. Having rendered the service of a greeting, I ask that you never mix the untaught compositions of schoolmen with your holy writings. It is enough for me to find in your thoughts what I admire and what I ought to follow, if I am worthy.
XIX. Ennodius to Agnellus.

My mind hung long in uncertainty. Should I, out of eagerness for your acquaintance, knock with affectionate presumption at the door of a letter and by this path enter the heart of a most excellent man? Or should I be content with a passing greeting through your men, and so break through the hesitations that besieged me? For it seemed to me that one whom the mightiest of men did not know was not to be counted among men. And plainly neither character nor nature gives confidence to one who is hidden from those set on the heights, and especially from you. Both worlds embrace you in a friendly and allied diversity. The fear of God, confirmed by the kindness of his grace, has already made you bestow the highest honours and, what even eminent men are scarcely brought to do, give those beneath you the glory of a good name. The heights are to be praised, but they are scarcely reached even with the greatest sweat. Yet, be it said with good omen, the summits are among your gifts. So, greeting you with reverence, I close my letter briefly, lest my praise seem importunate before you have shown me your favour. After a written reply befitting your character and your power, you will read more at length, with Mundus bearing witness alongside me.
XX. Ennodius to Mascator.

It is right for me to hope for what is godly, and right for you to grant it. By different paths, an intention that deserves reward moves toward one end. You spend practical help on their affairs, while all that is asked of me is the slender aid of words. So it happens that a man whose office obliges him to provide greater things can scarcely provide small ones. Let the man of the palace restore their free status, since the church can do nothing more than pray. You know from whom the reward comes for [?], if they are helped. Come to the aid of those whom even their native land holds captive, who share [?] with the native inhabitants and a pitiable condition with refugees. A Christian and a wise man needs no longer admonition, or a long entreaty might come to claim for itself the fruit of another's labour. I therefore greet you with fitting humility, and I beg you to send the people I have mentioned back to me with joy.
XXI. ENNODIUS TO HELPIDIUS.

Even if Pontic inhumanity makes you forget me, it does not become me to imitate what I complain of. So you flew off from the city of Milan like Icarus, and did not even deign to send me a greeting. That is how people behave when an unexpected companionship joins them to the sides of the powerful. [?] is right, but if you cannot manage it by nature, let my example draw you to affection: others may be more useful to you because of their abundant means, but they cannot be sweeter. But I come back to your homeland, to which you owe your forgetfulness of kindnesses and the misery you suffer from. Now, then, having paid the honour of a greeting, I have sent your servant to report to your son the lord prefect and to you, in the name of Christ, that I have received the lawful documents for that suburban estate, so that you may not fail to do what seems necessary together with your lord Triggua.
XXII. ENNODIUS TO FAUSTUS.

I hope in our God the Trinity, through the venerable intercessions of the saints, that he will guard his servants wherever they are, as the pupil of the eye is protected, and restore to good health whatever a hostile imbalance has broken. As for me, though I cannot follow you in body, I follow you with my services: at the command of my anxiety I have let my words go, begging to be told how well you are. See, I can hardly bear a short absence, and I am to be worn down by a long one. But the lords your friends, to whom your holy soul entrusted you, are powerful, and I go to them without ceasing to remind them to keep what has been entrusted to them. They will stand by their part and will keep undiminished what they have taken on. To this I add that, by the gift of almighty God's mercy, your servants have already returned from Venetia and produced documents confirmed by law, and that the formal taking of possession was carried out here at once. Now consider, with your usual maturity, whether you ought to say anything to the friend.
XXIII. ENNODIUS TO LIBERIUS.

By the infusion of a heavenly mystery I have been granted the freedom to judge freely, even though I am bound by benefits. It is a gift from above when a man under obligation gives a frank opinion, and the vigour of his judgement is not charmed by the vastness of the favour. It is divine when someone on whom you have conferred much speaks of you without corruption, and, though overwhelmed by the wealth of your gifts, puts nothing unjust on the scales of truth. For when the subject is the greatest matters, and words are being shaped that will pass into the ears of the world, why should private dealings overshadow public testimony? I indeed owe your Highness more than the whole world does. But I do not wish to put forward anything greater than the mouths of all can utter, and, content with the law of a letter's brevity, I offer a modest foretaste of that harvest of merits. Most fortunate of men, hostility labours with the whole expense of its strength only so that you alone, throughout the whole world, may set in order what has been scattered. One may judge what sort of man he is whom you serve, when things fallen, burned and ruined recover as soon as they see you. Italy was barely being fed at the sweat of public expense when you changed it, with no lapse of time, both to the hope of restoration and to the paying of tribute. Under your governance we joyfully began to bring into the public treasuries what we used to receive with the greatest distress. Our abundance has always been your management. Heaven aided your venerable counsel. For the strength of the revenues you either nourished for the public good or gave away. A man loftier than all the heights, you were the first to make the royal resources flow without the evil of private extortion. It is owed to you, after God, that we can admit our riches without fear before our most mighty lord, victorious everywhere: the wealth of subjects is safe when the emperor is not in need. And what of this, that you enriched those countless hosts of Goths with a generous grant of estates, while the Romans hardly noticed? The victors desire nothing more, and the conquered felt no loss. Out of regard for the limits of a letter I say nothing of the honey of your fellowship and your charm, ordered by heavenly precepts and ennobled no less by deeds than by words. I turn my speech to the prayers that are owed to your Eminence, since the Gauls join me in this pledge: that, Christ the living God disposing, once those people are set in order to whom you brought civil government after many cycles of years, who before you had never chanced to taste Roman liberty, you may be brought back to your Italy, at our request and while they still hold you. So, a native of both worlds through your holy deeds, may you exalt your venerable house and your most eminent sons, together with all who possess Italy, by the gift of your happy presence. For my part, having rendered the service of greeting, I report that I am well, and I await from you news that may satisfy my wish.
XXIV. ENNODIUS TO AVIENUS.

My mind would be at ease if even a frequent opportunity of couriers offered itself for writing. For ancient providence devised the gift of letters as a remedy for longing: shaped to stand in place of presence, a letter soothes the burning heart with conversation. And although the mind of the absent grows sick from these very remedies, and care is doubled by the medicine for anxiety, still what alone remains must not be given up. So, as the boy Valentinus was setting out for Rome, I snatched as much as I could in haste of what had to be said, briefly letting you know that my bodily health has been disturbed. Yet it is enough if, at news of your prosperity, my soul becomes cheerful and I recover. My lord, having discharged the duties of greeting as your reverence requires, I ask you now to relieve me by a letter that tells me of the fulfilment of my wishes and of your welfare.
XXV. ENNODIUS TO AGNELLA.

It is a pleasure to me to send the gift of a letter to your Magnificence, for this honour is not so much bestowed on your family and your conscience as repaid to them. It is right that a man of religious profession should revere a holy widow, and a freeborn man a noble lady. I thank my God that the good fragrance of your reputation has reached us; may he who planted the good root in this worldly way of life grant its fruit until the end of life. You did well, lady Agnella, to reject the allurements of this world, and in pursuing loftier things to forgo even what could have come to you from lawful remedies: you knew how to seek not only pardon but a crown. Let the sick rejoice in their medicine; one who is granted happily to unlearn enticements is close to being next to integrity. Therefore, my lady, paying you the courtesy and honour of a greeting, I ask you not to cease praying at the thresholds of the apostles for me, your friend and kinsman, that I may deserve to keep what I preach and not neglect myself what I praise in others.
XXVI. ENNODIUS TO MESSALA.

I know indeed that you were taken away to my sorrow, but from your attentiveness I had expected something else. Had you remembered me, I would have learned both how the lord, by God's grace, has fared and what our itinerary was. But what am I to do, when even by suggesting a model of affection I cannot overcome your negligence? So if, by the gift of Christ our God, the hope of marriage has breathed upon you, you will not drive away the memory of Ennodius, provided that [?] no greater diligence has given way, and godly love is shut out from your heart only as far as I shall be removed from your eyes. Be well, and may your father and brother be kept safe; God do you good. Let them learn what may feed their hearing [?]. Show me whatever disposition you wish. One thing I ask of you, having paid the honour of a greeting: deign to offer prayers for me at the shrines of the lord apostles, that they may heal my miseries like physicians and not allow me to want anything unbecoming; let them chastise the presumptions of mind and body. If you do this, I believe that, because of your innocence and purity, you will be heard better on my behalf than if I were there in person.
XXVII. ENNODIUS TO BISHOP AURELIAN.

I owe a voice to my grief, but silence to your reverence. And perhaps a mute pretence would better express my sorrow at your refusal to write: it would be urbane and subtle to strike at the faults of my betters with the very lines by which I am wronged, so that the fault would carry its own punishment. But where shall I turn, when I do not cease to pursue with stubborn love one who has forgotten me and spurns acquaintance with the lowly? Is not the importunity of a rejected man the mother of loathing, since the desire to please by persistence provides matter for displeasing? For whatever we shun in our minds we scarcely look at when it is thrust before our eyes. If only I could still compete with your Beatitude on equal terms! But the privileges of kinship sleep before your crown, now that you have been found worthy to be a father. Does anyone hold that the rights of kinship perish for his own people through his advancement, and that the bonds of family and affection are dissolved by the accession of a holy dignity? Was it fitting, then, that I should learn of the elevation your merit earned through unstable rumour, and be content to hang on hearsay about our common joy? Was I chosen as the one from whom the general good was to be kept quiet, so that I alone, because of the obscurity of my standing, should be ignorant of something belonging to the golden age? A life noble in conduct and in birth has climbed to the summit of ecclesiastical honour, and disdains to address me. Truly such a deed, whether it came about by design or by negligence, cannot be approved. Nevertheless I pay the service of greeting, and with Italian simplicity I reveal without pretence why I have been sad.
XXVIII. ENNODIUS TO AGAPITUS.

Harshly has the courtesy of an eager soul called my mind back to the memory of sorrows, to be goaded by recollection. Forgetfulness is always the remedy for grief, since what we cannot bury by reason we bury by length of time. It is good that affliction grows old with time, and consolation for a great grief is more quickly obtained through silence; in matters of this kind more is done by doing nothing.
