But what am I to do, when the reading of your letter tears open the depths of a wound already scarred over and, by a bitter lot, brings back to life the buried memory of an untimely death? Could I then give consolation to our common brother, when, if there is believed to be any humanity in me, I grieve as I do? Or has a weeping comforter ever pleased anyone? Is medicine to be expected from the sick? No. You judge well of me, lord Agapitus, if, in your brother's grief and at the death of his spiritual son, I come forward as one who disputes your opinion. Healthy hearts find the way to a cure; no one frees another from what he himself suffers. But more on this another time. God is powerful, who alone can meet such things and lighten the weight of our common misfortune. For my part, offering you the honour of a respectful greeting, I ask you to grant me often the gift of an exchange of letters. In such pursuits it befits neither a lover nor an eloquent man to be slow.
XXIX. ENNODIUS TO LIBERIUS.

If the discipline of prose admitted the spirit of the poets, a hundred mouths and a voice of iron would hardly suffice to set out, with abundant words, what I owe your Highness. But since, indebted for great things, I am barely equal to small ones, I have found, after the mercy of God, someone to repay your kindness. For your brother lord Faustus, by declaring that he owes the benefit you bestowed on me, lifts the packs of a heavy load from weak shoulders. These things are shared between two most exalted men: you know how to give each other and to repay each other what is worthy of you. For me, placed under the burden of your gift, nothing remains but to confess my indebtedness, since the weight of your favour, coming to me before I could act, made me unequal to the very thing in which it granted my wish. Yet I stand by my part, and in my prayers, sinner though I am, I beg God to repay you on my behalf as well. See, these two things are enough: you expect from heaven on my account what you remember having bestowed, and on earth there is one of equal rank who confesses that he is in debt. Still, I await a speedy completion of your kindness, that I may receive letters such as I asked for through the illustrious Tranquillinus. Besides this, knowing your good character, I will show you another way to show mercy. My kinswoman Camilla in Gaul is said to have sunk under both the misery of widowhood and the hardships of a twofold captivity. No one but your Highness can avert so many needs. May the patron of my family not refuse in Gaul what he provided to those living in Italy, so that, by your arrangement, if the burdens of the treasury are diverted from her little properties, they may at least suffice for the said lady's support. My lord, paying the service of greeting, I ask that your Eminence, with God's inspiration, order the bearer of this letter, my man, whom I have appointed to see to these matters, to travel on my business. Should one who knows he has obtained even what he did not ask for have any doubt about his requests?
XXX. IN THE SIGN OF CHRIST.

It is the nature of things that even one who is able in speech or in mind can be blamed for presumption. For any advantage of words that oversteps the bounds of humility is trampled underfoot, and just as what is requested is held in value, so what is thrust on people grows cheap. Importunity strips the eloquent of the nobility of their reputation, and clothes the unlearned with disgrace. But I support myself with this reasoning: it is bold indeed, but lovable, to have spoken first; and though it borders on rashness, opening a road that leads to charity is close to diligence. Among men of the churches, is it a crime if those unequal in dignity compete in equal love? Or do those exceed the narrow limits of a modest rank who wish to be compared with the highest in the support of grace? No. It is he who has a proud conscience who does not measure himself only in the duties of affection [?]. I venture to say that it is the straightforward ardour of subordinates that anticipates their superiors in this matter. See, in this way I have cleared my part of the cloud that darkened it, as though my address were merely voluntary. But I add what makes the fullest defence: your son lord Rhodanius required me to break out into the use of this present pen. Yet I confess that what he ordered was already my own desire, for whoever compels the willing has no hard task. Let us give thanks to God in the first place and throughout the whole composition of this letter: since the Roman members have at last come together in fellowship with their head, it was right that the blessed apostle Peter, through the Lord, should restore to his see its churches and to a freer senate its due share. A worthy ruler, and worthy those in whose time the sum of their prayers has come to pass! For even if this happiness continues and passes on to posterity, special praise must be offered to those with whom it began. You prayed effectively to God that his power might rescue you, whose clemency is able to preserve you. You have learned of the prosperous fortunes of the one whom you see followed by victory whenever he orders war. Little remains except that you should regard the gentleness of his mind as so deep that he might seem a stranger to campaigns. With God's gift his peace cannot be disturbed by doubts [?], nor his fortitude broken by any opposition. Nothing is safer with him than a suppliant: the only one who escaped the battle lines was the one who asked; the one who devotedly offered obedience overcame the onset of arms. What the old emperors scarcely won by the sweat of their own presence, a brief letter from our king has always secured. His fortunate army is directed through its campaigns to triumph. Who would believe that his soldiers, in their toil and its completion, have the glory of the conqueror but the restraint of the conquered? When the battles are over, nothing remains of the legacy of anger: those whom his adversaries once saw as deadly, they now find gentle as they pay their tribute. And these things are prepared by heavenly support in return for this: that our faith, though he himself follows another, is safe in harbour with him. Marvellous patience, when, holding fast to his own position, he does not overshadow the brightness of another's! He even groans if the patrimonies of our churches slip back instead of increasing. So it has come about that those that are rich keep their standing as the substance of the poor, and those of modest means grow strong to the greatest wealth. In priests he cherishes the virtues that are innate and inspires those that are lacking. But why should I forestall your Beatitude with the prejudice of a long-winded speech? Your experience and that spiritual perfection of yours will at once accuse me of having been meagre in praising your son, and, since deeds are usually amplified in conversation, will charge me with being a barren reporter of the harvest of his virtues. How he now restores secular honours, the curule chairs and the trabea, and even patrician dignities, either to birth or to merit, let the bearer from your household make known by his confirmation. For he makes the old families endure in the ancient light of their lineage, and he lights up new men with the splendour of an unexpected brilliance. The state, overflowing with the good of his administration, more readily passes into private wealth than the property of those who serve him is turned into gain for the palace. Now, for what remains, accept the service of my greeting and see to it by your prayer that Christ our Redeemer may preserve for a long age the gifts he has conferred through this most clement king on those who serve him, and may grant him a successor to the kingdom from his own offspring, so that the blessings of so great a man may not grow old in a single lifetime and, made antiquated by time, be named only as a memory of a golden age.
XXXI. ENNODIUS TO AVIENUS.

While, by God's dispensation, I was still enjoying the delightful sight of you close at hand, and my hearing still held, by a venerable deception, the lovely honey of our conversations, an occasion for writing was offered me. I confess that for a long time I did not wish to break in on one medicine for longing while another was being supplied. The image, flattered by a pious trick, delighted my mind; I did not wish knowingly to expose the deception that fed me in my love. A seduction that humours our desires tastes good, and we gladly accept images of sweet messages as true. Whenever pleasant dreams are put to flight by waking, we groan, and that likeness of death is loved all the more for its peaceful deceptions. So now, since what I have described could not last, I must carry out what remains. Does any man labour so under the weight of his own sin? I would be afflicted if I did not see you; brought to what I longed for, I waste away, because what we asked for has, by God's gift, been granted. Has anything tormenting ever come to anyone from an occasion of gladness, or has a plant of sadness ever sprung up from a harvest of joy? Thanks be to the inseparable Trinity, the true God, who, to fulfil our prayers, sometimes disregards our prayers. May he, then, look upon the bond of your union; may he make one out of two, he who formed both in the body of the first man while he still rejoiced in his native and undefiled immortality. May your wife be joined to you as Sarah was united to Abraham, Rebecca to Isaac, and Rachel to Jacob, with heavenly blessing. May you have the reward of the continent and the fruit and sweetness of the married. Let the loosing of virginity obey the law of God, as what it takes from itself it restores in offspring. May your well-founded union know no affection outside it. May she restore your mother in character and way of life, and you your father. Let not the form of your ancestors, so worthy to be embraced, perish from the world, while it is born again in you. You need no foreign or borrowed examples of life: follow those set before your eyes. See, I who could not be present at your wedding share in it by this escort of my prayers; in return, give me frequent letters. My lord, paying the love and reverence of a greeting, I ask that, if you do not thrust the memory of me out of that rich store of recollection, you will relieve me with both prayers and letters.
XXXII. ENNODIUS TO ADEODATUS THE PRIEST.

How much more illustrious you are than I, in merit and in conduct, the effect of your prayers has revealed. See, you will now hold the greatest part of my comfort, taken away from me, the part that belongs to lord Faustus your son. I, indeed, did not obstruct holy and lawful desires with my prayers; but the departure of lord Avienus struck me so hard, because of my love for him, that I followed him with tears even as he went toward what was wished for. In this case the contradictory way human affairs are shaped was laid bare. Answered prayers summon him, under Christ's guidance, and they wound me; the nearness of union delights him, the separation pierces me. See, the fruit of my prayers troubles me, and, if it may be said with Christ's peace, I groan that we have obtained whatever was asked for in this matter. Yet amid all this I am sustained by this consolation for my care: that we have returned lord Avienus even greater than we had hoped. Rome boasts of his origin, Liguria of his progress. There a son was granted to lord Faustus by the law of nature; here he was revealed as such by education. It was a lesser thing for a man to be born as all are born than to be shown, as seemed beyond imitation, the true offspring of Faustus. Let us refer God's benefits back to him, and give thanks for Avienus to the one from whom we asked what we now hold. Receive the homage of my greeting with the purity of your holy heart, and when you return my book, send it together with the one you promised.
XXXIII. ENNODIUS TO BISHOP CAESARIUS.

Your letter reported what I had already anticipated in hope. From the announcement in your venerable letter I learned what the heavenly Emperor had compelled the lord king to do for you. Once your merit had become plain, the happy outcome of the affair could not be hidden from me. Who does not know that earthly powers are subject to a bishop, the noblest of men in the service of Christ, and that the threatening might of a king is overcome by the shield of innocence? When has the imperial purple ever looked down on sackcloth or the pallium? When has that supreme freedom believed it was allowed to do as it pleased in the face of Christian humility? Or when has it been allowed even to wish for what would do harm? And if, alongside these, we recall examples from hoary antiquity and bring before our eyes the tyrants' savagery against the worshippers of God, we know that the followers of our faith were slain by them so that they might never die. Then that everlasting Captain bestowed life and eternity on his soldiers through the obliging sword: by the service of their enemies they lost their native lowliness. You, my lord, were born of the divine law into a world already Christian, and nourished by it with the milk of the apostolic breast. You surpass all others as the great sun surpasses the lesser stars. Whoever has looked upon you with the eyes of the inner man has been instructed. For since even your very countenance cherishes purity, you rebuke wrongdoers without opening your mouth. Wherever you go, the good find in your way of life things to imitate, and the wicked are shown things to flee. Blessed are you, to whom God has granted that you teach both by counsel and by example, for you have always gone before and invited others onto the straight road of piety. Who, when you are speaking, would not choose to forgo reading in order to learn more? While your reading aloud wins favour for books, you also instruct the teachers; even the greatest of writers is in your debt, because you enlarge him with the gift of your delivery. In you the light of word and of deed meet together. Whence comes this privilege to the people beyond the Alps? Whence this unexpected eminence to my kinsfolk, that they should send such a man? But why look among earthly things for a heavenly cause? Could any haughtiness of the palace, then, fail to bow before you? Could he withhold from you what you desired, he who is gentler than sheep and is made combative only by wrongdoing? Both your merit and your diligence call me to speak at greater length, but the rule of the letter keeps my talkativeness within bounds. For the rest, kindly accept this tribute of my service, commend me to our God with the support of your prayers, and inform me often of what is being done or has been done in your affairs. I also beg you to let me know by letter what has come of the petition of Rusticus, who, as I hear, clothes his fornications with the name of wives and thinks that a crime can be excused by the vocabulary of the law.
34. Ennodius to Avienus.

Where are those who say that affection does not last between people who live apart, that the warmth of love cools when lands divide them, and that the mind cannot reach farther than the eyes? See, the fullness of my love boils over under the violence of separation, and the remedy of conversation, though weaker, is not confined to where the body dwells. Yet I bless God, who has had regard for our prayers on your behalf and has given you a wife not only noble but, as report announces, holy in character. The worshippers of Christ [?] gain all things perfect: to them alone, in marriage, is the splendour of wealth, of mind and of blood not denied. I hoped and anticipated that such a woman could be found as I now hear has come to you. What I think of the progress of a man who, I hear, has made his beginning from the best of things passes my power to estimate. My lord, in offering you the courtesy of a greeting, I hope that you will be so good as to carry out without delay the request of the holy bishop your father, and to grant to his man [?] that favourable disposition about which I am confident.
35. Ennodius to Messala.

Unexpected good fortune usually softens the necks of proud minds, and new joy tempers the brows of a sterner purpose. For whatever answers to our prayers sows kindness, and nothing humbles the most powerful more than the eminence they longed for. Reaching the summit should be a mark of fellowship and courtesy. Yet you, once advanced to what you desired, despise me with a pride unknown till now; and forgetting what you ought to regard in your sweetness, you scorn your old friends solely on account of your future wife's wealth, not knowing that a burden comes from the very place from which you suppose a reward is arriving. First, it is not fitting for one who does not darken the rays of his origin to be fickle; second, I shall be avenged by the very thing for which I am despised. So turn back graciously to keeping your promise, lest I should seem to have suspected what is plainly true. Because you have so far refrained from the duty of writing, I have burst out into these words: it is fitting that you, with the nobility of your speech, either wash away the deed or affirm your innocence. My lord, in paying you the duties of the fullest greeting, I hope that you who neglected me when I loved you will at least deem me worthy of conversation now that I reproach you.
